+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 56.2
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The transfer vessel's air filtration system hums with a persistent mechanical drone, a sound at once comforting and accusatory. In the confined cabin assigned to Arthur Neegan, every vibration of the hull seemed to ask the same question in a dozen metallic tones: Well, Neegan, what have you done now? He sat strapped into a molded acceleration couch that had been designed for a different age of spaceflight—sleek in intention, clumsy in execution, all polished alloy ribs and cracked green padding. Opposite him, a blank-faced man in dark Antarean gray watched without appearing to watch. On the man's collar gleamed the insignia Arthur had seen on the shoulders of the retinue that had arrived at his home an hour after sunset Mars-time: the split-star over a ringed globe, emblem of the Antares Diplomatic Corps. Diplomatic in name only. On Mars, everyone knew that much. Arthur turned his head slightly and peered through the narrow porthole. Mars had already dwindled to a rusty coin, crossed by haze and polar white. Beyond it lay the hard black brilliance of space, impersonal and ancient. In that darkness men had built empires, or what they called empires when they wished to conceal trade monopolies under banners and anthems. The guard spoke for the first time in nearly forty minutes. “You are uncomfortable, Mister Neegan.” Arthur looked back at him. “You say that as though it surprises you.” “The journey is brief.” “So was the conversation on my porch, and that was no less educational.” The man's expression did not change. “You were invited with all courtesy.” Arthur gave a short laugh. “Six armed men and a sealed transport are courtesy where you come from?” “In Antares space, yes.” “Then I am grateful I settled on Mars.” The guard's mouth twitched, though whether in amusement or irritation Arthur could not tell. “You will find the party you are to meet more congenial than I.” “That would depend on whether he tells me why I’ve been taken off my claim.” “You have not been taken. You have been conveyed.” Arthur leaned his head back and closed his eyes for a moment. “Conveyed. Of course.” He remembered the knock—firm, almost ceremonious. He remembered opening the door to find gray uniforms standing in the thin evening dust, their boots bright under the porch lamp, their weapons held low but not hidden. The leader had bowed, actually bowed, and informed him that his presence was requested in orbit by a personage of significance. Refusal had not been mentioned, which was the neatest way to make it impossible. The vessel altered course with a gentle thrust. Somewhere below the deck plates machinery clicked in relay patterns. Arthur opened his eyes again. “Who is it?” he asked. The guard folded his hands. “You will be informed shortly.” “Government?” “No.” “Corporate?” A pause. “Not precisely.” Arthur frowned. “That narrows things not at all.” “That is not my responsibility.” The hatch behind the guard hissed. A woman in the same gray uniform entered, carrying a slim case and a tablet. Her features were severe enough to seem sculpted, but her voice was unexpectedly mild. “Mister Neegan. We arrive in six minutes. You will, before disembarkation, surrender all personal recording devices.” “I don’t own any.” “Your wrist chronometer.” “It barely keeps time.” “That will not be a difficulty.” He unstrapped the chronometer and handed it over. She placed it in the case. “Am I under arrest?” Arthur asked. “No.” “Then I’d like some explanation.” “You will receive one. It may not satisfy you.” “That much I had guessed.” She regarded him a moment. “You are an engineer, Mister Neegan.” “Yes.” “You understand systems.” “When they’re honestly diagrammed.” “Then understand this one: a minor event on a frontier world may become a major event elsewhere. A single ore assay on Mars can alter shipping allocations at Vesta, naval budgets at Deneb, elections in the inner markets, and the private ambitions of men who have never seen red soil except in stereos. Your landholding is no longer a local matter.” Arthur stared at her. “Because of the Azra vein.” She did not answer directly. “You have become visible.” “That sounds very much like a threat.” “It is a fact. We do not manufacture facts.” The transfer vessel docked with a muted clang that reverberated through the cabin. The mechanical hum altered pitch; pumps compensated, seals tested, pressures equalized. Arthur rose as the door unlocked. “Come, Mister Neegan,” the woman said. The station beyond was no Martian orbital freight ring. That was Arthur’s first realization. The corridor was too spacious, too carefully lit, too hushed. Thick carpets in dark blue ran beneath metal arches polished to a mirror luster. The air smelled faintly of ozone and citrus. This was not utility; this was wealth arranged to appear inevitable. At intervals stood more gray-uniformed personnel, each with the same split-star insignia. Through one broad observation pane Arthur saw the curve of an anchored vessel outside—a spindle-bodied yacht or courier with clustered radiators folded like black wings. Its hull carried no registry visible to him. He was led into a circular chamber paneled in lacquered wood imitation, the kind that old Earth architects had once assumed would always signify refinement, even in orbit. A broad window occupied half the wall. Stars blazed beyond it with unbearable steadiness. There was only one other person in the room. He was a small man, silver-haired, seated comfortably in a low chair beside a table on which rested a coffee service of extravagant antiquity. He wore no uniform. His suit was dark, severe, and perfectly cut. His hands, folded over one knee, were the hands of a pianist or a surgeon. He rose. “Mister Neegan,” he said. “My apologies for the manner of your arrival. Please believe that on Mars, discretion and force are regrettably difficult to separate.” Arthur remained standing. “I’ll believe that when I know who you are.” The man inclined his head. “A reasonable standard. I am Lucian Vale.” The name meant nothing to Arthur, but he knew enough not to show disappointment. Men like this often preferred to be known by effect rather than biography. Vale gestured toward the chair opposite him. “Sit, please. Coffee?” Arthur sat slowly. “If it’s not drugged.” Vale smiled. “If I intended compulsion, we would not be wasting one another’s time with porcelain.” He poured. The aroma was rich and bitter, absurdly terrestrial. Arthur took the cup and held it without drinking. Vale settled back into his chair. “You discovered an Azra vein beneath your registered homestead. Not merely a vein, according to the preliminary analyses available to me, but a lode of uncommon purity and geometrical regularity.” “You have good informants.” “I purchase what the age makes available.” “I haven’t put anything up for sale.” “No,” said Vale softly. “That is what makes you troublesome.” Arthur set the cup down. “To whom?” “To everyone.” There was no melodrama in the answer, and for that reason it struck harder. Vale continued. “Mars has always been a peripheral equation—too costly to ignore, too distant to govern efficiently. It survives by imbalance. Corporations lease labor under contracts no civilized legislature would admit to drafting. Colonial offices denounce abuses while taxing their output. The Antares people, among others, maintain consulates with armored basements. It is all untidy, but stable.” “And my claim upsets the stability.” “Potentially. Azra has already disturbed the strategic arithmetic of half the settled systems. Before its discovery, deterrence was a matter of distance, fuel, and industrial patience. Now decay acceleration changes everything. Drives can be made compact beyond previous limits. Warheads can be made dreadful in ways military theoreticians describe with enthusiasm and admirals with insomnia. If one bloc gains reliable control of high-grade Azra—” “Then the arms race ends,” Arthur said. Vale shook his head. “No. It begins properly.” For a moment only the ventilation and the faint tick of cooling metal sounded in the room. Arthur said, “Why tell me this? I’m not a senator. I’m not a financier. I’m a mining engineer with a patch of bad land that suddenly turned miraculous.” “Exactly,” Vale said. “You are not yet aligned. You are local. You are authentic. Those are rare commodities, Mister Neegan. Sometimes rarer than Azra.” Arthur gave him a hard look. “Now we approach the offer.” Vale spread his hands. “Very well. I represent an association of interests concerned that your discovery not pass wholly into the custody of any corporation or polity currently equipped to misuse it.” “That sounds noble.” “It sounds prudent. Nobility is expensive and rarely budgeted.” “And what do these interests want from me?” “Cooperation. Publicly, you retain control of your claim. Privately, you grant extraction rights to a trust we establish on your behalf. The ore is removed gradually, under independent oversight, and distributed in quantities insufficient to grant strategic primacy to any one power.” Arthur blinked. “You propose to ration the most valuable material in human space through a private arrangement?” “Human civilization,” said Vale, “has often depended on private arrangements masquerading as principle.” “That’s a polished way to say conspiracy.” “Only if one dislikes the word stewardship.” Arthur leaned forward. “What do I get?” “Protection. Legal counsel. Transport. Technical resources. A percentage that will make your grandchildren offensively comfortable. Most of all, survival.” Arthur’s jaw tightened. “There it is.” “Yes,” Vale said. “There it is.” The stars beyond the window seemed colder now. “You think I’ll be killed if I refuse.” Vale regarded him steadily. “I think refusal has many forms. Some are theatrical and brief. Some involve litigation, tax reassessment, labor unrest, accidental hull breaches, or the sudden appearance of rival deeds predating your own by twenty years. In frontier economies, murder is considered inelegant because it leaves evidence of haste.” Arthur let out a slow breath. “And Antares sent the welcoming committee because your ‘association’ has arrangements there too?” Vale’s expression did not change, but something in it hardened by a fraction. “The Antares Diplomatic Corps is useful in matters requiring speed. Their title is incidental.” “Who are you really, Vale?” The silver-haired man looked toward the stars. “A servant of continuity, if I am allowed one vanity. Long ago, before Mars was more than a parliamentary headache and a geological curiosity, people imagined that expansion into the system would enlarge mankind morally. Instead it enlarged our logistics. We carry the same appetites farther, that is all. Men like me exist to prevent appetite from becoming catastrophe.” Arthur stood abruptly and crossed to the window. His reflection stared back at him superimposed on the starfield: a broad-shouldered settler in a dust-stained shirt borrowed into an orbital salon. “Suppose I say no,” he said. Vale’s reply came without delay. “Then I return you to Mars with every courtesy. Within a week, at least three delegations larger and less patient than mine will arrive. One will be corporate. One governmental. One, I think, neither. You will discover that ownership is a philosophical concept and force a practical one.” Arthur turned. “And if I say yes?” “Then you step into history knowingly instead of being dragged into it blind.” There was a long silence. At last Arthur said, “You make a generous case for blackmail.” Vale smiled faintly. “I make a realistic case for adulthood.” Arthur looked at the untouched coffee, the polished table, the immaculate suit, the silent guards beyond the door. Then he looked again at Mars, a red spark in the distance now, already reduced by perspective but not by consequence. “You came quickly,” he said. “We had to.” “Because of my vein?” Vale met his eyes. “Because your vein may not be the first.” Arthur felt something tighten in his chest. Vale continued, very quietly. “There are indications of prior Azra extraction—small quantities, decades old, impossible by any accepted record. If that is true, then someone has known more than they should for a very long time. Your discovery has frightened them. It has also exposed them.” Arthur said nothing. Vale rose. “Consider my offer, Mister Neegan. But do not take too long. In politics, as in mining, pressure seeks the fault lines first.” Outside the window, the stars remained fixed. Yet Arthur had the uncomfortable sense that everything in the Solar colonies had just lurched, silently, onto a new and dangerous orbit.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of Asimov-pastiche science fiction. The chapter opens aboard the transfer vessel as instructed, delivers a dialogue-heavy meeting with an unknown party (Vale), and sows intrigue effectively — the twist about prior Azra extraction is a good hook. The prose is clean, controlled, and appropriately retrofuturistic. Vale's dialogue is the highlight: aphoristic, chess-like, reminiscent of Asimov's cerebral conversational duels. The world-building (colonial economics, arms race logic, "murder is inelegant because it leaves evidence of haste") is delivered largely through dialogue, which suits the style. Weaknesses: Arthur is somewhat thin as a character — a competent straight man but not much more. Some of Vale's exposition is on-the-nose ("You have become visible"). The "prior extraction" reveal, while effective, is a familiar trope. A few lines flirt with cleverness for its own sake. The ending metaphor of orbits is serviceable but slightly pat. Overall, however, the piece is coherent, well-paced, and faithful to the prompt's requirements including length (~1000 words target, slightly exceeded but acceptable). + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first time I noticed Elliot, he was wearing a black lace shirt under a frayed army jacket, like a goth choirboy who’d robbed a surplus store on the way to class. Most people in Experimental Photography just looked like they were trying to look like artists. Elliot looked like he’d assembled himself in the dark from beautiful leftovers and somehow come out more honest for it. He never took up much space. That was part of what got me. I’m not exactly subtle. I’m twenty-five, I know what I like, and usually what I like is obvious to me before I’ve even finished my coffee. I’ve spent years perfecting the art of entering a room like I own the lease. In relationships, too. I make plans. I kiss first. I ask dangerous questions and don’t apologize for wanting things. But Elliot made me careful. Maybe because he was nineteen and had that soft, self-contained way of moving through the world, like every gesture had been negotiated in advance with gravity. Maybe because when he did speak, it was always worth hearing. Maybe because there was something about him that felt unfinalized, not in an immature way, but in the way a photograph in developer slowly reveals itself: already there, just not yet visible. So of course Professor Klein paired us for the final. “A study in transformation,” she’d said, handing out project prompts with a sadistic little smile. “You’ll need the darkroom.” Naturally. By the third late night in the basement lab, I’d gotten used to the smell of developer and stop bath clinging to my clothes, the red safelight making everything look half-wounded, half-sacred. In there, time did weird things. You lost track of hours. Conversations got looser around the edges. Elliot was better in the darkroom than I expected. Not more competent—I already knew he was good—but less hesitant. His hands, usually tucked into sleeves or wrapped around a notebook, became precise and sure under the red light. He moved trays like he was conducting something private. He’d lean over a print as it surfaced in the chemical bath, and his face would soften into this expression of startled devotion that made my chest feel crowded. That night, rain tapped at the basement windows near the ceiling, just audible over the ventilation hum. We were contact-printing negatives from our latest shoot—self-portraits, layered exposures, mirrors and fabric and fragments of hands. The whole project had drifted into stranger, more intimate territory than either of us had planned. “Can you hand me the tongs?” he asked. I passed them over. Our fingers brushed. He pulled back first, then looked at me like he was annoyed with himself for doing it. “You okay?” I asked. He gave a short laugh. “That depends on how broad your definition of okay is.” I leaned against the counter, folding my arms. “Broad. Very broad.” He dipped the print, watched the liquid sheet over it. “I’ve been meaning to tell you something.” There are moments when every instinct in me wants to seize control, to make the opening easier by charging through it. Usually I’m good at that. Usually people like it. But something in his voice stopped me. It wasn’t fear exactly. It was delicacy. Like he was holding up a glass object and asking me not to breathe too hard. So I said, “Okay,” and nothing else. He nodded, as if my not pushing had answered a question for him. “I think…” He stopped. Tried again. “I think I’m not as attached to being a guy as everyone assumes I am.” The safelight buzzed faintly above us. Somewhere down the hall a door slammed, muffled and far away. He kept his eyes on the tray. “Or maybe that’s not right. It’s more like—I don’t know if ‘boy’ fits in the way it’s supposed to. Sometimes it feels fine. Sometimes it feels like a costume everyone’s congratulating me on wearing correctly when I didn’t mean to put it on.” I swallowed. “Have you told anyone else?” He shook his head. “Not in a way that counted.” I wanted to step closer. I wanted to ask ten sharp, useful questions and build him a structure to stand on. I wanted, stupidly and tenderly, to fight anybody who’d ever made him feel like he had to apologize for uncertainty. What I actually did was grip the edge of the counter and say, “Thank you for telling me.” He finally looked at me. Under red light, his eyes were almost black. “I didn’t know if you’d think it was ridiculous,” he said. “Elliot.” I heard my own voice go firmer, warmer. “Nothing about you has ever struck me as ridiculous.” That made him smile, small and crooked. “I just…” He exhaled. “You seem very sure of things. Of yourself.” I barked out a laugh before I could stop it. “That is an incredible branding success on my part.” “No, really.” “I’m sure of some things,” I said. “Mostly logistical things. Where to stand. When to leave. Which ex to never text back.” He smiled again, and I felt absurdly rewarded. “Identity’s messier.” I didn’t add that he was making mine messier in real time. Because here was the thing I hadn’t admitted to myself cleanly: my attraction had always felt organized around legibility. I liked femmes who knew they were femmes, butches who wore it like architecture, men whose masculinity had edges I could push against. I liked presentation as declaration. Elliot was undoing something in me, not because he was androgynous in a simple, aesthetic way, but because whatever he was becoming seemed alive, shifting, resistant to categories I normally leaned on. It should have made me back off. Instead, it made me want to pay closer attention. He lifted a dripping print from the developer. It was one of his self-portraits: his face doubled in the frame, one exposure in shadow, one turned toward the camera, veil-thin fabric crossing his mouth. Even unfinished, it hit hard. “It’s beautiful,” I said. He looked embarrassed. “You don’t have to—” “I know.” I stepped up beside him, not touching. “It is.” Our shoulders almost met. I could feel the heat of him through two layers of black cotton. He said, very quietly, “Sometimes I think I want to look less like myself. And sometimes I think I want to look more like myself than I’m allowed to.” The honesty of it opened something in me so fast it was almost painful. “Yeah,” I said. “I know that feeling. Not the same way, probably. But… yeah.” He turned toward me then, tentative but direct. “Can I ask you something weird?” “Please.” “Do you—” He paused. “Do you still see me as a guy?” I could have answered too fast. I almost did. That’s my reflex: certainty on impact. But this felt like one of those prints you ruin by pulling it from the tray too soon. “I see you as Elliot,” I said. “And I get that that might not be enough of an answer.” He considered that. “No. It’s… actually kind of a relief.” I smiled. “Good.” “And,” I added, before I could overthink it, “if the answer changes, or gets more specific, or less specific, you get to tell me.” Something in his expression loosened. “You really do make everything sound manageable.” “That’s because I’m hot and bossy.” He laughed, louder this time, and bumped my arm with his shoulder. The contact was accidental, I think. Maybe not entirely. My whole body noticed. Then I turned to reach for the unopened box of photo paper with the ease of someone who has done this a hundred times, and my elbow caught the lid. The stack inside slid sideways, fanned open like a magician’s trick directly under the safelight spill from the door someone had failed to fully close. Elliot and I both froze. “No,” I said. He lunged for the box. I slapped the lid down. Too late. A pale bloom had already kissed the top sheets. We stared at it in collective horror. “Well,” he said after a beat, “that’s probably unusable.” I pressed my palms to my eyes and groaned. “Professor Klein is going to turn my skin into a camera strap.” That did it—he started laughing again, helplessly now, shoulders shaking. It infected me immediately. In the red gloom, with chemicals on our gloves and ruined paper between us, we laughed so hard I had to brace myself against the sink. “I’m sorry,” he said, still grinning. “It’s just—you were being so calm and wise and then instantly—disaster.” “Rude,” I said. “I contain multitudes. One of them is catastrophic.” He looked beautiful when he laughed. Not handsome, not pretty, not any single word that behaved itself. Just beautiful, in a way that made classification feel cheap. The laughter tapered off. The room felt smaller afterward, softer. “We can share what’s left of mine,” I said. “You sure?” “Yeah.” I hesitated. “Maybe we should both stop pretending this project isn’t about becoming visible to ourselves.” He met my eyes. “That’s terrifying.” “Usually means it’s good art.” “Or a bad coping mechanism.” “Those are not mutually exclusive.” He smiled, then went shy again, gaze dropping to my mouth and away so fast I might have imagined it. Except I didn’t think I did. My pulse changed shape. Here was the usual moment, the one I knew by heart: I’d close the distance, set the terms, make it easy. But this wasn’t usual, and he wasn’t a puzzle for me to solve with confidence. Wanting him wasn’t the same as understanding what he needed. For once, my restraint felt less like hesitation than respect. So I only said, “You can tell me if I overstep.” He looked back up. “I think you’re the first person who’s made me feel like stepping could be my decision.” That landed somewhere deep. I reached for a fresh sheet from my box and held it out to him. He took it, our gloved fingers touching carefully this time, intentionally. The chemistry smell, the red light, the ruined stack, the rain, all of it seemed to gather around that tiny point of contact. Uncharted territory, absolutely. For him, for me. Maybe that was why I felt so alert, so tender. I didn’t know what he would call himself in a month, or a year. I didn’t know what it meant about me that I wanted him not in spite of that uncertainty but partly because of the fierce, fragile honesty inside it. What I knew was smaller and stranger and enough for the moment. Under the red light, beside the trays, Elliot was becoming. And I wanted, more than I wanted to lead, to witness it well.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of first-person literary fiction that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with skill and restraint. Dani's voice is consistent throughout: wry, confident, self-aware, and observant, with a habit of aphoristic phrasing ("entering a room like I own the lease") that characterizes her without tipping into caricature. The central tension—her assertiveness complicated by a desire to give Elliot agency—is dramatized rather than merely stated, most effectively in moments where she consciously withholds her reflex to take charge ("So I said, 'Okay,' and nothing else"). The darkroom setting is used well thematically: the developing-print metaphor for Elliot's unfinalized identity is introduced early ("already there, just not yet visible") and pays off in the closing line ("Elliot was becoming"). The red light's "confessional atmosphere" requested by the prompt is achieved through sensory detail and pacing rather than assertion. The ruined photo paper incident is a smart structural choice—it releases tension, generates genuine chemistry, and grounds the intimacy in shared clumsiness rather than melodrama. Weaknesses exist. The prose occasionally strains for cleverness: "assembled himself in the dark from beautiful leftovers" is lovely, but phrases like "my pulse changed shape" and "the honesty of it opened something in me so fast it was almost painful" flirt with overwrought territory. The metaphor load is heavy in places—photography metaphors, glass objects, architecture, blooming paper—and a few lines ("half-wounded, half-sacred") are more decorative than earned. Some of Elliot's dialogue is almost too articulate for a nineteen-year-old first articulating gender questioning ("Sometimes I think I want to look less like myself. And sometimes I think I want to look more like myself than I'm allowed to"), though it's beautiful and defensible as written dialogue. The identity-confusion thread on Dani's side is handled with nuance but is somewhat compressed—her "attraction organized around legibility" passage is one of the best moments, though it arrives and resolves quickly. The ending is earned: it resists both a neat romantic resolution and a false crisis, landing on witness rather than possession, which suits both characters. Dialogue is generally strong, naturalistic, and character-differentiated, with the humor landing ("That is an incredible branding success on my part"). The piece is coherent, well-paced at roughly the requested length, and emotionally layered without sentimentality. Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By ten in the morning, Rome had already become a performance. Water flung itself in white lace from the Trevi Fountain. Tourists stood in clumps, arms raised, phones tilted, coins pinched between fingers as if making wishes required documentation. The air smelled of stone warming under the spring sun, espresso from the bar on the corner, and perfume—too much of it—left in the wake of passing women. Ben Harcourt stood too close to the curb with a guidebook opened in both hands and the expression of a man trying very hard not to be lost. He was reading a paragraph about Bernini, or possibly about Roman hydraulic engineering, when a horn split the square. A red motorcycle shot through the congestion like a thought no one had approved. “Attento!” Ben looked up. The scooter missed him by inches. The front wheel skidded, corrected, and stopped at an angle so dramatic it seemed rehearsed. The rider planted one boot on the cobblestones and glared at him through the visor. Ben, pulse suddenly in his throat, took an apologetic step backward. “I’m so sorry,” he blurted. “Entirely my fault. I mean—I was standing. But in the wrong way.” The rider lifted the visor. She was all dark eyes, sun-browned skin, and an expression sharpened by impatience. A black helmet had compressed her hair into rebellious waves, and there was a smear of grease on one wrist. She looked at him as if deciding whether he was stupid, dangerous, or entertaining. “Ma sei impazzito?” she snapped. “You want to die under a Vespa near Trevi? Very poetic. Very stupid.” Ben swallowed. “Yes. No. I mean—not especially.” Her gaze dropped to his guidebook. “Ah. Inglese.” “British, yes.” “Worse.” He gave a startled laugh before he could stop himself. That seemed to annoy her for half a second. Then, against her will perhaps, one corner of her mouth tilted. Ben noticed the motorcycle then: red, compact, scarred in one place along the side panel by a long turquoise scrape, edged with yellow paint, as though it had once collided with a carnival. He nodded at it, because nerves made him observant in useless directions. “That looks... colorful.” She glanced back. “Ah, this?” Her smile sharpened. “An old love story.” “I’m not sure that is reassuring.” “It isn’t.” She killed the engine, swung one leg over, and approached him with quick, feline confidence. “Let me see.” Before Ben understood what she meant, she had plucked the guidebook from his hands. “Excuse me—” She flipped through it with contemptuous speed. “Trevi, Pantheon, Spanish Steps. Mamma mia. They sell the same Rome to all of you.” “It seemed a sensible place to start.” “Sensible.” She said the word as though it were a skin condition. He should have been offended. Instead he watched sunlight catch in her eyes and felt a strange, embarrassing curiosity. She closed the book and tapped it against his chest. “You nearly die because of this. I should charge the publisher.” “I can write a complaint.” “In very polite English?” “I’m capable of stern disappointment.” That made her laugh properly, sudden and bright. “Okay, Professore. You are funny by accident.” “Ben,” he said. She considered him, then handed back the guidebook. “Alessandra.” A delivery app buzzed from her jacket pocket. She glanced at the screen, rolled her eyes, and silenced it. “You have somewhere to be,” Ben said. “Always. It’s boring.” She looked him up and down: linen shirt already creased, messenger bag, sensible shoes, the awkward gentleness of someone unused to being looked at too directly. “You are on holiday?” “Sabbatical. I teach history at King’s College.” “Of course you do.” She leaned in a little. “And today, Professor History, what is your great Roman plan?” Ben looked at the guidebook, then at the fountain, then at her. “I was going to continue not dying, if possible.” “Too ambitious.” She took his sleeve and tugged once. “Come on.” “Where?” “Rome.” “I’m already in Rome.” She was already walking toward the motorcycle. “No. You’re in a queue with architecture.” He should have refused. Everything in his life had trained him to refuse women who looked like bad ideas in leather jackets. Yet five minutes later he was on the back of her motorcycle, clutching the rail instead of her waist because he was trying to remain a person of principle. “Hold on,” Alessandra called over her shoulder. “I am.” “To me, idiota.” The bike leapt into traffic before he could negotiate. Rome became velocity. They shot through alleys too narrow to deserve vehicles, skirted delivery vans, and slipped between buses with a confidence Ben found morally compromising. Alessandra drove as though the city belonged to her by inheritance and spite. Her laughter was snatched backward by the wind. At a red light near Piazza Navona, she reached out casually and removed a pair of sunglasses from a street vendor’s unattended display. Ben stared. “Did you just—” The light changed. She accelerated. “Alessandra!” “They look better on me,” she shouted. “You can’t simply steal things!” She glanced back just long enough for him to see the wicked delight in her grin. “Can’t I?” His heart pounded for several reasons. “That is illegal.” “So is this turn.” They emerged into a side street and stopped by a coffee bar where men in suits threw back espressos like medicine. Alessandra parked crookedly, slid off the motorcycle, and put on the stolen sunglasses. “You are impossible,” Ben said, dismounting with considerably less grace. “And yet you came.” He opened his mouth, then closed it. Inside the bar she ordered for both of them in machine-gun Roman dialect. Ben caught only caffè and cornetto. When the cups arrived, she drank hers in one swallow and watched him attempt the same. He coughed so hard she slapped the counter laughing. “Piano, Professore. It’s coffee, not war.” “It feels more aggressive than British coffee.” “Everything is more aggressive than British coffee.” He smiled despite himself. “True.” Outside, she stole the sugar packet from his saucer and tucked it into her jacket without comment. Then, as if to distract him from noticing he had noticed, she said, “Show me your hands.” “My hands?” She took them anyway. His were long-fingered, ink-smudged near the side of one finger. Scholar’s hands. She turned one palm up, studying him as though reading a text. “You don’t do enough stupid things,” she said. “I’m beginning to suspect I’ve done one.” Her thumb brushed his wrist, light and unhurried. “Beginning?” The contact lasted one second too long. Or perhaps exactly long enough. They spent noon crossing Trastevere on foot because Alessandra declared the bike “too civilized for these streets.” She walked fast, talking with her whole body. She pointed out laundry strung like flags between buildings, the bakery that sold maritozzi “worth cheating on someone for,” the church where her cousin had once hidden from police after a protest, and a tiny locksmith’s shop from which she distractedly pocketed a brass keychain while arguing with Ben about whether emperors were simply celebrities with better tailoring. He saw it disappear into her palm. She saw him see. Neither of them mentioned it. Instead she led him to a rooftop terrace above a friend’s restaurant, officially closed until evening. A cook downstairs shouted when he saw her; she shouted back something involving affection, insult, and a promise. Moments later two plates of cacio e pepe appeared, smuggled up by a laughing waiter who kissed Alessandra on both cheeks and gave Ben a long, assessing look. “Your boyfriend is too pale,” the waiter said in Italian. Ben caught only one word. “What did he say?” “That you need sun.” “Ah.” Alessandra twirled pasta. “And?” “And what?” “Do you?” “Need sun?” She looked at him over the rim of her glass. “Need me to translate everything?” Heat rose, absurdly, to his face. “I should probably manage some ambiguity on my own.” “Good.” She lifted her glass in salute. “Rome is made of ambiguity.” By late afternoon, Ben had done things he would not have believed at breakfast. He had ridden helmetless down the Janiculum while Alessandra sang badly in his ear. He had entered a deserted palazzo courtyard through a gate marked private because she insisted there was “the best echo in the city.” He had shouted his own name into the cool, empty air and listened as it came back sounding bolder than he felt. He had watched her slip a silver lighter off an outdoor café table when its owner wasn’t looking, spin it over her knuckles, then place it in his breast pocket with a wink. “For your criminal development,” she said. He pulled it out at once. “No.” She laughed. “See? Scholar.” Yet he kept it for three full blocks before thrusting it into her hand again. Toward evening they climbed the Aventine in amber light. Rome spread below them in domes and terraces, ancient bones under modern skin. Traffic hummed at a distance. Somewhere nearby, orange blossoms scented the air. At the keyhole of the Priory gate, Alessandra insisted he look first. Ben bent and peered through. The famous view aligned perfectly: a tunnel of clipped hedges framing the dome of St. Peter’s, far away and impossibly centered. “It’s beautiful,” he murmured. “Yes,” Alessandra said, but she was looking at him. When he turned, she was closer than before. The city, the gate, the whole day seemed briefly to hold its breath. “I had plans today,” he said quietly. “Terrible plans.” “Yes.” He smiled. “Probably.” “And now?” “Now I’m not sure what’s happened.” “I stole your day.” He studied her face, trying to decide where the joke ended. “Did you?” Her expression flickered. Mischief, certainly. Something softer underneath, gone before he could name it. From below, her phone buzzed again with another delivery request. She ignored it. Then, with theatrical reluctance, she checked the time and groaned. “Basta. I have to work before my boss kills me.” “You were working.” “No,” she said. “This was much worse.” They walked back to the motorcycle slowly, as if neither wanted to be the first to make the ending official. At the curb, Alessandra handed him his guidebook. He had forgotten she was carrying it. Something bright marked his page. A small card had been tucked inside: a tram ticket, expired, with a phone number written across the back in black ink. Ben looked up. “Is this stolen too?” She tilted her head. “Maybe. Maybe I bought it with money from a life of crime.” “Should I be concerned?” “You should call before I change my mind.” The evening traffic thickened around them. Gold light slid over the turquoise-and-yellow scar on her bike. Ben held the ticket between two fingers, suddenly absurdly careful with it. “And if I do?” Alessandra stepped close, close enough that he could smell coffee and city dust and the faint citrus of her shampoo beneath the leather. She adjusted his collar with mock severity. “Then maybe tomorrow,” she said, “I teach you how to do one stupid thing on purpose.” “And if I don’t call?” She put on her helmet and dropped the visor. Through it, her smile was a dark, dazzling shape. “Then you go back to your guidebook, Professore. And Rome remains completely wasted on you.” She kicked the motorcycle alive. On impulse—his own, unmistakably his own—Ben touched her arm before she could pull away. She turned. He kissed her quickly, awkwardly, more brave than skilled. For one suspended second she did not move. Then she laughed, low and delighted, and caught his chin in her gloved hand. “There you are,” she said. The engine growled. She pulled into traffic and was gone in a flash of red and sunlight and that impossible painted scar, leaving Ben at the curb with his pulse stumbling, his orderly mind in ruins, and Rome at last beginning to feel real.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a polished, confident piece of commercial romance writing. The prose is economical and rhythmic, with a wry narrative voice that suits both characters ("a thought no one had approved," "bad ideas in leather jackets"). The scene structure — Trevi collision, coffee bar, Trastevere, rooftop lunch, Janiculum, Aventine keyhole, parting — gives the single day a satisfying arc of escalating intimacy and risk. Characterization is the piece's strongest asset. Alessandra's kleptomania is handled exactly as instructed: never named, shown through escalating small thefts (sunglasses, sugar packet, keychain, lighter), with the keychain moment ("He saw it disappear into her palm. She saw him see. Neither of them mentioned it.") being the story's best beat — understated, charged, and characterful. Ben's politeness, flustered apologies, and slow loosening ("he kept it for three full blocks") are believable and charming. The dialogue is sharp, funny, and differentiated; Alessandra's clipped, idiom-flavored English reads authentically Italian without becoming caricature. Weaknesses: the arc is somewhat formulaic — manic-pixie-courier meets repressed academic is a well-worn trope, and the beats (stolen day, "teach you to do one stupid thing," the kiss) are predictable genre furniture. Alessandra's inner life stays deliberately opaque, which is per the prompt, but it means her softness at the end ("There you are") is a touch unearned — we haven't seen enough cracks in her armor for the tenderness to feel fully motivated. The kiss is initiated by Ben, which is a nice reversal, but his transformation from timid to bold happens quickly, though the story does seed it (the lighter, the echo, riding helmetless). Some lines flirt with cuteness ("Rome is made of ambiguity"), and the ending is a bit more romantic-neat than the ambiguous tension fully supports, though the prompt did permit a payoff. Imagery is vivid without purple excess; the turquoise-and-yellow scar on the bike is a nice recurring motif. Pacing is tight for ~1000 words of instruction (the piece runs longer, but the prompt asked for a full day of scenes, so expansion is defensible). No meandering, no tonal drift, no amateurish tics. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By station-night, The Last Outpost always sounds like a ship deciding not to fall apart. The vents wheeze warm air that smells faintly of ion scrubbers and old cinnamon. The long front window shows the slow carousel of the belt outside—asteroids gliding past like dark, thoughtful animals, their mining lights blinking in patient code. Above the bottles, our sign buzzes in tired pink: THE LAST OUTPOST, though the S dies every third hour, so for stretches of the evening we become THE LA T OUTPO T, which somehow suits us better. I polish a glass that is already clean and keep one eye on table six, where Jori and Pel are conducting the latest stage of their six-month breakup. “I’m just saying,” Jori says, all offended dignity and excellent cheekbones, “you cannot call salvage rights on gifts given during courtship.” Pel’s lower set of hands spread in exasperation. “The moonstone fern is not a gift, it is a shared asset.” “It lived in my quarters.” “It died in my quarters.” “Because you overwatered it out of spite.” I set the glass down. “Children, if I draft a custody schedule for the dead plant, will you both promise to stop using the phrase shared asset in my bar?” Pel turns. “Nets, be reasonable.” “I am always reasonable,” I say. From two stools down, Miro the fuel broker snorts into his ale. “That is not your reputation.” “My reputation,” I tell him, “is slander manufactured by people I’ve refused to overpour.” Jori points at me like I’m a court clerk. “Tell Pel the fern was mine.” Pel points with two fingers and one thumb. “Tell Jori attachment does not supersede ownership.” “Tell both of you,” I say, “that if your voices go up another notch, Talla in the kitchen will come out here with the ladle, and none of us want to explain that to station security again.” From the kitchen hatch, without appearing, Talla calls, “I heard that.” The room ripples with laughter. Jori subsides first; Pel follows a moment later, muttering something about precedent. I slide them each a dish of salt-roasted kelp twists on the house, the universal solvent for romantic litigation. “You’re bribing us to be civil,” Jori says. “Yes,” I say. “And it’s working.” The evening settles back into its usual drift. Sefa and Rin play a low-stakes card game near the recycler, cheating in ways so polite they might as well call it choreography. Old Beren nurses one drink for three hours and watches cargo manifests on his wristpad as if any one of them might suddenly confess. A pair of ore haulers fresh off shift glow red-faced with fatigue and tell the same story about a cracked drill line to anyone who’ll listen. This is the part of the night I like best: the hum after the first rush, when everyone has decided where they belong. I belong behind the bar, where I can keep my hands busy and my history shelved in unmarked bottles. The hatch sighs open. Cold dock-air rolls in first, carrying metal dust and the bitter tang of ship coolant. Then the stranger steps through. They’re tall, though that’s hard to judge with the slight fold in their posture, and wrapped in a travel coat gone shiny at the seams. Their skin has the pale oil-slick sheen of someone from the water moons, and their hair—if hair is the word—is a mass of tentacled dreads, several of them half-unbound and askew as if they’ve been running hands through them for hours. One small case is handcuffed to their wrist. Not expensive luggage. Important luggage. They pause just inside the threshold and scan the room. Not like a tourist. Like someone counting exits. I have learned to notice that difference. They cross to the bar and sit in the third stool from the end, the one under the dead section of the sign where the light never quite hits. Up close, I can see the fine tremor in their left hand. “Vega whisky, neat,” they say quietly. Their voice is low and sanded rough with strain. “Better make that a double.” “Long haul?” I ask. Their mouth moves in something that is not interested in becoming a smile. “Something like that.” I reach for the Vega. “Tab open or settle now?” “Now.” A cred-chip lands on the bar between us. Untraceable black ceramic. Too much money for a double. I glance at it. “You know I make change.” “Keep it.” That gets Miro’s attention; I feel it from down the bar like static. Nobody on the rim tips that hard unless they’re showing off, desperate, or don’t expect to be here long. I pour the whisky. Amber catches in the low light. Their hand closes around the glass before I’ve fully set it down. They drink half in one go, shut their eyes, breathe once through their nose. “Better?” I ask. “No.” “Honest answer. Rare around here.” “Is it?” “Not really,” I say. “We just package our lies prettier.” That almost earns me the smile. Almost. “What should I call you?” I ask. They hesitate too long. “Nobody tonight.” “Tempting,” I say, “but for inventory purposes I prefer my patrons slightly more specific.” Their fingers tighten on the glass. “Aster.” It might be true. It might be the name of their first ship, their favorite weather pattern, or a lie grabbed at random from the nearest passing rock. I nod like I believe it. “Well, Aster. I’m Nets.” “I know.” I stop wiping the bar. Across the room, someone laughs too loud. A chair scrapes. The vents hiss on. I keep my tone light. “Do you.” “The bartender at The Last Outpost,” they say. “Nettle. Good at listening. Better at remembering. Keeps a scattergun under the sink and a stunner taped under the till because she trusts technology less than mechanics.” My hand stills on the rag. Miro looks over. Jori and Pel are mid-argument again, but quieter now. Talla slides a tray through the hatch with deliberate calm. Nobody else has noticed anything yet. “Sounds like I’ve got a fan,” I say. Aster opens their eyes and meets mine. Their pupils are blown wide. “It means someone told me to come here,” they say. “Specifically here. Specifically to you.” Before I can answer, there’s a sharp crash somewhere behind me near the service station—glass shattering across the floor. “Void take it,” Sefa says. “Sorry! Sorry, that one slipped.” The whole room flinches in chorus, then exhales. Talla swears from the kitchen. Rin starts laughing. “Leave it,” I call over my shoulder. “I’ll get the broom in a minute.” I don’t take my eyes off Aster. “Who sent you?” I ask. Aster sets down the whisky very carefully. “If I say the name, I need to know whether you’re going to run.” Now Miro is openly listening. I give him a look sharp enough to fillet ore and he pretends to become fascinated by his ale. “That depends on the name,” I say. Aster leans in. The cuff on the small case knocks softly against the bar. “Oran Vale.” Everything under my ribs goes cold. The room doesn’t change, but it feels like it does. The belt still turns beyond the window. The sign still buzzes. Jori says, “That was not overwatering, that was grief,” and Pel groans. Someone orders another round from the far end. The broken glass near the service station glitters under the lights. Oran Vale. There are names that belong to your old life so completely that hearing them is like finding a door where you bricked one over. I pick up a clean glass because my hands need a reason to move. “That’s not a name I hear often,” I say. “No,” Aster says. “I gathered.” “From who?” “From the man himself.” I laugh, because if I don’t I might do something messier. “Then either you’re lying, or the galaxy’s gotten considerably crueler since breakfast.” Aster reaches into their coat. My shoulders tighten. So do Miro’s. Talla appears in the kitchen hatch, ladle in hand, taking in the room in one sweep. Aster stops, notices all of it, and slowly withdraws not a weapon but a folded datafilm, creased and old enough to have physical edges. “I’m not armed,” they say. “Everybody says that right before making my night difficult.” They place the datafilm on the bar but keep two fingers on it. “He said if I found you,” Aster says, “I should give you this and tell you he’s sorry.” The station seems to tilt half a degree. I stare at the film and do not touch it. From the end of the bar, Beren says mildly, without looking up from his wristpad, “Dock authority just flagged an incoming security cutter. Fast approach. No posted cargo.” Nobody speaks for one beat, then two. Aster’s face drains what little color it has left. “They found me,” they whisper. I look from the film to the handcuffed case, to the door, to the frightened stranger who knows my name and carries one from the grave. Then I set the clean glass down. “Everyone,” I say, louder than I mean to, “finish your drinks or hide them. We may be about to have company.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted cozy sci-fi chapter that fulfills nearly every instruction with skill. The first-person present-tense voice is consistent and distinctive — wry, observant, economical. The opening establishes the bar's rhythm through warm, characterful dialogue (the Jori/Pel dead-fern custody dispute is a charming bit of low-stakes comedy that earns its space), and the ~60% dialogue target is met naturally. The stranger's entrance is handled with genuine craft: the shift from cozy to tense is gradual and well-paced. Details do real work — the untraceable cred-chip, the case handcuffed to the wrist, the "counting exits" observation, the dead letters in the sign. The reveal of Nets's old life via the name "Oran Vale" is an effective hook, and the chapter correctly ends on unresolved conflict (the incoming security cutter) rather than closure. Strengths: dialogue is sharp and differentiated (each character has a distinct verbal fingerprint); the prose is clean with occasional striking images ("asteroids gliding past like dark, thoughtful animals," "finding a door where you bricked one over"); the bartender's interiority is economical but present. The supporting cast (Miro, Talla, Beren) is sketched efficiently and used well for tension — Beren's mild announcement of the cutter is a great beat. Minor weaknesses: some of the cozy banter runs slightly long relative to the word budget; the "I know" / "The bartender at The Last Outpost" exchange flirts with genre cliché (the mysterious stranger who knows too much is a familiar trope, though executed competently); a couple of aphorisms ("we just package our lies prettier") edge toward writerly self-regard. The tremor/wide pupils/blown pupils are standard-issue fear signals — shown, but somewhat stock. The ending line is a touch melodramatic ("louder than I mean to") but functional. Nothing here is purple, overwrought, or amateurish. The emotional register is controlled, the lightness early on is earned and makes the darkness land harder. This is professional-grade commercial fiction. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 62.5
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The saxophone got to me before the city did. Not the buildings, not the heat, not the trash-sweet stink rising off the sidewalk like the whole place had been left out in the sun too long. The saxophone. Some guy on a corner in the French Quarter, eyes half-closed like he was praying through brass, pulling this low, aching sound out of the air that made everything feel cinematic and unreal. Like I hadn't slept in a gas station bathroom in Mississippi six hours ago. Like I wasn't sixteen, broke, gross, and very possibly making the worst decision of my life. I stopped in the middle of the sidewalk because of course I did, and someone immediately shoulder-checked me and said, "Keep moving, sweetheart." Sweetheart. Sure. Great. No one can tell what I am if I keep my mouth shut, I thought. Maybe that's a superpower. Maybe it's just dissociation with better branding. I kept moving. New Orleans was loud in a way my town back in Tennessee never managed. Home had truck engines, church bells, lawnmowers, football games, people talking about other people in the Piggly Wiggly parking lot. This was noise stacked on noise: heels on concrete, a bus sighing at the curb, tourists yelling, a man laughing too hard, the saxophone threading through all of it like it knew a secret. Everything smelled like beer, fryer grease, piss, sugar, river water, and something floral trying its best. I had seventy-three dollars in my bra, a dead phone in my backpack, one extra T-shirt, and exactly zero plans beyond get gone. Which, okay. Mission accomplished. Now what? I passed shop windows with masks and beads and T-shirts that said things like I GOT BOURBON FACED ON SHIT STREET, and a group of college girls in matching tank tops, and a man painted entirely silver. Every single person looked like they belonged to some version of the city except me. I looked like what I was: some kid who ran. I kept waiting for the panic to catch up to me fully. It had been taking little bites all morning. In the truck with the guy who picked me up outside Jackson, I was mostly numb. When he dropped me off with a "Good luck, buddy," like this was summer camp and not me blowing up my whole life, the numbness cracked. Now every feeling in my body was fighting for first place. Relief, obviously. Relief so sharp it was almost joy. I had done it. I had actually left. I didn't have to hear my mom say, in that flat voice she'd used two nights ago, "I don't understand why you're doing this to us," like my existence was a prank with bad timing. I didn't have to watch my stepdad's face go red while he called me confused and selfish and sick. I didn't have to sit in that house while everybody kept using my old name like they were trying to nail me to it. But also: guilt. Fear. Hunger. A weird fizzing thrill that made me feel like maybe I was the kind of person who could survive anything, right up until I remembered I had no place to sleep tonight and no clue where kids like me were supposed to go. I stopped under a balcony dripping ferns and dug around in my backpack for my charger before remembering, again, that a charger was useless without an outlet, and an outlet was useless without somewhere to stay long enough to use it. "You're gonna get pickpocketed standing there like that." The voice came from my left. I looked up fast. The speaker was leaning against the wall in the shade of a souvenir shop, maybe my age, maybe a little older. Seventeen, tops. They had close-cropped dark hair under a Saints cap, a loose gray T-shirt, black jeans with one knee blown out, and the kind of watchful face that made me think stray cat, not in a cute way. Their eyes flicked over me, my backpack, my shoes, taking inventory. "I have like twelve dollars worth of stuff that can be pickpocketed," I said. They snorted. "Then they'd take the bag." "Cool. Thanks. Extremely comforting." "You're welcome." I should've walked away. This is the part in every cautionary tale where the idiot trusts the wrong person because they seem interesting and not immediately threatening. But they weren't smiling in a manipulative way, weren't stepping into my space, weren't doing that fake-friendly adult thing. They just looked tired. "You local?" they asked. "No." "Yeah, I got that." I crossed my arms. "Then why ask?" They tilted their head. "To see if you'd lie." The saxophone wailed behind us, long and lonely. I stared at this person and had the deeply inconvenient thought that they were the first person all day who seemed even remotely real. "Okay," I said. "I'm not local." "No kidding." "I just got here." "Also obvious." "Do you always talk like a jerk, or is today special?" One corner of their mouth twitched. "Depends. You always announce to strangers that you're fresh off the bus?" "I didn't get here on a bus." That made them actually smile, small and fast. "Congratulations?" I nearly smiled back, which felt like a moral failing. They pushed off the wall. "You got somewhere to be?" It was a simple question, and I hated how much it punched through me. "No," I said. Their eyes changed a little. Softer, maybe. Or more careful. "Name?" There was half a second where everything in me braced. My old name sat there like a landmine. "Taylor." "Taylor," they repeated, like they were trying it on for size. "I'm Jude." Could be real. Could be fake. Mine was real, but only sort of. I had chosen it six months ago and only ever heard it out loud in my own room, whispered to the mirror with the fan running so nobody'd catch me. Hearing a stranger say it on a street in New Orleans made something in my chest go painfully bright. "Okay," Jude said. "Here's the deal, Taylor. You look lost enough that somebody's gonna notice, and not everybody who notices is nice. Don't follow anyone anywhere private. Don't tell anyone how much money you have. If somebody offers you a job today, it's a scam, prostitution, or both. And if a guy named Rene with a neck tattoo says he knows a cheap hostel, he does not." I blinked. "That is... weirdly specific." "Because it's true." "You say that like experience." Jude's face shut down so fast I almost wondered if I'd imagined the expression before. "I say it because I live here." That, also, could be true or not true. Everybody was a possible liar now. Maybe that's what running away does: turns every interaction into a test you don't know how to grade. "Why are you helping me?" I asked. Jude shrugged, but not casually. "Maybe nobody helped me the first day." We stood there with the saxophone pouring sadness into the heat. I should've said no thanks. I should've gone to a police station, except absolutely not. I should've found a shelter, except I didn't know where, and the thought of explaining myself to one more adult made my skin crawl. I should've done lots of things. Instead I said, "So what, you give all baby runaways a safety lecture?" Jude looked at me for a beat. "Only the ones who look like they might bolt if I offer them food too fast." My stomach betrayed me with a loud, humiliating growl. That got a real grin out of them. "There it is." "I hate you already." "That's healthy. Come on." They started walking, not looking back to see if I followed. Which was maybe the smartest thing they could've done, because if they'd tried to coax me, I would've run on principle. I followed. We cut away from the thickest tourist crowd into narrower streets where laundry hung from balconies and murals bloomed across brick walls and the city felt less like a performance. Jude walked like someone who knew exactly which cracks in the sidewalk to avoid. I kept three steps behind, rehearsing contingencies. If they turned into an alley, I was gone. If they reached for my bag, I was gone. If a van appeared, I was gone. Congratulations to me on developing survival instincts approximately twelve hours after hitchhiking across state lines. "There's a church on Dauphine does lunch some days," Jude said over their shoulder. "No sermon requirement, which is nice." "Wow. Luxury." "You joke, but one place made me listen to a man compare sin to mold for forty minutes before giving me half a sandwich." "Very Jesus." Jude barked a laugh. And just like that, against every sensible impulse, I felt some tiny dangerous thing uncurl in me. Not trust. Definitely not. But the idea of it. The possibility. I looked at the back of Jude's neck, at the faint scar disappearing under their collar, at the way they kept checking reflections in windows instead of turning their head outright. Issues and secrets, I thought, recognizing the type because, hello, same. The saxophone was gone now, swallowed by distance, but I could still hear it in my head as we turned the corner into whatever came next. I had no map for this city, for this life, for who I was going to be by nightfall. I just knew the day was happening whether I was ready or not. And for the first time since leaving home, I wasn't facing it completely alone.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted YA opening chapter. The first-person voice is sharply defined: sardonic, defensive, self-aware, with a distinctive rhythm of short punchy lines and wry asides ("dissociation with better branding"). The prose does a lot of work with sensory detail — the saxophone as an opening hook, the layered smells of the city, the "trash-sweet stink" — grounding New Orleans as a character in itself without tipping into travel-brochure excess. Taylor's internal monologue is the strongest element. The conflicting emotions (relief/guilt/fear/thrill) are named but also dramatized through behavior: the contingency rehearsals, the refusal to be coaxed, the stomach growl. The trans identity is handled with specificity rather than tokenism — the "old name like a landmine" moment and the mirror-whispered chosen name are genuinely affecting, and hearing "Taylor" spoken aloud by a stranger lands as a small, earned emotional beat. Jude is a good foil: guarded, deflective, with hints of backstory (the scar, the shut-down face, the Rene warning) that seed future chapters without dumping exposition. The dialogue crackles — clipped, adversarial-flirtatious, believable teen register. "To see if you'd lie" is a nice characterizing line. Weaknesses: the plot is thin — essentially a meet-cute plus a walk; the chapter is more atmosphere and character than event, and the word count falls short of the 1000-word seed. Some metaphors are slightly overworked ("panic taking little bites," "fizzing thrill"). The ending's "not completely alone" is a touch neat, though it's earned by the preceding wariness rather than sudden trust. Jude's helpfulness flirts with the convenient-stranger trope, though the text itself flags this ("this is the part in every cautionary tale"), which partially inoculates it. Minor clichés: stray cat comparison, "landmine." Overall: voice-driven, emotionally layered, coherent, and engaging with only minor craft blemishes.
