+ Dystopic-comedy: My Apocalypse Buddy — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. The story begins with the pair deliberating their predicament and intent for the day's mission, details the ways in which the mission inevitably goes sideways, and returns them to home base in multiple ways, worse for wear. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the time the sun had dragged itself over the broken ribs of the city, Midas was already having a disagreement with the future. This was not unusual. Midas disagreed with the future on most mornings, largely because the future kept arriving wearing different boots but somehow stepping on the same sore places. Today it arrived cold, misty, and smelling faintly of wet rust. He sat on the roof of Home Base—which was a grand title for three connected bus shells, a greenhouse made of old windows, and a rain barrel with ambitions—turning a bent spoon in his fingers and staring out at the old motorway overgrown with nettles, thorn, and the occasional philosophical goat. Beside him sat Chewy. Chewy was an animo-tronic stuffed koala from some long-forgotten Before Time, back when people had apparently considered it sensible to make children’s toys capable of blinking, making comments, and, in Chewy’s case, surviving the collapse of industrial civilisation with all the grim persistence of mildew. His fur was patchy, one ear had been reattached with copper wire, and when he spoke there was a faint grinding sound, as if every sentence had to be negotiated with internal components no one alive understood. “Well,” said Chewy, in the tone of one delivering a verdict on a disappointing casserole, “we remain alive.” Midas sighed. “For now.” “Yes. One mustn’t be greedy.” He unfolded the scrap of cloth he’d found nailed to the wall of the old underpass two days before. On it, in tar-black paint, someone had scrawled: WHEN THE RED GIANT LOOKS WEST, FOLLOW THE THREE WHITE STONES. BENEATH THE THORN THAT DRINKS NO RAIN, THE QUIET LANTERN WAITS. Chewy regarded this in silence. Then he said, “A hidden refuge.” “Or directions to a murder.” “Those are not mutually exclusive.” Midas rubbed his face. He had the gaunt, weathered look of a man who had lost several arguments with weather and one memorable one with bees. “If it’s a refuge, there might be stores. Tools. Maybe dry bedding that hasn’t previously belonged to rats.” “And if it is a murder, we may finally discover what all the excitement is about.” Midas ignored that. “We need salt, lamp oil, and something that isn’t turnip.” Chewy’s head clicked as he turned to look at him. “Ah. Desperation, the mother of navigation.” The plan, such as it was, involved following the old canal out past the skeletal warehouses, finding something that might conceivably be a red giant looking west, identifying three white stones in a world that was mostly made of stones trying to be grey, and then hoping the thorn in question was botanically inclined toward secrecy. The day’s mission therefore consisted of vague directions, inadequate footwear, and confidence neither of them had actually packed. They set out after breakfast, which had been boiled nettle mash and the last of the acorn cakes. Home Base waved them off in the silent way homes do when they suspect they’ll be seeing their owners again sooner and in a poorer condition than expected. The city beyond was what happened when mankind left in a hurry and nature came back with opinions. Buildings leaned into one another like old gossips. Vines throttled lampposts. The canal ran green and thick as soup no one should ever trust. Here and there, relics of the Before Time still jutted from the foliage: a traffic signal blinking one weak amber eye at eternity, a half-buried sign advertising luxury apartments to a species that had mostly reverted to practical caves. Midas climbed over a fallen delivery van and landed in a puddle up to his ankle. “This,” he said through clenched teeth, “is a bad omen.” Chewy, strapped to his pack and peering over his shoulder, said, “No, a bad omen would be crows spelling your name. This is merely damp.” The first thing to go sideways was the goat. There is, in every ruined landscape, at least one goat that has mistaken feral self-confidence for a philosophy. This one emerged from a collapsed garden centre wearing a curtain of ivy around its horns and looked at Midas with the steady contempt of an animal who believes all human suffering is either deserved or hilarious. “I don’t like its expression,” said Midas. “It has your expression.” The goat charged. Midas had enough time to leap onto the bonnet of a rusted car before the animal slammed into it hard enough to set off a small avalanche of flakes and one deeply embarrassed car horn, which emitted a feeble bwoop after twenty years of silence. The goat took this as encouragement. By the time Midas escaped—via a greenhouse roof, a bramble hedge, and what he later maintained had been a deliberate swing from a hanging sign—his trousers were torn, his dignity perforated, and Chewy had somehow acquired a cabbage leaf on one ear. “That,” said Chewy, “was a strategic withdrawal.” “That,” said Midas, panting, “was attempted murder by livestock.” “Again, not mutually exclusive.” They found the red giant around noon. It was an old communications tower on a hill beyond the canal, painted in peeling red bands and leaning westward as if exhausted by history. At its foot lay, wonderfully enough, three white stones arranged in a rough line, almost as if the universe had once accidentally employed a signpost. “See?” said Midas. “It’s real.” Chewy’s eyes whirred shut and open. “I am never happier than when cryptic instructions prove only moderately stupid.” They followed the line of stones into the wilds beyond the old city edge, where the world became less ruin and more argument between forest and memory. Here the trees crowded close and the air smelled of damp bark and mushrooms and old secrets. Birds erupted from branches with the indignation of tiny aristocrats. The thorn that drinks no rain turned out to be a dead hawthorn growing from the roof of a buried structure, its roots clutching cracked concrete. Midas knelt and brushed away leaves, revealing a metal hatch hidden under moss. For one shining, impossible moment, things had gone right. Then he pulled the hatch open. There was a click. Chewy said, with impressive calm, “Ah.” The old security alarm, asleep for decades in some deep electronic coma, woke in a fit of existential outrage. A siren began to howl beneath the earth—wavering, distorted, but very much alive. The forest froze. Then everything in it decided to become involved. Birds exploded upward. Something large crashed through underbrush to their left. Farther off came the unmistakable barking shriek of scavenger dogs, the sort that travelled in packs and considered hesitation a seasoning. Midas stared into the dark opening below. “Can we still do the refuge?” “We can certainly die near it.” They dropped through the hatch and pulled it shut over them just as paws scrabbled above. Below was a concrete chamber lined with shelves, many collapsed, some still bearing dusty tins, mouldered blankets, and jars of what might once have been medicinal herbs or might now be a form of revenge. In the far corner hung an old oil lantern, painted blue. “The Quiet Lantern,” whispered Midas. “Not especially quiet upstairs,” said Chewy. There were supplies—some salvageable, some less so—and a second tunnel leading away into darkness. Naturally, because the universe enjoys rhythm, this was when the floor gave way. It wasn’t the whole floor. That would at least have been decisive. It was merely the section Midas was standing on, which crumbled with tired malice and deposited him, a crate of antique turnips, and Chewy into an underground drainage channel full of black water. The current seized them at once. For a few seconds there was only cold, darkness, and the sort of panic that leaves no room for thought except a sincere regret at one’s previous life choices. Midas flailed, hit a wall, swallowed half the old world, and grabbed wildly at Chewy just as the toy’s internal voice box began repeating, in clipped mechanical tones, “UNSCHEDULED AQUATIC EVENT. UNSCHEDULED AQUATIC EVENT.” “Not helping!” spluttered Midas. The drain spat them out at sunset into the canal half a mile from Home Base. This was the first way they returned. The second way was on foot, because after dragging themselves ashore coated in black slime and aquatic vegetation, they still had to stagger back carrying a sack of tins, a bundle of damp blankets, and the blue lantern, which Midas had somehow retained through the flood by the simple principle that if one is going to suffer, one may as well suffer profitably. The third way was by being chased the final stretch by the same goat, or one of its theological relatives, which objected to Midas crossing its patch of wasteland and accelerated their homecoming considerably. They tumbled through Home Base’s gate after dark, soaked, scratched, bruised, and smelling like an argument between a swamp and a cellar. Midas collapsed onto an upturned crate. Chewy, set carefully on the table to drip, regarded the blue lantern. “Well,” said the koala, after a while, “we found the hidden refuge.” Midas gave a weak laugh. “And it nearly killed us.” “Yes. But then, so does everything. The important distinction is whether it does so usefully.” Midas looked at the tins they’d salvaged, the lantern, the blankets. Enough, perhaps, for another week. Maybe two, if the turnips inside the tins had the decency to be something else. Outside, the wind moved through the bus shells with a low, ghostly hum. Inside, Home Base held around them like a patched coat. “Same time tomorrow?” said Midas. Chewy’s eyes glowed faintly in the dark. “Certainly. Survival, after all, is just a habit with worse scenery.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, disciplined piece of comic post-apocalyptic fiction that understands its assignment remarkably well. The Pratchett influence is present in the right places—footnote-adjacent wry asides, personified abstractions ("the future kept arriving wearing different boots"), and the deadpan exchange rhythm between Midas and Chewy—without tipping into slavish imitation. Strengths: The dialogue is the engine of the piece, and it's genuinely funny. "Those are not mutually exclusive" as a running gag is well-deployed, and Chewy's clipped mechanical pronouncements ("UNSCHEDULED AQUATIC EVENT") land as both character work and comedy. The structure follows the brief precisely: deliberation at Home Base, a mission that goes sideways in escalating stages (goat, alarm, floor collapse, flood), and a return home "in multiple ways"—which the story cheekily literalizes as three modes of return rather than three separate endings. That's a clever, self-aware reading of the prompt. The prose is economical and image-rich without purple excess; lines like "the canal ran green and thick as soup no one should ever trust" and "a traffic signal blinking one weak amber eye at eternity" are Pratchett-adjacent without being stolen. The ending earns its small warmth: they return worse for wear, with modest salvage, and the closing exchange ("Survival, after all, is just a habit with worse scenery") is tonally perfect. Weaknesses: The plot is thin and the riddle-map is resolved a bit too neatly and quickly—the "red giant" and "three white stones" are found without real friction, which slightly deflates the middle act. The goat is funny but borders on stock comic device. Chewy's animatronic nature is more flavor than function; his internal mechanics never create a real complication, which is a missed opportunity given the character brief. Some metaphors ("philosophical goat," "theological relatives") gesture at cleverness without quite earning it. The alarm-dogs sequence resolves off-screen rather than on the page, which is a small cop-out. Emotionally, the piece stays in one wry register throughout—entertaining, but not layered; there's little beneath the jokes. Overall, this is skilled comic writing with strong voice control, minor structural softness, and limited emotional depth. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 58.7
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door gave a prim little chime, and then the door itself slammed hard enough to rattle the display of local history paperbacks in the window. “Sorry—am I being murdered, or are you just closed?” The man who’d come in shoved a hand through rain-damp hair and bent double, peering through the lace-edged lower pane of the front window. Outside, on the narrow high street, a pair of photographers in black jackets hovered beneath the butcher’s striped awning across the road, cameras tucked under their arms like rifles waiting for a war to resume. From behind the till, Elin Price looked up from her ledger. “We close at five,” she said. “It is currently four twenty-seven. So no, not closed. Also probably not murdered. Though it’s early yet.” He turned. Even before she knew who he was, he had the sort of face that explained a great many poor decisions. Beautiful, yes, but with that extra degree of trouble in it—cheekbones too sharp to be kind, a mouth built for smiling and lying with equal fluency, and dark brows lifted now in theatrical gratitude. “Oh, thank God. A sanctuary.” He pressed a hand to his chest. “I was beginning to think I’d have to hide in the post office, and I’ve always felt one should preserve a little dignity.” Elin shut the ledger. “You’re Rhys Vale.” He smiled as if she’d handed him exactly what he wanted. “I am. I’m delighted to find Wales still claims me.” “Mm.” She took in the expensive coat, the damp at the shoulders, the city polish that sat oddly among her shelves labelled MYTH, POETRY, CRIME, and WELSH LANGUAGE LEARNERS. “You’re dripping on my floor, Mr Vale.” “Rhys,” he said automatically. “On my floor, Rhys.” He looked down. “Right. Sorry.” She nodded toward the umbrella stand by the door. “If your pursuers have gone rabid, I’d rather not have them trampling through Travel and Biography. You can stay there until they wander off.” His expression flickered. “That’s all? No squeal, no autograph request, no solemn declaration that your auntie loved me in The Glass Harbour?” “Elin,” she said. “Sorry?” “My name. Since we’re on first names and all.” His mouth tilted. “Elin. Lovely. Soft at the edges. Dangerous in the middle.” She stared at him. He cleared his throat. “That usually goes over better.” “I imagine it does.” For a second, something like embarrassment crossed his face, so quick she nearly missed it. Then he recovered and sauntered—actually sauntered—toward the front table stacked with new fiction. “This is a very nice shop,” he said. “Charming. Tasteful. Smells like rain and second chances.” “It smells like old paper and the café next door over-roasts its coffee.” “See? You do have poetry in you.” “I stock poetry. That’s not the same thing.” He picked up a novel, looked at the cover without seeing it, and set it down again. The cameras outside flashed once through the window, bright and vulgar. Instantly his shoulders tightened. Elin noticed. “Persistent, aren’t they?” “They’re bored,” he said lightly. “Bored people are the most dangerous people in Britain.” “And what exactly are they hoping to catch? You buying a dictionary?” “An exclusive picture of me in exile. ‘Beloved screen idol takes refuge among the common paperbacks.’” “You think rather highly of yourself.” “I have to,” he said, too quickly. Then he laughed, but there was a nick in it. “Occupational hazard.” She leaned one hip against the till. “You could go out the back, if you like. There’s an alley by the bins. Very glamorous. Really improves a person’s mystique.” “I might. In a minute.” He glanced around again, this time slower. “Do many people come in?” “In this weather? No. In this town? Also no.” “That bad?” “That honest.” He grinned despite himself. “And here I thought booksellers were meant to be gentle with the public.” “We are. You’re not the public. You’re a disruption.” “That’s devastating, Elin.” “Yes, you look crushed.” He set both palms on the edge of the front table and looked at her more directly now, charm softened into curiosity. “Do you genuinely not care who I am?” “Oh, I know who you are. That isn’t the same thing.” “And which is it? Moral superiority? Professional reserve? Or do you just dislike actors on principle?” “I dislike being expected to perform enthusiasm on demand.” His brows rose. “That was very nearly aimed at me.” “It landed where it landed.” A laugh escaped him, real this time. He tipped his head back, and she had the ridiculous, unhelpful thought that his throat was unfairly elegant. “Well,” he said, “I deserve that more often than I get it.” “I’m sure.” He wandered toward the Welsh fiction shelf. “You really are immune.” “No. Just Welsh.” He turned with a hand over his heart. “Cruel.” “Elin!” A voice came from the curtained doorway at the back, where the stockroom and tiny kitchen lay beyond. “Did that box of—” Megan, sixteen and all elbows, skidded to a halt. Her eyes went wide enough to swallow the room. “Oh my God.” Rhys straightened automatically, smile clicking into place with practised warmth. “Hello.” Megan made a strangled sound. “You’re—” “Yes,” Elin said. “He is. And if you scream, you can mop the floor after.” “I wasn’t going to scream,” Megan lied, visibly vibrating. “I just—wow. Sorry. Huge fan.” There it was, Elin thought: the way he came alive under admiration as if someone had struck a match beneath his skin. The tension left his shoulders. His eyes warmed. He became easy, luminous. “That’s very kind,” he said, and meant it too much to be entirely vain. “What’s your name?” “Megan.” “Megan, I’m honoured.” Megan shot Elin a look that plainly said are you seeing this, and Elin gave her a look back that plainly said boil the kettle and survive. Megan fled into the back room with both hands over her mouth. Rhys watched her go, smiling faintly. “See? Not everyone in here thinks I’m a plague of frogs.” “I never said frogs.” “No, but the implication lingered.” He moved nearer the till. Close enough now that she could smell rain, wool, and some clean, expensive cologne that seemed a little wasted on this tiny shop in Aberaeron. Up close, he also looked more tired. Fine strain around the eyes. The sort no camera ever admitted. “So,” he said, lowering his voice. “What have I done to offend you, Elin Price, besides arrive wet and famous?” She folded her arms. “Nothing. That’s what unsettles you.” His smile faded at the edges. “You think everyone should like you,” she said. “Maybe because mostly they do.” He held her gaze for a beat too long. “Should they not?” “Not automatically.” He glanced at the window, where one paparazzo was now pretending to inspect his phone while very obviously watching the shop. “It’s not as pleasant as it looks, you know.” “No?” “No.” He leaned a shoulder against the shelf, all careless lines over something tauter. “When I was fourteen, I had a drama teacher who told me if I went onstage and made them love me quickly, they wouldn’t have time to notice I was frightened.” His mouth twitched. “I’ve been treating it as sacred wisdom ever since.” Something in Elin eased before she could stop it. “Frightened of what?” He looked down at the spine of a book, tracing the title with one finger. “Being forgettable.” He said it lightly, but not enough. “My father had a remarkable talent for leaving rooms in the middle of things. Conversations, birthdays, Christmas dinner once. One minute there, one minute gone. I think I got it into my head that if I were dazzling enough, no one would walk away before the end.” The shop seemed quieter around that. Rain ticked at the window. In the back, a kettle clicked on. Elin said, more gently than she meant to, “That’s a rotten thing to teach a child.” His eyes lifted to hers. “Yes. Well. We all make art from the damage, don’t we?” There was an ache in the space between them now, inconvenient and alive. “You’re very good at this,” she said. “At what?” “Making women forgive you.” His grin came back, but smaller, less certain. “And are you forgiving me?” “No.” “Liar.” She should have rebuked him. Instead she found herself almost smiling. “Careful.” “With you?” “Yes.” “That sounds suspiciously like hope.” She looked at him for one reckless second too long, and his expression changed. The practised charm thinned. What remained was younger, startled, and far more dangerous. From the back room, Megan called, “Tea’s on!” Neither of them moved. Rhys spoke first, voice quiet. “Tell me something true about you, then. Fair exchange.” Elin hesitated. “I don’t like locked doors.” His face softened. “No?” “When I was ten, my brother thought it was funny to shut me in the airing cupboard. Only for a few minutes, but…” She shrugged, hating that she’d offered it, hating more that she wanted him to understand. “I still keep every internal door in the flat half open. Even in winter.” He didn’t smile at that. Thank God. “That sounds lonely,” he said. “It sounds ridiculous.” “No.” He shook his head. “It sounds like surviving in the shape available to you.” The kettle clicked off. Outside, one of the photographers gave up and ducked away toward the harbour. The other followed, shoulders hunched against the rain. Rhys glanced toward the window, then back at her. “It appears your kingdom is secure.” “For now.” He nodded, but made no move to leave. “Would it be terribly improper of me to buy a book I don’t need in order to prolong my welcome?” “You were never welcome,” Elin said. “Mm.” “But I suppose I can sell to refugees.” His smile was slow and unexpectedly warm. “There you are. I knew you liked me.” She came around the till before she could think better of it. “Don’t be unbearable.” “Too late.” They stopped close by the fiction table, both reaching for the same novel. His fingers brushed hers—brief, accidental, enough to send a ridiculous current up her arm. He looked at her hand, then at her face. “Elin.” “Rhys.” “Is this the part where the bookseller throws me out?” “Not today.” A pause. “Good,” he said softly. And from the back room, Megan, with all the tact of youth, shouted, “If you two are done staring at each other, the tea is getting cold!”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a polished, well-executed romance scene that hits nearly all the prompt's requirements: Welsh setting (Aberaeron, Welsh-language shelf, local color), famous actor fleeing paparazzi, a bookstore owner superficially immune to his charm, an undercurrent of mutual attraction, dialogue-forward construction, and a rogue with a fragile ego who visibly wilts without admiration and blooms when Megan fawns over him. Elin's internal fluster is shown through small physical tells (the "unfairly elegant" throat, the reckless second too long, the almost-smile), which is largely showing rather than telling. Strengths: The dialogue is genuinely good—crisp, voice-differentiated, and carrying the "It landed where it landed" / "No. Just Welsh." exchange, which is both funny and characterful. The Megan interruption is a smart structural device that externalizes Rhys's need for approval without narration, and the observation "he came alive under admiration as if someone had struck a match beneath his skin" is one of the few permitted tells that earns its place. The backstories (father leaving rooms; the airing cupboard) arrive at the right pace and do real work, and "surviving in the shape available to you" is a strong line. Prose is clean, controlled, with light Welsh-inflected dryness. Weaknesses: The story follows the rom-com beat sheet quite predictably—brushed fingers, shared vulnerabilities, the knowing teenager shouting from the back room is a stock device, and the closing line is a touch sitcom-neat. Rhys's confession about his father and his "sacred wisdom" arrives a little easily and fully formed for a first meeting; the intimacy accelerates faster than is fully credible, nudging toward Unearned Transformations, though the mutual confession structure partly excuses it. Elin's vulnerability dump ("I don't like locked doors") is somewhat convenient for a woman established as guarded. The paparazzi simply leaving is tidily resolved. Some lines ("smells like rain and second chances") flirt with cuteness, but Elin's deflation of them keeps overwrought tendencies in check. Imagery is serviceable rather than lush, which suits the piece but limits the top score on descriptive quality. Overall: a competent-to-excellent genre scene, charming, coherent, not especially surprising. + Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 83.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The iron-banded door gave beneath Aya’s hand with a groan that seemed too loud for the hush beyond it. She had expected the usual underhold music: the drip of old water through stonework, the clink of chain from the pulley-shafts, the mutter of sentries, the ceaseless breath of boilers from the machine-rooms above. Instead there was a stillness so complete it felt staged, as if the very dark had been instructed to hold its tongue. Cold air issued up from the chamber beyond, touched with lamp-oil, brine, wet limestone, and that faint metallic taint that belonged to old blood scrubbed poorly from stone. Aya stepped across the threshold first, one gloved hand near the inside pocket where she kept her chalk, her silver filings, the little obsidian token she prayed she would not need. Katra followed close at her shoulder, compact and hard-eyed, with a stiletto hidden somewhere in every fold of her coat. Simeon came last, broad as a dock gate, his beard still damp with the mist outside, his boots soft despite their size. The underhold opened beneath a low vault of sweating brick. Iron pillars rose from black water pooled between the flagstones. At the far end, upon a dais enclosed by rusted railings and sigil-cut plates of whalebone riveted into the floor, stood the reliquary vault itself: a coffin-shaped cabinet of greened brass, all keyholes and warding seals, fed by copper conduits that ran up into the dark like veins. And before it, in a chair placed with theatrical leisure upon the stones, sat Madam Veleris. Alive. At liberty. Very much not in gaol. She wore black wool and sealskin, a high collar fastened with jet. One leg crossed over the other. In one hand she held a slim cane-sword unsheathed by three inches, enough for the steel to catch the gaslight with a chill and wicked line. Around her stood six bodyguards in leather harness and oilskin coats, pistols holstered, cudgels loose in hand, one man with a brass shock-prod that ticked blue at its tip. Two more shapes watched from the gallery overhead, rifles nested on the railing. Aya stopped so abruptly Katra nearly struck her back. “Well,” said Madam Veleris, and her voice carried with all the softness of velvet laid atop a coffin lid. “My industrious little moon-calves. How punctual.” Katra swore under her breath. Simeon’s hand twitched toward his belt and then thought better of it. Aya felt the blood leave her face, though she prayed the half-mask and shadow might hide it. A feint. The arrest had been a feint. Of course it had. Of course no woman kept the Morska Guild by being stupid enough to be taken in her bed. “Do shut the door,” said Veleris. No one moved. One of the bodyguards did it for them. He shoved the slab with his shoulder, and the clang of the bolt landing home rolled through the chamber like a judge’s gavel. Aya forced herself to breathe slowly. The underhold was warded. She could feel the old scythan script laid through the masonry like hooks beneath the skin of the place. The immateria disliked such places. It could be done, perhaps—but not cleanly, not quickly, and certainly not with six pistols pointed the instant anyone scented witchery. Veleris studied them one by one. “You gave me a most diverting afternoon. Half the upper rooms torn apart, three quartermasters accusing each other of treachery, and Bors dead in the counting-house with his tongue black in his mouth. That was your work, was it not?” Katra smiled thinly. “Could’ve been his cooking.” A bodyguard cuffed her sharply across the mouth before Veleris even nodded. Katra staggered, spat blood, and laughed, though her eyes glittered murder. “Still insolent,” said Veleris. “Reassuring. I should hate to think prison manners had overtaken us all.” “You were never in prison,” Simeon rumbled. “No,” said Veleris. “But a great many useful people were persuaded that I was. I wished to know who among my enterprising children would come scratching at the old bones beneath the house.” Her gaze settled on Aya. Not on the mask—through it. Aya knew then, with a sick and sinking certainty, that she had been measured long before this night. “You in particular,” said Veleris. “Come here.” Aya did not move. A pistol clicked. Simeon shifted forward half a pace, and instantly three weapons found his chest. “Do not make me have him ventilated,” said Veleris, sounding bored. “The floor is damp enough.” Aya stepped down from her companions and crossed the stones alone. Every footfall rang in her bones. She felt Katra’s stare between her shoulder blades, Simeon’s helpless fury hanging in the air like heat before lightning. When she was an arm’s length away, Veleris rose. She was not a large woman, but command made a second stature of her. She reached out with one gloved hand and took hold of Aya’s mask. “For months,” she said quietly, “you have played spectre in my halls. Whispered to the gullible. Rose very quickly, did you not? A lady phantom with uncommon talents and uncommon ambition.” Her fingers tightened. “Let us have a look at the face of ambition.” She tore the mask free. The cold struck Aya’s skin. So did the light. There was a tiny silence after that—small, but catastrophic. One bodyguard inhaled sharply. Another muttered, “Saints preserve us.” Aya had forgotten, absurdly, how recognizable her own face might be. Not to these dock-thieves, perhaps, but enough: the cut of her coat too fine even in disguise, the line of her jaw echoing portraits in newspaper etchings, her mother’s dark eyes, famous once in scandal sheets before they had become the eyes of a hanged witch. Veleris smiled without warmth. “Ah. There she is. The black sheep of House Vale.” Katra’s expression changed by a hair; not surprise, exactly. Confirmation. Simeon closed his eyes for a single beat. “Aya…” It was not accusation. It was worse. It was hurt. Aya’s stomach turned over. So this was the shape of it. Not merely death, but exposure. Her father’s household dragged into inquiry. The clubs and parliament rooms whispering over breakfast. Her brothers denying knowledge. The family solicitor purchasing silence where he could. And her mother’s ghost, if ghosts kept counsel, laughing bitterly to see the daughter brought round at last to the same noose by a more circuitous road. “Take them,” said Veleris. The bodyguards moved at once. Simeon was clubbed behind the knee and forced down, his wrists cinched with chain. Katra fought the grip by instinct alone, earning an elbow in the ribs and a twist of her arm that drove a hiss between her teeth. Aya did not resist when they seized her; resistance would invite panic, and panic would invite the dark thing inside her to answer. She could feel it already, brushing at the edges of her mind like wet velvet, eager for a slit in the world. Not here, she thought fiercely. Not warded, not watched, not with them so near. A chain was looped about her wrists. Another around her waist. One guard patted her down and found the chalk, the filings, the obsidian token. He recoiled from the last of these and flung it skittering across the floor as though it might bite him. “Filth,” he muttered. “Careful,” said Veleris. “She is delicate stock.” Aya lifted her chin. If she let them see fear they would feed upon it. If she spoke too boldly they would break her teeth. Somewhere between those cliffs there might yet be a channel. “You know what I am worth,” she said. Katra gave a short incredulous bark. “Aya—” “Hush,” Aya said, not taking her eyes off Veleris. “You know exactly what I am worth.” Veleris tilted her head. “Do enlighten me.” “The daughter of Alistair Vale. Sister to one magistrate and one naval undersecretary. Niece to a bishop. If I vanish into harbor mud, there will be inquiry. If I am returned discreetly, perhaps in exchange for consideration, there will be gratitude. If held—” She swallowed the bile that rose with the word. “If held, I am worth more than any relic in this hole.” Simeon stared at her as if she had become a stranger twice over. Katra wiped blood from her lip with bound hands. “Now she remembers she’s rich.” Aya ignored her because to meet that look would be fatal. Veleris walked a slow circle around her. Cane-sword point whispering over stone. “A ransom, then? How patrician. How very clean. But there is the difficulty of your extracurricular pursuits. Men of office are terribly sensitive where scandal is concerned. They might pay less to recover you than to ensure you are never spoken of again.” Aya’s pulse thudded in her throat. “Then use me otherwise.” “Otherwise?” “You have enemies in parliament, in customs, in the harbor board. Men who smile at your shipments while sending constables after your runners. Through me, doors open. Names are obtained. Papers copied. Questions diverted.” She forced the words out with a steadiness she did not feel. “Kill me and you possess a corpse with an interesting pedigree. Keep me and you possess leverage.” Veleris stopped before her. “And why,” she asked softly, “would I trust the issue of a house that would hang a woman for sorcery?” Because I am my mother’s daughter, Aya thought. Because I learned long ago what mercy aristocrats offer those who embarrass them. Aloud she said, “You should not trust me. You should simply value me.” For the first time, Veleris laughed—a low, genuine sound, though there was little mirth in it. “There. That is almost honest.” From far beyond the guild walls, through layers of brick and fog and sleeping streets, a harbor horn sounded. Once. The note came long and mournful, like some leviathan calling through iron lungs. Twice. The guards shifted uneasily. Old sailors said three calls before dawn meant a bad tide or a body in the lockgates. Thrice. The last note lingered in the underhold until even the lamp flames seemed to shiver. Veleris’s eyes remained on Aya. “I have not yet decided,” she said. “Whether to sell you, use you, or cut your occult little heart out and lock it in the reliquary for luck.” Katra muttered, “Charming woman.” “Take them to the lower cells,” Veleris said. “Separate the gentleman. Search the ladies again. Thoroughly.” Simeon strained against his chains. “Touch her and I’ll—” A rifle butt silenced him. Aya stood very still as hands closed on her arms and began to drag her toward the stair. Beneath the fear, beneath the shame, beneath the ruin yawning open before her, another feeling stirred—thin and cold and patient. Not hope. Calculation. If Veleris had not killed them here, then the game was not done. And in the black country beyond reason, where her mother’s art still breathed through cracks in the world, some listening thing had heard the horn call and turned its face toward the door.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece is a strong execution of a demanding brief. It hits every requested story beat: the trio enters the underhold, finds Veleris free and armed, Aya is unmasked, all three are captured without a fight scene, and Aya stalls via hostage-negotiation while internally reckoning with exposure. The dialogue is heavy, period-flavored, and distinct per character—Veleris's velvet menace ("The floor is damp enough"), Katra's gallows insolence ("Could've been his cooking"), Simeon's protective rumble. The whalepunk/Victorian texture is well rendered: whalebone sigil-plates, sealskin, gaslight, harbor horns, brass shock-prods. Gothic horror elements (the warded masonry, the "wet velvet" entity brushing Aya's mind) are integrated rather than pasted on. Strengths: pacing, atmosphere, the unmasking beat lands with genuine weight ("It was not accusation. It was worse. It was hurt."), and Aya's internal monologue about family ruin is specific and affecting. The closing horn-call is an effective omen, and the final "Not hope. Calculation." is a well-earned tonal note. Weaknesses: some familiar genre furniture (the bored villain, the "I should hate to think..." quips, the theatrical chair on a dais) edges toward convention. Veleris is sketched as a type rather than a person. The horn-call omen is slightly convenient as scene punctuation. A few lines flirt with over-polish ("velvet laid atop a coffin lid") but mostly stay controlled. The prose is confident and largely show-don't-tell; occasional summarizing ("Aya knew then... that she had been measured long before this night") is acceptable as interiority. + Fanfic-crossover: Gunpowder Rendezvous — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bar squats between a pawn shop and a shuttered massage parlor, its neon beer signs buzzing like dying insects in the rain. Inside, the air is thick with cigarette smoke, spilled whiskey, and the kind of old grease that never leaves the walls. A neon jukebox in the corner keeps coughing up the same scratchy rock track on repeat, the guitar riff warped and thin, as if it’s being dragged back from the grave each time it starts over. Spike Spiegel leans against the bar like he grew there, long legs crossed at the ankle, a cigarette hanging from his mouth. His suit is rumpled, one sleeve darkened by rain, and he looks half-asleep in the yellow light. But his good eye moves constantly, taking inventory of exits, mirrors, hands. The other eye catches the neon wrong, making the room feel a little distant, a little unreal. He’s on his second cheap bourbon and thinking about dinner he can’t afford when the front door opens. She walks in like she owns every bad decision ever made under this roof. Shorts. Boots. Black crop top. Dragon ink winding down one arm. A pair of pistols riding low and easy like they’re part of her skeleton. Revy scans the room with flat, predatory disinterest, then heads for the bar. Spike exhales smoke and says, without looking at her, “You’re blocking my light.” Revy snorts and climbs onto the stool beside him. “Cry about it.” Her voice is rough from cigarettes and disuse. Up close she smells like cordite, sweat, and rum. Spike glances sideways, and her eyes are already on him, sharp and amused in a way that promises trouble. The bartender slouches over. “What’s it gonna be?” “Whatever’ll erase this place,” Revy says. “Then you need a gun, not a drink,” Spike mutters. She turns to him, grin flashing mean and bright. “You volunteering?” “Depends. You buying?” The bartender pours her something brown and hostile in a glass that isn’t clean enough to matter. She knocks half of it back in one swallow, wipes her mouth with the back of her hand, and finally says, “You here for Volkov?” Spike takes his cigarette from his mouth. “Maybe.” “Funny,” Revy says. “I’m here for Volkov too.” There it is. The thing beneath the banter. It settles between them as naturally as smoke. Volkov is a low-grade trafficker with a medium-grade body count and a high-grade price on his head. The kind of man who gets careless when he thinks his money can buy another week. Last report puts him in the rooms upstairs, with two guards, a suitcase of bearer chips, and a girlfriend young enough to still believe his promises. Spike shrugs. “Big city.” Revy laughs once. “You’re not good at playing dumb.” “You’re not good at playing nice.” “I don’t play nice.” “Yeah,” Spike says, studying the angle of her jaw, the scar near her lip, the calm way her fingers rest close to her guns. “I noticed.” For a second the scratchy guitar from the jukebox fills the silence. It starts over again. Same opening riff. Same miserable little resurrection. Revy signals for another drink. “How do you wanna do this, cowboy? Split the bounty? Flip a coin? Or we shoot it out and save Volkov the suspense?” Spike lifts his glass. “I hate coins.” “Then maybe I’ll just take your legs out and drag him downstairs myself.” “You flirt with everybody like that?” She turns on the stool until one knee brushes his thigh. It doesn’t feel accidental. “Only the broke ones.” Spike smiles around his cigarette, lazy and dangerous. “Good. I’m definitely your type.” The gunfire upstairs starts with a muffled pop and turns the whole bar inside out. Everybody moves at once. Chairs slam back. Somebody screams. The bartender drops below the counter. Spike and Revy are already off their stools before the second shot. “Guess someone got impatient,” Spike says. “No shit.” They hit the stairs side by side, not together exactly, but in rhythm. On the landing, Volkov’s first guard barrels through the hallway door with a shotgun. Spike slides low, one hand on the filthy carpet, and the blast goes over him, shredding wallpaper. Revy steps into the opening and fires twice. Her pistols buck in clean, efficient flashes. The guard folds backward into the room. Spike rises in the same motion and kicks the shotgun away. “Show-off.” “Keep up.” The second guard comes from the bathroom with a submachine gun. Spike sees the muzzle, grabs Revy by the waist, and yanks her flat against the wall as bullets chew splinters from the doorframe. She snarls at being handled, but only for a second. Then she twists free, leans out with both arms extended, and returns fire so fast it sounds like tearing cloth. The guard stumbles, spraying the ceiling, and Spike plants a shot through the man’s shoulder, then another through his chest. Silence drops hard. Volkov crashes through the room’s far window. “Son of a—” Revy sprints for it. Spike follows, flicking his cigarette aside. Outside, the fire escape rattles under Volkov’s weight as he clambers down into the alley. Rain slicks the metal. Neon bleeds pink and blue across puddles below. Revy vaults the sill first. Spike is right behind her. They descend fast, boots ringing steel, Volkov slipping lower in a panic. On the last ladder he loses his footing and drops, hits the pavement badly, scrambles anyway. He gets three limping steps before Revy puts a round into the dumpster beside his head and sends sparks into his face. “Move again,” she shouts, “and I ventilate your balls.” Volkov freezes. Spike lands lightly, gun up. “That’s persuasive.” They close in from opposite sides, both weapons aimed at Volkov, and for a ridiculous moment all three of them stand in the rain while the jukebox upstairs keeps bleeding that same scratchy song through the open window. Volkov lifts his hands, panting. “You can’t both collect.” “No,” Revy says. “But we can both drag.” Spike crouches, pats Volkov down, finds the bearer chips. “Huh. Dinner money.” Revy snatches the case from him. “Our dinner money.” He looks up at her. Rain beads on her bare skin, traces the edge of her collarbone, catches in the loose strands of her hair. Her chest rises slow and hard from the chase. She looks alive in the ugliest way possible. Spike feels the old instinct kick in—that warning in his bones that attraction and danger are usually the same thing wearing different suits. “Fifty-fifty?” he says. She gives him a long look. “You trust me that much?” “Not even a little.” “Good answer.” Volkov takes that as his chance. He lunges. Spike and Revy fire at the same time. Volkov slams back against the alley wall and slides down, dead before he hits the ground. For a second there’s only rain and smoke drifting from their barrels. Then Revy says, “Now we’ve got a problem.” “Yeah,” Spike says. “Paperwork.” She laughs despite herself. “No. No live bounty, genius.” Spike stands and holsters his pistol. “Depends who you know.” “Or who you bribe.” “That too.” They end up in a motel three blocks away because the alley is no place to divide chips, and because both of them know better than to settle accounts in public. The place advertises hourly rates and air conditioning that rattles like a dying engine. The room smells of bleach, mildew, and old sex. Outside, red neon from the vacancy sign pulses through the blinds. The suitcase lies open on the bed between them. Spike sits in the chair by the window, one ankle over a knee, smoking like he plans to outlast the wallpaper. Revy leans against the dresser with a bottle of rum she found in her bag, one pistol loose at her side. Neither of them has counted the chips yet. “You grabbed me in the hall again,” she says. “You’re welcome.” “Do it a third time, I break your wrist.” “Probably.” The scratchy rock song from the bar has followed them somehow, still lodged in Spike’s head, still circling. He watches her take a drink. Watches the tilt of her throat. Watches her mouth wipe against her wrist. “You always this friendly after work?” he asks. Revy looks at him over the bottle. “You always stare this much?” “Occupational hazard.” “Try it again and I’ll charge.” Spike smiles faintly. “How much?” Instead of answering, she raises her gun. A beat later, Spike raises his. It happens so smoothly it almost feels rehearsed. Two professionals, perfectly still, aiming center mass across ten feet of stained carpet and humid air. Neither one blinks. The tension in the room changes shape. It’s not just mistrust now. It’s heat with nowhere to go, sharpened into something reckless. Spike can feel it in the drag of his cigarette, in the pulse beating slow under his skin. Revy’s expression is hard, but not empty. There’s anger there, yes. And curiosity. And the same dangerous pull he knows is mirrored in his own face. “You thinking about shooting me,” she says, “or something else?” Spike lets smoke out through his nose. “Both.” That makes her grin, small and vicious. “Good.” The red neon pulses over them. Gunmetal glints. The bed sags under the weight of the open case between them like an invitation neither one trusts. No one lowers their weapon. No one looks away. And for one suspended, electric moment, it’s impossible to tell which one of them is going to pull the trigger first— or close the distance.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent, atmospheric noir crossover that hits nearly all the prompt's beats: seedy bar, shared bounty, banter, gunplay, drinking, and a motel-room standoff ending on unresolved tension. The prose is lean and rhythmic, with strong sensory grounding (neon, rain, cordite, scratchy jukebox) and a consistent hard-boiled register appropriate to both source materials. Character voices are well captured—Spike's fatalistic laziness and Revy's profanity-adjacent menace come through in clipped, credible dialogue. The recurring jukebox motif is a nice unifying device. Strengths: the dialogue is punchy and character-distinct; the action choreography is clear and spatially coherent; the mutual-attraction/mistrust dynamic is shown through posture, gunplay, and negotiation rather than stated outright; the ending withholds resolution in a way true to both characters. Weaknesses: the plot is formulaic—bounty target flees, dies, chips become the new stake—with no surprises in structure. Some lines flirt with cliché ("she walks in like she owns every bad decision ever made under this roof" is stylish but borderline precious). Revy's vulnerability is barely present; she's mostly surface menace, which flattens her complexity compared to the prompt's description. The Volkov chase resolves too easily, and the "both fire at once" beat is convenient. The piece is polished but safe, never transcending genre pastiche into anything genuinely surprising or emotionally deep. Still, it's professional, coherent, and engaging throughout, with no amateurish lapses, no purple excess, and an ending whose ambiguity is earned by the established dynamic. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 87.2
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
By November I had learned that darkness in the north was not the same thing as darkness in Stockholm. In the city, night still belonged to people: windows lit in stacked rows, buses sighing at stops, the orange wash of streetlamps making even empty places feel watched. In the village, once you stepped beyond the last yard light, the dark seemed to begin at your face. It had depth. It had weather. It pressed against your eyes as if there were miles of it waiting. That was the night Astrid took me to sit out on the mound. She never called it anything as dramatic as a ritual. She said it the way someone might suggest sneaking cigarettes behind the gym. We were in her room after school, half doing homework, half cutting pictures from an old mail-order catalogue, and she said, “We can try útiseta tonight if you want. Properly, I mean. Not like when Johan and them sat on the sawmill roof and shouted for ghosts.” I asked what “properly” meant, and she shrugged like it was obvious. “You sit on a grave mound at midnight and stay quiet until something tells you what you asked. Or shows you. Mormor says people used to do it for knowledge. About winter, cattle, sickness, thieves, marriages. We can use it for other things too.” “Like what?” She gave me a sideways look, amused that I needed it spelled out. “Like whether Malin actually stole that silver ring from Birgitta’s locker. Or whether Andreas likes you.” I said I did not care whether Andreas liked me, too fast, and she laughed. That was part of Astrid’s talent. She could wrap anything old and solemn in the language of ordinary teenage cruelty and make it seem harmless. We had already played at things she called games: whispering names over running water, dropping pins into melted candle wax, tying knots in thread while speaking questions we wanted answered. Most of it had produced exactly what such things always produce—coincidences, suggestibility, the excitement of pretending there are secret levers behind people’s faces. Yet once or twice there had been moments I still do not sort comfortably. A teacher calling on the exact person Astrid had named under her breath. A girl bursting into tears the morning after Astrid said she’d dreamed where the girl hid her cigarettes. Small things, explainable things, but accumulating. “Where is this mound?” I asked. “In the pasture above the old road. The one with the ring of pines.” “You’re not supposed to be up there.” “No,” she said. “That’s why it works.” She came to my house after eleven carrying a thermos, a folded wool blanket, and a little paper packet tied with red thread. My parents were asleep, or meant to be. I left a note saying I was staying over at Astrid’s, though of course that made no sense because she was visibly standing in our kitchen in her father’s army surplus jacket, mud on the hem of her jeans. It did not matter. My mother had reached the stage of the move where she was too tired to notice contradictions. Outside, the cold had the clean metallic smell of deep winter approaching. Snow had not settled yet, but the ground was iron-hard. Frost filmed the grass silver where our flashlights passed over it. Astrid walked quickly, not wasting the beam except when we crossed ditches or wire. She seemed to know every hollow and rise by memory. “What’s in the packet?” I asked. “Things for sitting out.” “That tells me nothing.” She sighed. “A little salt. A bit of bread. Juniper. Mormor said not to go empty-handed. And don’t bring anything with steel if you can help it.” “I have keys.” “That’s fine. Just don’t jingle them. And if you need to pee, do it now.” I stopped short. “You could have said that earlier.” “I am saying it now.” I went behind a stand of birch saplings while she stood in the road, humming to herself. I remember feeling faintly ridiculous then, shivering and annoyed and thinking this was exactly the sort of thing girls in villages did to pass the time because there was nowhere else to go. I wanted to belong badly enough to follow. That is the simple truth of it. The mound rose from the pasture so gradually that at first it looked like only a swell in the ground. As we got closer, I saw the shape was too round, too deliberate. A ring of old pines stood around it, black trunks evenly spaced as if planted to guard it. Their roots broke through the turf like knuckles. The road below had long ago shifted away, leaving the mound by itself above the field. Astrid switched off her flashlight. I did the same a second later, unwilling to be the only weak one with a light. For a moment there was nothing. Then the dark arranged itself: a paling strip of cloud, the rougher black of the trees, the sheen of frost on the grass. The sky was clear enough that stars showed between moving bands of high cloud. Our breaths drifted white. “Listen,” Astrid said quietly. “From here on, don’t say anyone’s full name. Don’t answer if you hear yours from behind you. Don’t take food or drink if you’re offered it.” “Offered by who?” She looked at me. Even in the dark I could feel the steadiness of it. “That’s exactly the kind of question you shouldn’t ask up here.” I almost told her to stop, that she was laying it on too thick, but the words felt childish in my mouth. She climbed the mound first, her boots making soft tearing sounds in the frozen grass. At the top she spread the blanket and knelt, opening the paper packet with practical care. The smell of juniper lifted sharp and resinous in the cold. She crumbled bread into four pieces and set them at the edges of the blanket. Then she pinched salt into a ring, not complete but horseshoe-shaped, open toward the north. “Why leave it open?” I whispered. “So something can come and something can go. Otherwise it stays.” She said it as if explaining how to prop a door. “What are we asking?” “You ask what you want. But ask once. If you keep asking, it thinks you don’t trust the answer.” “Who thinks?” Astrid ignored that. She sat cross-legged within the broken salt ring and gestured for me to do the same. “Hands on your knees. Don’t fidget. If you get scared, don’t run downhill. Walk. And don’t step on the bread.” “You make this sound very safe.” “It’s not unsafe if you aren’t stupid.” There was, beneath her confidence, something rehearsed. Not performative exactly. More like inherited precision. I wondered how many nights she had listened to her grandmother say these things, in a kitchen smelling of coffee and boiled potatoes, while snow pressed at the windows. I wondered how much had been altered in the retelling, roughened by adolescent daring into something more glamorous. We sat. At first all I could feel was discomfort. The cold seeped through the blanket. My toes began to ache. Somewhere far off a dog barked once and was silent. The pines made no sound at all. Astrid had told me to form the question in my mind and hold it there, so I thought, with embarrassed intensity, Tell me what they say about me when I’m not there. It seemed petty even then, but pettiness is often what drives these experiments with forbidden knowledge. Not wisdom. Not transcendence. Just the desire to be less helpless among other people. Time loosened strangely. The longer we sat without speaking, the more every sensation swelled. A drop of melted frost slid from a pine branch and hit the ground with a tick loud as a knuckle on glass. My own pulse became an intrusion. I found myself listening for patterns, for words hidden in the tiny sounds of the field. Then, from very far away, a church bell chimed once. The sound arrived thinned by distance, but unmistakable. One clear note, hanging in the frozen air. I turned to Astrid. In the dark her face was only a pale oval. “Is there—” She caught my wrist hard enough to hurt. I remembered: no speaking after midnight. Or perhaps she had never said that and I only believed she had. Memory has a way of making rules multiply after the fact. We sat motionless while the bell’s echo disappeared. There was no service scheduled anywhere that I knew of. The village church stood locked at night. I told myself there must be some ordinary reason: a clock mechanism, a caretaker, a fault. But the sound had changed the quality of the dark. It no longer felt empty. It felt attentive. A few minutes later—I think it was minutes; it could have been seconds—I heard someone moving below the mound. Not walking on the road. Not crossing the pasture. Circling. Slow steps in the grass, stopping now and then as if whoever it was were feeling their way by hand. I could not see anything through the pines. The sound might have been wind worrying at dead stalks, except there was no wind. Astrid’s fingers tightened once around my wrist and then let go. The steps stopped behind me. Every childish warning I had ever heard about the dead, about forest things, about never turning when called, rose at once in my body so that I could hardly breathe. I knew with complete rational certainty that there was probably some person down there, or an animal, or nothing at all. My certainty did not help. I became aware of the back of my neck as a separate vulnerable object. Something touched my hair. Very lightly. Not a grasp. More like a curious lift of one strand, then another. I made a noise then, a tiny involuntary intake of breath. Astrid moved beside me, quick as a striking animal, and threw a pinch of juniper over my shoulder. The smell burst green and bitter. The circling sound began again at once, farther away now. Or perhaps only masked by the blood pounding in my ears. We stayed until Astrid decided we could leave. That, more than anything, was what frightened me later: not the sound, not the bell, not the impossible sensation at my hair, but how completely I surrendered my judgment to hers. When she finally stood, brushed salt from her knees, and whispered, “Don’t look back,” I obeyed. We walked down from the mound without our flashlights. At the bottom I stepped around the bread pieces automatically, as if that mattered. Only when we reached the road did I realize my right braid had come half undone. Neither of us spoke until the village lights showed through the trees. Then I said, trying to sound mocking and failing, “So did we receive knowledge from beyond?” Astrid unscrewed the thermos and drank. “You’ll know tomorrow,” she said. I wanted to ask what had touched me. I wanted to ask whether she had heard the steps too, whether she had planned the bell somehow, whether all of this was just another of her games sharpened by local superstition and my own suggestible city nerves. But I did not ask. Some part of me was afraid that if she said it had been nothing, I would have to admit how ready I had been to believe. And if she said it had been something, I would have to live in a world that contained it. The next morning, at school, I learned what people said about me when I was not there. That is another story. But I have never since been able to smell crushed juniper in cold air without feeling a hand, or a branch, or my own panicked imagination, lifting the hair at the back of my neck on that mound while the dark listened.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of folk horror that fulfills the brief with notable skill. The prose is controlled and atmospheric, with a mature first-person retrospective voice that stays transparent as instructed. The opening meditation on northern darkness is genuinely evocative and establishes the narrator's adult recollection without belaboring the device. Strengths: The ambiguity is sustained expertly throughout—the bell, the circling footsteps, the touch on the hair all remain explicable (wind, an animal, suggestibility) while feeling genuinely threatening. Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions ("if you need to pee, do it now") perfectly capture the requested mix of teenage ordinariness and eerily specific tradition. The salt ring left open "so something can come and something can go" is a superb detail. The narrator's self-awareness about her own motives ("pettiness is often what drives these experiments") adds psychological depth. The ending—"You'll know tomorrow"—is an excellent withholding, and the final line about juniper ties the trauma to sensory memory convincingly. Weaknesses: Some minor inconsistencies—the narrator says she left a note claiming to be at Astrid's while Astrid stands visibly in the kitchen, which the text acknowledges but strains plausibility slightly. The braid coming undone is a nice touch but slightly underexploited. Occasional sentences lean toward the aphoristic ("It had depth. It had weather.") which borders on stylistic self-consciousness, though it largely works. The dialogue, while functional and characterful, occasionally serves exposition a bit neatly ("Mormor says people used to do it for knowledge..."). The piece is otherwise remarkably free of amateurish tells, overwrought sentiment, or purple prose. The word count appears close to target. The tone is consistent, the pacing tight, and the closing ambiguity lands well without incongruent positivity or unearned transformation.
