Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By the time I learn the studio numbers, I’ve already learned the smell of this place: pine disinfectant, hot rosin, sweat dried and rewarmed under LED panels. Studio 4B is at the end of a white hallway so clean it makes me walk softer than I ever have in my life. Inside, the floor is pale maple with black tape making a perfect center cross. The mirrored wall runs the whole front length, broken only by the sound system mounted high in the left corner. Windows line the right wall from waist height up, looking down on Seoul like it’s another stage I haven’t earned. There are twelve of us in formation when Instructor Han enters. Three rows of four, each dancer standing on a tape mark. I’m back row, far left from the mirror’s perspective, which means if I’m facing front, I’m near the back-right corner of the room. Jisoo is one mark in front of me. Minjae is to my immediate right. Everybody has exactly one arm’s length between shoulders and another half-step between rows. I know because Han made us measure it with our own bodies at the start of rehearsal, palms out, fingertips almost touching. He doesn’t raise his voice when he comes in. He just closes the black hand fan in one sharp crack against his palm and the room seals itself around that sound. “From count one,” he says. The track starts with a four-beat synth pulse and a sub-bass drop on five. Commercial style. Idol style. Everything cut clean enough to edit with a ruler. Count one: right foot steps out to second position, just wider than shoulders. Both fists chamber at ribs. Two: left shoulder hits forward while the right knee angles in. A diagonal line, sternum front. Three-and-four: right arm shoots to high diagonal, left arm extends low behind the hip, torso twists left, then snaps square. Han wants the hit to stop like a frame freeze, no overswing, no residual groove. “Picture-based,” he says. “The audience must read it in one glance.” That’s the first place my body betrays me. Where they stop, I melt. Not on purpose. It’s years of battling under train tracks, finding the pocket in a beat-up speaker, letting the groove travel from ankle to knee to hip before it blooms in the chest. My shoulder hit rolls. My sternum follows through. My wrist loosens at the top of the diagonal instead of locking. Tiny things, but in the mirror they scream. Eleven bodies make angles; mine makes weather. Han pauses the music with a remote. Fan crack. He walks straight toward the back row. He wears slate practice clothes, no logo, hair iron-gray at the temples, face calm in a way that feels more dangerous than yelling. He stops two feet in front of me, reflected and real. “You are arriving after the count,” he says. “I’m on beat.” “No. You are inside the beat. That is different.” A couple of the others keep their eyes on themselves in the mirror, pretending not to listen. I can feel the heat in my ears. My Korean is good enough for correction, not good enough to defend myself without sounding stupid. Han demonstrates. He takes my spot on the tape mark and has me step aside half a meter toward the right wall. “Watch.” He marks the first four counts. On one his right foot lands and all his weight settles instantly to center. On two the shoulder hit isn’t a ripple; it’s a switchblade. On three-and-four the diagonal arm line cuts and stops so hard it looks edited. There’s no bounce under it, no groove leaking between counts. Every transition is hidden in the counts before it, prepared by core engagement and exact weight transfer. Clean. Efficient. Inhuman. “Again,” he says, and I retake my mark. We run eight counts. One, out. Two, shoulder. Three-and-four, diagonal. Five: both feet gather under hips on the bass drop as the hands slice inward, forearms crossing at the wrists in front of the face. Six: drop to a deep second-position plié, knees tracking over toes, elbows opening to a flat T. Seven: pivot a quarter-turn right on the balls of both feet while the left hand spears forward and the right retracts to the jawline. Eight: rebound to front, chin down. I know how to make ugly look beautiful. I know how to catch a snare in my scapula, how to let a glide skim sideways like I’m on oil. But this is architecture. They want every line pre-decided. On six, when we hit the deep plié, my hips sit naturally lower and looser than theirs. I’ve spent too many years in a crouch, too many rounds with my center of gravity near the floor. The problem comes on seven. Instead of the sharp quarter-turn pivot Han drilled, my left heel peels late and my torso initiates before my feet do, making the spear read as a body lead instead of a shape lead. Street habit. I move from groove outward. Here, they move from picture to picture. “Stop.” Fan crack. Han points with the closed fan. “Your body tells stories between the counts. I did not ask for stories.” The class titters, nervy, not cruel. Still, my jaw locks. He resets us. “Travel section. Front line, do not drift. Back line, close your diagonals.” We start from count nine. Formation shifts matter more than the choreography itself here. At nine, front row advances two small runs toward the mirror, center row fans outward, back row—my row—threads through the gaps to become the new center line. From my back-right corner position, I move on a left-right-left chasse path diagonally toward center, passing behind Jisoo’s left shoulder and in front of Minjae by less than a foot. If I overtravel, I clip Minjae’s elbow on eleven when his arm extends to side. If I undertravel, I leave a hole in the center picture. Han has us repeat the pathway six times without music until our spacing is mathematically boring. Then he adds counts. Nine-and-ten: chasse left-right-left, torso pitched five degrees forward, arms tight to body. Eleven: plant both feet parallel under hips on the new center mark, right arm punches side at shoulder height, left hand at sternum. Twelve: head whips left. The head whip gets me. In battles, a head throw is attitude; it drags the spine, invites the shoulders, talks back. Here it’s only neck to focus point, nothing more. My shoulders answer when they shouldn’t. The whip becomes a groove accent. In the mirror my line shivers while everyone else snaps. Han is beside me before the count finishes. He doesn’t touch me often, but now he places two fingers at the top of my shoulder blade, another at my clavicle. “Quiet here,” he says. “Only here.” He taps just behind my ear. The next run, I try to isolate it. Try to turn off everything except what is assigned. The choreography continues: thirteen, left foot steps back into a lunge; fourteen, chest pop forward; fifteen-and-sixteen, a tutting sequence at face level—right forearm horizontal, left vertical, wrists flexed to ninety degrees, then switch, then frame the jaw. My wrists know waacking circles, know flexion with sass, know how to draw halos. But this tut is measured, elbows level, corners exact. Mine comes out too round, too alive. Sweat drops from my chin to the floor and darkens the maple between the tape lines. By the fifth full-out run, my shirt sticks to my spine. Seoul is still new enough that every correction feels like translation stacked on top of translation. It’s not just the language. It’s bowing at the right depth. It’s pretending I don’t notice the brands on everyone’s duffels. It’s hearing kids who started jazz-funk at six talk about “cleaning details” like cleanliness was something families could afford. Back home, dancing was the only thing that didn’t ask me to become presentable first. We reset one last time. Han stands front center, fan open now, stirring air at his throat. He studies us in the mirror. “You,” he says to me. “Scholarship.” I hate that title in his mouth more than my name. “Yes, sir.” “I selected you because your movement is dangerous.” He closes the fan slowly. “But if you protect your habits, they will remain small. If you abandon them completely, you become ordinary. Decide.” Then the fan snaps shut. The track begins again. We hit one, two, three-and-four. I feel the old impulse under my skin, the urge to ride through the hit, to make the angle breathe. On five I gather. On six I drop. On seven the quarter-turn asks me to become a blade. The whole room moves with machine precision: twelve bodies clicking through designed impact, shoulders squared to mirror, knees matching, focus slicing left on twelve like a school of fish changing direction. And there, in the half-count before thirteen, I choose. Not rebellion like blowing up the combo. Not surrender like killing everything I am. I lock the shape exactly where Han wants it—feet planted on the center tape, lunge length equal, forearms forming clean boxes at count fifteen—but I place my intention differently. I keep the pathways strict and the endpoints ruthless, and inside the transitions I change only the texture, microscopic, almost private. A tensile pull through the ribs before the chest pop. A grounded weight in the chasse that comes from the sidewalk, not the conservatory. Not extra counts. Not delay. Just truth distributed so precisely it can survive in uniform. When we finish on sixteen—right knee down, left foot flat, torso hinged forward, left hand braced on thigh, right hand framing the eye—I hold still. Completely still. For the first time my stillness doesn’t feel like death. It feels loaded, like a crouch before a cipher opens. No one moves. In the mirror I see Han looking directly at me. He says nothing for so long I hear the AC kick on overhead. Then: fan crack. “Again,” he says. But this time he’s smiling, only a little, like he hasn’t broken me yet and maybe now he won’t have to.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of controlled first-person dance writing. Its greatest asset is spatial and kinetic precision: the narrator's position (back row, far left from the mirror's perspective), the formation shifts, the counts, and the specific mechanics of each betrayal (heel peeling late on seven, torso initiating before feet) are all tracked with unusual clarity. The prompt demanded complete physical coherence, and the piece delivers it, even using the mirror to double-check positions. The central conflict—groove versus picture, "inside the beat" versus "on beat"—is dramatized through movement rather than stated, and the technical vocabulary (tutting, waacking, chasse, plié, chest pop) is deployed to show the collision of street and commercial styles rather than as decoration. Han is efficiently characterized through the fan, the quiet voice, and lines like "Your body tells stories between the counts. I did not ask for stories"—a genuinely good line that carries the whole theme. The class/culture anxiety is present but slightly underdeveloped relative to the dance material; a few paragraphs ("It's pretending I don't notice the brands...") gesture at it efficiently, though the emotional interior is thinner than the kinetic one. The ending is the riskiest element: the narrator's compromise solution (keeping strict pathways, altering only internal texture) is conceptually elegant and true to the character, but Han's smile arrives quickly, and the resolution feels a touch neat—"maybe now he won't have to" softens what could have been a harder, more ambiguous beat. Minor unearned transformation risk, though it's mitigated by the fact that the narrator's choice is a synthesis, not a conversion. Prose is clean and rhythmic, occasionally aphoristic ("Eleven bodies make angles; mine makes weather"), with only faint traces of overreach. Dialogue is sparse but sharp. No meandering; the ~1000-word target is respected. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 85.2
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The courtroom of the Dreaming was full in the way graveyards were full: quietly, attentively, and with a general sense that no one present had any real business being comfortable. At the center of it all sat Dream upon his high black seat, robed in shadows that seemed too tired to move. His expression, as ever, suggested that existence itself had submitted inferior paperwork. Today, however, there was a particular stillness to him that in lesser beings would have been called irritation. Below him, on the left, stood First Love. First Love was pink-cheeked, earnest, and looked as if he had been assembled from pressed flowers, awkward silences, and the memory of nearly touching someone’s hand in a cinema. He clutched a sheaf of luminous dream-filings to his chest and tried not to look at the opposing table. At the opposing table lounged Mora. She sat like a stain in candlelight. Beautiful in the way deep water was beautiful. Her smile had all the warmth of old iron. When she crossed one leg over the other, several minor phobias in attendance took notes. The bailiff, a gaunt herald stitched from thunder and etiquette, struck the floor with the butt of his staff. “Oyez,” he boomed, making the stars in the ceiling tremble. “The Court of the Dreaming now hears the matter of Furst Luff versus Morrow.” First Love winced. “First Love,” he whispered. Mora lifted a hand. “Mora,” she said pleasantly. The bailiff inclined his head with funereal dignity. “As I have declared.” Dream said nothing. This somehow conveyed disapproval more completely than speech. At a gesture from his long pale hand, proceedings began. First Love rose first, because of course he did. He looked as if he had rehearsed this many times and disliked himself for all of them. “My lord,” he began, “the dreamscape in question was an ongoing developmental sequence belonging to one Max—aged fourteen years, seven months, recurring on alternate Thursdays and periods of emotional distress. It was designed as a foundational romantic dream: field of wildflowers, late afternoon sun, subject reclining beside his beloved, increasing proximity, mutual laughter, a final near-kiss, and then awakening with harmless longing and a productive level of emotional bewilderment.” Dream regarded him. “And your claim?” “That it is mine by authorship, stewardship, and prior occupation,” said First Love, gaining confidence. “I built it carefully. The petals opened on cue. The breeze was calibrated. I had just introduced hand contact.” He swallowed and glanced at Mora. “Then the defendant entered without notice or leave, altered the central figure into a predatory manifestation, pinned the dreamer beneath her, induced paralysis, and fed upon his breath.” Mora raised a finger. “Very pejorative phrasing.” First Love colored. “It is factually accurate phrasing.” “Mm,” said Mora. “Debatable.” Dream turned his dark gaze to her. “Your response.” Mora stood. She did not bother with papers. The shadows around her behaved like loyal dogs. “My lord, learned colleagues, assorted anxieties,” she said, with a nod toward the gallery, where several Teeth-Falling-Out dreams shifted self-consciously. “The complainant presents this as vandalism. I submit that it is adaptation.” First Love stared. “Adaptation?” “Yes. The boy is fourteen.” Mora spread her hands. “His dreamscape was already unstable. Flowers. Crush. Mounting. Breathlessness. Confusion. I merely followed the emotional logic to its natural conclusion.” A murmur moved through the room. First Love made a strangled sound. “Its natural conclusion was not chest-sitting predation!” Mora looked at him with mild pity. “For you, perhaps.” Then she turned to Dream, and her smile sharpened just a little. “My lord, a girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” There was a pause. In the back row, a Night Terror made a tiny choking noise that might have been a laugh. Dream’s eyes flicked toward the gallery. Silence returned at once. He steepled his fingers. “This Court is not unsympathetic to appetite,” he said. “It is, however, traditionally wary of trespass.” Mora inclined her head. “Then I would argue implied invitation.” First Love’s papers slipped from his hands. “Implied—” He bent to gather them in visible distress. “He did not invite you. He invited tenderness.” “And received an unforgettable formative experience,” said Mora. “Trauma!” “Memory,” she corrected. Dream closed his eyes for the span of one patient breath, as if considering whether the universe had improved at all since last Tuesday. “Call your witness,” he said. First Love, looking grateful to be doing something procedural, nodded to the bailiff. The herald struck the floor again. “Call Maxmillian— Maximal— Macks, son of alarm clocks!” A thin, translucent schoolboy appeared in the witness stand, wearing the expression of someone who had gone to sleep in a modest suburb and awakened to legal metaphysics. “Is that him?” asked Dream. “Yes, my lord,” said First Love. Max looked around the courtroom at the assembled embodiments of things he did not have names for, then spotted Dream and immediately decided to become more respectful than he had ever been in his life. The bailiff boomed, “Do you swear to tell the truth, the partial truth, and such distortions as are customary under dream conditions?” “I— yes?” “Accepted.” First Love approached gently, as one might approach a skittish deer or a teenager. “Max,” he said, “can you describe the dream as it was before the intrusion?” Max swallowed. “Um. There was this field. And Ellie was there. We were just lying in the flowers talking, except I can never remember what about. And then she’d laugh and sort of lean over me and I thought maybe we were going to kiss, but then I’d wake up. It was nice. Sort of horrible. But nice.” First Love nodded eagerly. “And after the defendant’s involvement?” Max went red to the ears. “In the interest of judicial economy,” said Dream, “answer plainly.” Max looked at Mora, then away, then very determinedly at the witness rail. “She still leaned over me,” he muttered. “But then she sort of changed.” “Into what?” asked First Love. Max hesitated. “Something bad.” Mora folded her arms. “Be specific.” Dream’s gaze shifted to her. “You may refrain from coaching the witness.” “My apologies, my lord. Old habits.” Max cleared his throat. “She got, um, scary. Eyes wrong. Teeth. Too many shadows. But also…” He frowned, with the misery of adolescence distilled to a single expression. “Not entirely unlike Ellie. Which was confusing. Then she sat on my chest and I couldn’t move, and I couldn’t breathe, and I thought I was going to die.” First Love looked quietly triumphant. “Thank you, Max.” Mora rose for cross-examination. She approached the witness stand with the unhurried grace of an incoming weather event. “Max,” she said softly, “when I appeared—when the dream changed—you were frightened?” “Yes.” “And fascinated?” Max made the mistake of telling the truth in Dream’s court. “…Yes.” First Love covered his face. Mora nodded as if this settled a great legal principle. “And when you awoke, did you continue thinking about the dream?” Max stared at the floor. “Yes.” “For how many days?” “I don’t know.” “A week?” “…Maybe.” Mora spread her hands toward the bench. “Durability of impact.” First Love sprang up. “Objection!” “On what grounds?” asked Dream. “It is monstrous!” Dream considered this. “Overruled. Monstrous is not, in itself, disqualifying here.” Mora smiled faintly and returned to counsel table. First Love called his second witness: a Dream Architect from the Bureau of Recurrence, a fussy figure made entirely of graph paper and dew. The bailiff announced him as “Mister Arkitex of the Bureau of Reoccurring Adolescent Discomfort,” which was near enough. The Architect testified that the dream bore First Love’s unmistakable design signatures: looping sunlight, controlled pulse acceleration, floral symbolism, “Category Two consensual almost-kiss protocol.” He also noted invasive nightmare residue, chest-pressure markers, and unauthorized predatory overlays. Mora did not dispute the alteration. She only seemed bored by the outrage. When it was her turn, she called no witnesses at all. “I am my own best authority,” she said. “An alarming statement,” said Dream. “Usually a correct one.” She stood in the center of the court for her defense. “My lord, let us be practical. The complainant made a dream of yearning. Fine. Very tasteful. Delicate. Pollinated by blushes. But adolescence is not a neat jurisdiction. Fear leaks into desire. Desire leaks into fear. Bodies misbehave. Minds embroider. I entered where the walls were already thin.” First Love looked scandalized. “You exploited vulnerability!” “Yes,” said Mora. “That is literally my office.” Even Dream’s expression shifted by the smallest degree. It was not amusement. It was perhaps the idea of amusement, denied entry. Mora continued. “I do not contest that he made the field. I do not contest that he set the girl there first. But the moment she climbed atop the boy and all his little mortal alarms rang at once, the territory became mixed-use. If the Court denies every nightmare access to erotic confusion, half the Dreaming will collapse by morning.” There was, regrettably, some force to this. Dream sat in silence. The silence went on long enough that several people in the gallery became old enough to regret things. At last he spoke. “This Court finds that the original dreamscape was indeed authored by First Love and unlawfully invaded by Mora.” First Love exhaled in visible relief. Mora merely tilted her head. “However,” Dream continued, “the Court also finds that the underlying emotional terrain contains natural fault lines between longing, terror, shame, and fascination, rendering total exclusion… impractical.” First Love’s relief died in infancy. “My lord—” Dream raised one hand. The protest stopped. “Ownership of the field remains with First Love. Mora is prohibited from further chest-sitting, breath-feeding, paralysis induction, and predatory substitution within that dream without leave of Court.” First Love brightened again. “However,” Dream said, and now there was something in his voice that suggested he had decided to amuse himself after all, “the defendant shall be granted limited, supervised visitation rights.” Mora’s brows rose. Dream’s eyes were stars in a well. “On no more than one night per lunar cycle, Mora may appear in the dream only as an indistinct sense that the kiss would change everything and perhaps not for the better. No crushing. No feeding. No teeth beyond what puberty already provides.” The courtroom was utterly still. First Love looked horrified. Mora looked intrigued. Max looked as if this explained far too much about the human condition. Dream went on. “In exchange, First Love is ordered to revise the recurring sequence. The boy cannot remain forever in a field failing to kiss the same girl. Progress must occur. Add dialogue. Perhaps a hand-hold of substance.” First Love opened and closed his mouth. “My lord, that is advanced work.” “Yes,” said Dream. “Try.” Mora lifted a hand. “And if I violate the terms?” Dream looked directly at her. “Then I will assign you,” he said, “three centuries in the dreams of tax attorneys who have begun jogging.” For the first time that day, Mora appeared genuinely unsettled. The bailiff struck the floor. “Case of Furst Luff versus Morrow resolved! Long live the—” “Enough,” said Dream. The court dissolved in whispers. Max faded from the witness stand, back toward sleep and morning and the vague suspicion that tonight might be emotionally educational in several unfortunate ways. First Love gathered his papers with trembling care. Mora passed him on her way out. “You should thank me,” she said. “Your dream was becoming sentimental.” He clutched the files to his chest. “And yours was becoming actionable.” She laughed, low and delighted, and vanished into the dim. Above them, Dream remained on his throne, looking as he always looked: ancient, severe, and not to be troubled by trivialities. Yet as the last of the court emptied away, one corner of his mouth nearly, almost, in a manner not admissible as evidence, moved.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a highly competent piece of dark comic fantasy that executes the brief with unusual precision. The courtroom farce is well-constructed: the bailiff's mispronunciations ("Furst Luff versus Morrow"), the bureaucratic dream-logic ("Category Two consensual almost-kiss protocol"), and the gallery of anxious dreams (Teeth-Falling-Out dreams shifting self-consciously) all land the understated, droll tone requested. Dream's characterization is a particular strength. His irritation is conveyed through economical beats—the "particular stillness," the silence that "conveyed disapproval more completely than speech," the "idea of amusement, denied entry." The mischief in the resolution is exactly as specified: the visitation rights ruling, the order that First Love add "a hand-hold of substance," and the threat of "three centuries in the dreams of tax attorneys who have begun jogging" are all genuinely funny and in character. Mora is the standout: her cross-examination of Max ("And fascinated?") is a sharp piece of courtroom writing that earns her defense rather than merely asserting it. First Love is slightly thinner but serviceable as the flustered opposing counsel. Max's testimony is well-judged—adolescent inarticulacy rendered without condescension. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally reaches for aphorism and misses ("The silence went on long enough that several people in the gallery became old enough to regret things" is clever but strained). Some jokes are a touch over-explained ("It was not amusement. It was perhaps the idea of amusement"—though this one works). The ending's "not admissible as evidence" mouth-movement is a slightly pat callback. The piece runs somewhat past the seed length, though not egregiously. A few of the descriptive constructions ("assembled from pressed flowers, awkward silences, and the memory of nearly touching someone's hand in a cinema") flirt with preciousness, though they mostly stay on the right side of it. The emotional complexity is real: the piece treats adolescent fear/desire entanglement with genuine intelligence rather than just snickering at it, and Dream's ruling acknowledges that complexity diegetically. The darkness (breath-feeding, paralysis, predation) is never softened into harmlessness, and the lightness is earned by character and situation rather than by winking at the reader. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 81.3
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The moon rises swollen and red above the Carpathian ridges, staining the snowless peaks and black fir forests with the color of opened veins. Wolves howl in the distance at irregular intervals—sometimes one, sometimes three at once, sometimes silence long enough to make the next cry feel like a warning rather than an animal sound. The old road below the mountain pass lies empty except for a wrecked coach, its wheels broken, its horses dead, and the men who rode with it hanging in pieces from the pine branches. Yennefer of Vengerberg stands in the middle of the carnage with her hands folded into her sleeves, expression unimpressed. “It’s almost insulting,” she murmurs to the corpses. “If one is going to stage an ambush, one ought to survive long enough to make it memorable.” Lilac and gooseberries cut strangely through the smell of blood and wet earth. A purple spark crackles between her fingers, then dies. She studies the torn bodies, the manner of dismemberment, the drag marks, the absence of any ordinary feeding pattern. Not a ghoul. Not a katakan. Not anything she knows well enough to name, which irritates her. Behind her, a voice emerges from the darkness like velvet drawn over a knife. “And yet,” it says, “you stayed.” She does not turn at once. To whirl around would be to admit surprise, and Yennefer dislikes giving anything away for free. When she finally faces him, she finds a tall man in a red coat standing on the road as though he has stepped out of some feverish nobleman’s nightmare. Hat low. Orange lenses glowing in the moonlight. Hands gloved. Smile wrong. He should not belong in this century. He does not appear to belong to the human race. Yennefer’s eyes narrow. “You dress like a lunatic.” Alucard’s grin widens. “And you smell enchanting.” Her lip curls. “That line has probably worked on village girls.” “I’ve never needed lines.” The wolves howl again, farther off now, as if retreating from the pass. Yennefer feels the pressure of him before she fully measures it: ancient hunger held in the shape of a man, obscene vitality, a density of violence that presses against her senses. Vampire, certainly—but not like the higher vampires she has heard about in fragmented accounts, and not like the lesser creatures witchers dissect. There is something excessive about him, as though death itself found restraint tedious and made him instead. Alucard studies her with equal interest. She is beautiful in the way forged steel is beautiful: deliberately made, sharpened by suffering, expensive to touch. Magic clings to her skin like a second atmosphere, disciplined and dangerous. Not a peasant hedge-witch. Not prey. “How many did you kill?” Yennefer asks. “All of them.” “Why?” He lifts one shoulder. “They were there.” She almost laughs. “Refreshingly honest.” His gaze slips to the bodies in the trees. “You were expecting something else.” “I was tracking a thing that has been emptying crypts, murdering merchants, and leaving priests to invent explanations. Now I find you standing in its place.” Her voice cools further. “Convenient.” “Ah.” He takes one leisurely step closer. “So now we circle the tiresome question. Am I the monster you seek?” “I haven’t decided.” “No?” His teeth flash white. “Decide quickly.” The threat lands between them, but so does invitation. Yennefer raises one hand, and violet light blooms around her fingers. The air warps. Dust and blood begin to tremble on the road. “You first.” For an instant neither moves. Then Alucard vanishes. Not vanishes—moves too fast for ordinary sight. Yennefer throws up a shield on instinct. A heartbeat later a gloved hand slams against the invisible barrier inches from her throat. The impact rings like struck glass. Black shadows pour from beneath his coat, hounds’ shapes and human hands and darkness with eyes. Her shield buckles. She answers with a burst of force that detonates between them. The mountain pass lights blue-white. Alucard is thrown backward through the remains of the coach, wood exploding around him. Before the debris lands, he rises from it laughing. “Oh, marvelous.” His pistols appear in his hands as if conjured from the night itself. The guns are grotesque, oversized, engraved. Yennefer sees the muzzles swing toward her and teleports a body-length to the side just as thunder tears the road open where she stood. Silver fragments and stone spray across her skirts. “You use firearms,” she says, disgusted. “I use whatever kills.” “Crude.” “And you use vanity as architecture.” That earns him a smile as sharp as any blade. Yennefer flicks her wrist. A stream of fire whips toward him, twisting like a living serpent. Alucard allows it to strike him full in the chest. Flames engulf his red coat. Burned flesh blackens, splits, peels—and then crawls backward over itself, knitting whole before the fire has fully died. Yennefer’s fascination spikes despite herself. He notices. Of course he notices. “Yes,” Alucard says softly. “Go on. Look.” She hates that command because some part of her obeys it. She has spent years among mages and kings and monsters disguised as statesmen, and still she has rarely seen anything this indecently immortal. His body does not merely survive damage; it treats annihilation as inconvenience. There is pride in him, but also a kind of weariness so old it has curdled into amusement. “What are you?” she asks. His laughter quiets. “A man.” She glances at the torn corpses overhead. “No.” His smile becomes colder. “A monster, then. Are you more comfortable with honest words?” Yennefer takes another step, not back but forward. “Honesty is overrated. Accuracy matters more.” The wolves cry again, now from several directions, a ragged chorus under the red moon. Alucard lowers one pistol a fraction. “And what are you, sorceress? A miracle of correction? A masterpiece purchased with pain? You wear transformation better than most.” For a moment the pass goes very still. Very few people can look at Yennefer and perceive what was remade, what was taken, what was exchanged in blood and magic and ambition. Fewer still would dare mention it. Violet power ripples around her like storm heat. “Careful.” He leans into the warning. “Or what?” She stops pretending she is not angry. The spell she casts is old, elegant, and vicious. Chains of light erupt from the ground and the air together, winding around Alucard’s limbs, throat, torso, pinning him in a lattice of runes. The road groans under the force of it. For the first time his expression shifts—not to fear, but to delight so intense it looks almost reverent. “There,” he whispers. “There you are.” He pulls. The chains tighten, crack, shatter one by one. Black blood runs from his wrists; wolves made of shadow spill from his body and devour the fragments of light. He steps out of the ruined spell with the lazy inevitability of an avalanche. Yennefer teleports again, appearing behind him, palm raised to break his spine with a concentrated blast. His hand catches her wrist before the spell releases. Too fast. His grip is iron wrapped in courtly patience. Up close he smells not of rot but of gunpowder, old stone, and the copper edge of fresh blood. She suppresses the instinctive recoil. He lowers his head slightly, studying her face through orange lenses. “If I wanted you dead, sorceress, you would be.” “And if I believed that,” she says, voice silk over steel, “I’d be a fool.” For one charged second they remain like that: her captured wrist, his hand around it, both balanced on the knife-edge between seduction and murder. Then Yennefer smiles. Lightning explodes from her free hand straight into his chest. Alucard’s body convulses. The force tears a crater in the road and sends him sprawling across the stones in a storm of ozone and shattered pine needles. By the time the echoes die, he is already rising, smoke rolling off him, grin returned and wider than before. Yennefer flexes the wrist he held. “You were saying?” He removes his hat with a flourish and lets the red moon shine fully on his face. In his eyes she sees abyssal hunger, but also recognition—the rare pleasure of finding something neither fragile nor dull. “Merely,” he says, “that medieval Europe is less disappointing tonight than usual.” She almost answers with another insult, but movement catches her attention: shapes in the tree line. Not wolves. Too upright. Too many eyes. Pale things crawling from the dark, drawn by blood and magic. Grave-feeders, half-feral necrophages, and among them something larger, stitched from corpse parts and cemetery spite. The true source of the crypt desecrations has followed the scent of slaughter to this pass. Alucard glances toward them and sighs theatrically. “Interruption is such a vulgar habit.” Yennefer’s violet eyes gleam. “Try not to get in my way.” He bares his teeth. “Try to keep up.” Then they move at once, not together and not opposed, but in that more dangerous arrangement where each intends to dominate the field and neither is willing to concede the other the pleasure. The wolves’ howls stitch the night as gunfire roars, sorcery burns, and under the blood moon a vampire and a sorceress carve open the dark while already wondering which of them will blink first when the real contest resumes.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong crossover piece that captures both characters effectively. The prose is controlled and atmospheric, with the present-tense third-person instruction followed precisely. The word count lands close to the ~1000 target. Strengths: The power dynamic shifts constantly as requested — Yennefer and Alucard trade dominance through dialogue, spells, and physical positioning, and neither capitulates. Both characters are voiced well: Alucard's theatrical menace and death-weariness ("There you are" when she binds him, his delight at being challenged) and Yennefer's sarcasm, pride, and buried vulnerability (his perceiving her transformation lands as a genuine threat, and the story shows her rage without over-explaining it). The dialogue is sharp and in-character throughout — "You dress like a lunatic" / "And you smell enchanting" is efficient characterization for both. The imagery is vivid without tipping into excess: the blood moon, the wrecked coach, the shadow hounds. The ending's interruption by necrophages is a clever way to defer resolution while implying a continuing contest, matching the prompt's "neither willing to show weakness first." Weaknesses: The piece leans on familiar beats — the standoff, the "if I wanted you dead" moment, the mutual almost-respect — which are genre staples rather than fresh inventions. Some lines flirt with over-polish ("beautiful in the way forged steel is beautiful: deliberately made, sharpened by suffering, expensive to touch"), and a few aphoristic constructions ("velvet drawn over a knife," "silk over steel") are well-worn. The necrophage climax is somewhat convenient and the ending is more a pause than a resolution, though that suits the brief. Occasional tell-y narration ("She hates that command because some part of her obeys it") is mostly earned by interiority. Minor: Alucard's pistols and silver bullets are canon-accurate, but the "medieval Europe" setting makes firearms slightly anachronistic — though this is arguably a deliberate crossover quirk and Hellsing canon is loose on this. Overall the piece is coherent, engaging, tonally consistent, and does justice to both source characters. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 79.3
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
The prison squats at the edge of nowhere, a concrete ulcer ringed with chain-link, floodlights, and wards painted in ash and blood. It is the kind of place built by people who have seen too much and decided the answer is thicker walls. Officially, it does not exist. Unofficially, it houses things too strange for courtrooms and too dangerous for graves. Jolyne Cujoh hates it on sight. The air tastes wrong, metallic and humid, like a storm trapped indoors. Somewhere down the corridor, a man laughs and keeps laughing long after it stops sounding human. Fluorescent lights buzz overhead. The guards wear black uniforms without insignias, and every third door has old sutras nailed into the frame beneath steel bolts. Jolyne walks between two escorts with her wrists cuffed in front of her, chin lifted, green hair buns sharp against the gray. The butterfly tattoo on her arm peeks beneath the prison-issued sleeve. She looks like she belongs nowhere in this place, which is exactly why she survives it. “Real classy dump,” she mutters. “What, regular prison not creepy enough for you bastards?” Neither guard answers. At the intersection ahead, another figure waits as if she owns the hallway. Young woman. Neat black coat over white shirt. Auburn hair gathered with exact, boring elegance. Smile gentle enough to go on a recruitment poster. But the eyes stop Jolyne cold for half a second—yellow irises with concentric rings, like targets painted on glass. Makima. Jolyne doesn’t know her name yet, but instinctively, she dislikes her. The security camera above the intersection gives a sharp electronic whine. Its red indicator flickers, dies, returns, then dies again. One of the guards glances up and swallows. Rumor confirmed, Jolyne thinks. Cute. “Ah,” the woman says softly, stepping forward. “So this is Jolyne Cujoh.” Her voice is warm in the way a blanket can be warm over a corpse. The guards straighten. One actually lowers his head. “She’s under intake review, ma’am,” he says. Makima smiles at him. “Thank you. Leave us.” The order is quiet. Absolute. The guards hesitate only long enough to look ashamed of hesitating, then move away. Jolyne watches them go and clicks her tongue. “Seriously? That’s all it takes? You say jump, they ask how high?” Makima folds her hands before her. “People are relieved when someone else carries the burden of decision.” “Yeah? I call that being a sucker.” Makima’s eyes rest on Jolyne’s cuffs, then lift to her face. “I’ve read about you. Assault. Escape attempts. Destruction of property. Repeated insubordination. Deep attachment to a very small circle of people.” Jolyne smirks. “What, you make a hobby out of reading inmate files?” “I make a hobby out of understanding what stands before me.” That word catches. Stands. Jolyne’s expression does not change, but every muscle in her shoulders tightens. “You got some weird prison psych profile that says I’m a pain in the ass, congratulations.” Makima tilts her head. “Stone Free. A fascinating ability. Conversion of the body into string, partial or complete. Enhanced close-range combat. Sensory transmission through thread. Flexible, elegant. Very human.” For one ugly second, the corridor seems narrower. Jolyne’s cuffs clink as her fingers flex. “Who told you that?” Makima does not answer directly. “This facility attracts unusual talents. Curses. contracts. manifestations of will. I was curious which category you belong to.” “None of your damn business.” “No,” Makima says. “But it will become my business.” The camera overhead spits sparks. The feed monitor at the guard station around the corner pops with static. Somewhere nearby, an alarm chirps once and chokes itself silent. Jolyne stares at Makima’s smile and feels the same thing she feels around venomous animals at the zoo: the certainty that the glass is there for everyone else, not for the thing inside. She lets a thread slide from her fingertip, thin as hair, ghosting along the floor. Stone Free unravels in secret, feeding her the vibration of the corridor. Two guards at the corner. One nurse cart farther down. Three heartbeats in nearby cells. And Makima, standing impossibly still, heartbeat calm and steady, not a shred of tension in her posture. Like she already knows how this goes. “You’re not staff,” Jolyne says. Makima’s smile widens a fraction. “Observant.” “Then what the hell are you?” “A civil servant.” Jolyne laughs, sharp and joyless. “Bullshit.” Makima steps closer. She does not loom. She does not need to. Her politeness enters Jolyne’s space with the confidence of something that has never once been denied. “I help manage dangerous beings,” Makima says. “Some need direction. Some need affection. Some need a leash.” The word lands like a slap. Jolyne’s eyes narrow. “Try putting one on me and lose a hand.” “That spirit is admirable.” Makima studies her with open interest, like she’s examining a rare specimen. “You resist quickly. Most people want to be reassured before they realize they’re being cornered.” “Lady, you were cornering me the second you smiled.” For the first time, Makima looks genuinely pleased. “You really are different.” The thread on the floor reaches the corner, hooks around a metal table leg, and catches the tremor of movement. The guards are not leaving. They are waiting for instructions. Of course they are. Jolyne slowly raises her cuffed hands. “Let me guess. You’ve got this whole place wrapped around your finger.” “A prison is just another arrangement of obedience,” Makima says. “Bars are inefficient. Fear and devotion are much better.” “Devotion,” Jolyne repeats. “That what you call it when everybody acts brain-dead around you?” Makima’s expression stays soft. “You say that because you still believe choice is sacred. It’s an appealing belief.” “And you don’t?” “I believe most people are happiest when used correctly.” The air goes cold. There it is, Jolyne thinks. Not the fake sweetness. The thing under it. Not rage. Not sadism exactly. Worse. Certainty. A memory flashes: other inmates with dead eyes, corrupt authority smiling while lives get crushed, people deciding your future because they can. Jolyne has spent too long caged by systems built by bastards not to recognize one standing upright in a nice coat. Stone Free coils under her skin. Makima notices. “You’re preparing to attack.” “You’re preparing to own the room,” Jolyne shoots back. “Difference is, I’m honest about it.” A small sound comes from behind them. One of the cell doors across the hall rattles. An inmate presses his face to the reinforced window, staring at Makima like a starving man staring at meat or a saint. Hard to tell which. He begins mumbling, “Miss, miss, miss—” Makima does not even look at him. “Kneel.” The inmate drops out of sight with a thud. Jolyne’s stomach turns, not from fear but from disgust so immediate it almost tastes sweet. “What the fuck.” Makima finally glances toward the door. “He’s easier this way.” “You didn’t ask.” “I didn’t need to.” Jolyne moves. Stone Free bursts from her arms in a whip-crack bloom of string, shredding the cuffs apart. She lunges, fist driving straight for Makima’s face. Fast, direct, enough force to crack bone. Makima shifts half a step. The punch grazes her cheek instead of crushing it. Skin splits. Blood beads, bright and delicate. At the same instant, the two waiting guards round the corner with weapons raised. Jolyne’s threads snap out behind her, tangling one gun barrel, yanking it aside as it fires. The shot blasts sparks from the wall. She ducks, twists, and Stone Free hammers the second guard in the sternum hard enough to fold him. The first gets his own rifle slung around his neck by a string loop and slammed into the floor. By the time the echoes die, Makima has touched the blood on her cheek with one finger. She looks at it with distant interest. Then the wound closes. Not healing exactly. More like the damage decides it happened somewhere else. Jolyne sees it and understands, in one terrible intuitive leap, that this woman is not merely dangerous. She is the kind of danger institutions are built to hide because admitting it would break people. “Immortal?” Jolyne says. Makima smiles faintly. “Close enough.” More footsteps thunder down the corridor. The cameras all spark in sequence, one after another, going blind as Makima stands in the center of the hall like the eye of a storm. Red lights die. Static hisses from hidden speakers. “Jolyne,” Makima says, almost kindly, “if you cooperate, I can offer you purpose. Protection for those you love. A useful place at my side.” Jolyne wipes blood from her knuckles onto her uniform. “You think everybody’s a dog just waiting for a collar.” Makima’s yellow eyes shine in the failing light. “Almost everybody.” Stone Free rises behind Jolyne, humanoid and fierce, string muscles taut. Jolyne grins, all teeth and contempt. “Then you’re gonna have a rough time with me.” The prison shudders with approaching boots, alarms trying and failing to wake, and the electric death-rattle of cameras that cannot bear witness. In the blind corridor, sweet voice facing raw defiance, the battle stops pretending to be about force. It becomes what it always was. Control against freedom. And Jolyne, finally seeing the shape of Makima’s hunger, knows this place is not big enough to hold both of them for long.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This crossover fic delivers a tense, well-paced confrontation between Jolyne and Makima, and it largely succeeds on the strength of its atmosphere and character work. The prison setting is established efficiently with vivid, gothic-tinged detail ("a concrete ulcer ringed with chain-link," sutras nailed under steel bolts), and the escalating dread of failing cameras and dying alarms gives the supernatural facility a coherent internal logic. Jolyne's voice is the strongest element. Her foul-mouthed defiance, instinctive distrust, and adaptability in combat are all faithful to the source. The moment she unravels a thread to scout the corridor's vibrations is a clever, canon-accurate use of Stone Free's sensory capabilities. Makima is likewise well-rendered: her soft-spoken dominance, the casual "Kneel" command to the inmate, and the blood-wound that "decides it happened somewhere else" capture her uncanny menace without over-explaining. The prose is generally controlled, with strong rhythm and a few standout lines ("warm in the way a blanket can be warm over a corpse"). However, the piece leans on a repetitive sentence structure — many paragraphs are one or two short declarative sentences ending in punchy fragments ("Makima." / "That word catches. Stands.") — which becomes a stylistic tic rather than a choice. The fragment-heavy, hardboiled cadence occasionally tips into self-consciousness, and some lines ("the certainty that the glass is there for everyone else, not for the thing inside") are effective but border on over-polished aphorism. The dialogue is the engine of the piece and mostly crackles, though Makima's lines occasionally state her philosophy too explicitly ("I believe most people are happiest when used correctly"), telling the reader what her behavior has already shown. The ending is appropriately ominous and thematically tidy ("Control against freedom"), though the closing paragraphs verge on announcing the theme rather than letting it land. Minor weaknesses: the fight resolves too quickly and conveniently; the guards are pure furniture; and the ~1000-word target is met, but the piece feels like the opening chapter of something rather than a complete arc, ending on a cliffhanger rather than a resolution. The "memory flashes" paragraph is the weakest — a generic summary of Jolyne's backstory that tells rather than shows. Still, this is confident, atmospheric, character-true fanfiction with genuine tension and a strong sense of both franchises' tones. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 83.4
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-███ **Object Class:** Euclid **Author:** Researcher Elias Vann, Temporal Anomalies Division **Addendum Status:** Attached personal account approved for internal review only --- I wrote this because the standard report format stopped feeling honest somewhere around the sixth note. At first, the phenomenon seemed almost flattering. I had been assigned to Site-41’s lower archival wing, where “temporal anomalies” mostly meant mislabeled clocks, recursive filing errors, and once, a manila folder that insisted it had not yet been written. I was not important enough, in my own mind, to become the center of an event. Important things happened to senior staff, field agents, people with decisive jawlines and tragic service records. I catalogued improbable objects and signed transfer forms. The first note appeared on my desk at 09:14 on a Tuesday. I left for exactly four minutes to retrieve a document from Secure Storage Room C. When I returned, there was a square of yellow paper centered on my keyboard in tight, slanted handwriting I recognized instantly as my own. **DON’T LET THEM OPEN 4B. —E.** I stood looking at it long enough for my coffee to cool in my hand. Then I laughed, quietly and without humor, because there were only two explanations that came immediately to mind: either someone in the department was playing an exceptionally specific prank, or I had written myself a note and forgotten doing so. Complicating both theories, Chamber 4B had been sealed for eleven months following the transfer of SCP-███-1, an entity whose documented methods included auditory suggestion, mimetic contamination, and the inducement of directed paranoia in personnel exposed to it for prolonged periods. I had reviewed those files. Everyone in Site-41 had. I submitted the note to Document Analysis. Ink composition matched standard Foundation stock. Pressure patterns and letter formation were consistent with my handwriting. No latent prints except mine. Security reviewed the footage from my office. At 09:13:52, the camera image distorted—horizontal tearing, a burst of static, timestamp corruption for 1.8 seconds. At 09:13:54, the image restored. The note was on my desk. No hand entered frame. No door opened. No one appeared. That was when people stopped smiling politely and began using the phrase “contained inquiry.” The second note arrived that afternoon. Again the camera failed at the precise moment of manifestation. This one was written on the back of a requisition form in a shakier hand. **You thought this was small. It isn’t. When they tell you it’s stress, don’t agree. Check Marrow’s left sleeve. —You** Dr. Marrow, my supervisor, had no idea what I was talking about when I asked to see the cuff of his lab coat. He did, however, indulge me. There was a smear of gray particulate clinging to the inner seam of his left sleeve. It tested positive for dust from Chamber 4B’s outer service corridor. Marrow’s expression changed very subtly when he heard that. Not guilt. Annoyance first, then concern. “I was present for an inspection yesterday,” he said. “You could have found that out if you had asked a normal question.” He was right, and I hated him for being right. By the end of the week, the Foundation had split into two schools of thought around me. The first believed I was the focal point of a genuine temporal displacement event. The notes, in that model, originated from a future version of myself attempting to prevent an impending containment breach. The camera glitches were side effects: localized causality interference, electromagnetic disruption, all the language people use when they are naming a mystery instead of solving it. The second school believed SCP-███-1—or an associated, as yet unidentified entity—was manipulating me psychologically. The notes, according to this theory, were not from the future but generated through memetic insertion, hallucinatory reinforcement, or direct physical placement during periods of perceptual compromise. The camera failures might have been engineered to build credibility. I was tested for chemical exposure, hypnotic susceptibility, mnemonic intrusion, sleep debt, dissociation, latent telepathic contact, and one thing a medic refused to explain to me except to say, “You’d know if this came back positive.” All results were inconclusive or negative. Then the notes started mentioning things I had not told anyone. One appeared folded beneath my hand while I was writing an incident summary. I did not see it arrive. I only felt the change in thickness under the paper. **Stop checking reflections before you enter rooms. They notice when you do that. I know about the sink. I know about what you heard in the pipes. Don’t tell Dyer. Dyer dies first.** I had, in fact, begun checking reflections. Quietly, compulsively. In polished metal, in dark monitor glass, in the narrow wired window of my office door. It was stupid behavior, the kind of superstition intelligent people invent after enough exposure to impossible things. Three nights earlier I had heard a voice in the plumbing of the staff washroom say my name in my own voice. I had filed no report. I reported that note. Then I asked for a psychiatric evaluation. Dr. Sen met with me for two hours in an observation suite with no reflective surfaces. She asked whether I believed the notes were truly from my future self. “I believed,” I told her, “that something wanted me to believe that.” She called that a healthy distinction. The fourth note was longer. It appeared during the interview itself. The suite camera glitched; Sen’s wall monitor went black for one second. When the image returned, there was a lined page on the table between us. She read it before I could stop her. **This is not enough time. If Sen reads this, ask her if she remembers the boy with the paper lungs. She won’t. She should. Elias, listen: the breach doesn’t begin in 4B. 4B is the rehearsal. It begins when they evacuate 7. Do not let them move the mirrors. Whatever says it’s me by then, it isn’t.** Dr. Sen did not remember any “boy with paper lungs.” No such case existed in Foundation archives. Site-41 had no Sector 7 requiring mirror relocation. We did, however, have Storage Wing 7, which contained no mirrors whatsoever. That contradiction should have comforted me. Instead it frightened me more than the accurate details had. Because if the notes were fraudulent, they were becoming sloppy. If they were genuine, then reality itself might have been changing under our feet. A task force was assembled to test the temporal hypothesis. My office was stripped and rebuilt as a controlled environment. Pressure-sensitive flooring, redundant analog and digital surveillance, electromagnetic shielding, motion detection, continuous observation by two staff members rotating every thirty minutes. My hands were kept visible whenever possible. On one memorable afternoon, I was asked to sit motionless at my desk for three hours while waiting to see if my future self would interrupt the boredom. At 16:22, every camera in the room glitched simultaneously. Not just mine. Hallway feed, overhead thermal, pen camera on Observer Hale’s chest, the backup recorder mounted outside the shielding, all gone to static for 2.1 seconds. When the image returned, there were three notes on the desk. One was taped to the monitor. One was tucked inside my breast pocket. One was already unfolded in my lap. I do not remember touching any of them. The one in my lap read: **I tried all the controlled tests already. That’s why you’re there. That’s why I’m here. They keep making the room smaller by measuring it.** The one in my pocket read: **Marrow is lying but not about the dust.** The note on the monitor was nearly illegible. **When the red team gets to 4B tell them not to listen to me crying. I wasn’t in there yet when I wrote this. I mean I was. I mean—** It stopped. Observer Hale vomited into a wastebasket. Later he requested transfer. By then, command authorized limited interaction trials with SCP-███-1 under heavy shielding, on the premise that if it was responsible, some measurable response might occur when the notes were discussed in its presence. I watched through layered glass while Dr. Marrow addressed the entity. It had no stable anatomy worth describing; every report on it became metaphor under pressure. The chamber speakers crackled as Marrow asked whether it had communicated with me. For nine seconds, nothing happened. Then SCP-███-1 said, in my voice, “Which one?” The session ended immediately. I did not sleep for thirty-one hours after that. The next note was written on the inside of my own wrist. No camera saw it appear because I was in a blind corner between checkpoints, though the corridor feed glitched at 03:11 exactly as the others had. I found the words while washing my hands. **You let them ask the wrong question.** I scrubbed until my skin reddened. The ink did not smear. It faded on its own after eleven minutes. Around this time I began losing confidence in sequence. I remembered conversations that Marrow insisted had not happened. I found myself standing outside Chamber 4B twice in one day with no memory of walking there either time. Dyer—who, according to the note, died first—was reassigned off my case after I started flinching whenever he entered a room behind me. He was alive when I last saw him. I feel compelled to write that sentence because the alternative kept presenting itself in my head as a memory: Dyer on the floor beneath emergency lights, jaw moving without sound. There had been no breach. Not yet. That was the worst part. Everything remained anticipatory, hanging over us with bureaucratic patience. Every alarm test made me cold. Every mention of transfer schedules sent half the department to verify that no one was “moving mirrors,” whatever that meant. The final note arrived six days after the first. I say final because it was the last one I received before I was removed from active duty and this account was taken down under supervision. It came at 08:03, under full observation, in the controlled office, while I was reading over prior notes and trying to determine whether the handwriting had degraded over time or whether I was simply projecting desperation onto my own penmanship. The cameras glitched. When they returned, the note was not on the desk. It was in my hand. I do not remember picking it up. The paper was damp, as if carried in a closed fist for a long time. **If you are reading this then I failed to stop you from becoming me. Do not trust the notes after this one. I know I wrote that before. I know. 4B opens because you think the warning is the threat and not the mechanism. You keep following the handwriting like it belongs to you. When Marrow asks whether you want to see the footage, say no. If he shows you anyway, don’t look at the desk. Don’t look at what puts the note there.** I looked up at once. Marrow was standing on the other side of the glass, one hand on the intercom, his face pale in a way I had never seen before. Behind him, two security staff were speaking urgently over comms. Someone had triggered a containment response in the lower levels. Red lights had not yet started, but the system was preparing for them. You could feel it in the building, the shiver through ventilation and locks. Marrow entered two minutes later and asked me, very carefully, whether I wanted to see the footage. I said no. He hesitated. Then he told me Chamber 4B’s outer seal had opened without command authorization at 08:03. That was the exact moment the cameras glitched. I remember standing. I remember backing away from my own desk as if it had become an uncovered hole. I remember thinking, absurdly, that if I kept my eyes off the wood grain and the little cleared space between keyboard and blotter, then maybe causality would lose interest in me and choose someone else. I never saw the footage. Officially, this was because of prudent containment protocol and concern for my mental state. Unofficially, it was because I no longer trusted any version of myself enough to know whether refusal had been caution or obedience. I wrote this account three days later from a temporary office with no personal effects and no direct desk-facing camera. They said it was for my comfort. No more notes had appeared. That should have felt like relief. Instead it felt like the pause in a conversation when the other speaker had leaned in close enough that you could hear them breathing, and had not yet decided what to say next.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of SCP-format fiction that executes the prompt's requirements with notable skill. The first-person past-tense perspective is maintained throughout, with the notes interspersed effectively as physical artifacts rather than exposition dumps. The escalating desperation of the notes is well-modulated: from the terse, plausible "DON'T LET THEM OPEN 4B" to the genuinely incoherent final notes ("I mean I was. I mean—"), the degradation feels organic. The central ambiguity—temporal anomaly versus psychological manipulation—is handled with genuine craft. The Foundation's dual schools of thought are articulated clearly, and the piece refuses to resolve the question, which is the correct instinct. The strongest sequence is the controlled-environment test: the simultaneous glitching of every camera, the three notes appearing in impossible locations, and the note in the lap reading "They keep making the room smaller by measuring it"—a line that lands as both eerie and thematically resonant. The researcher's struggle to trust their own perception is convincingly rendered through behavioral detail: compulsively checking reflections, hearing his own voice in plumbing, standing outside 4B with no memory of walking there, the false "memory" of Dyer dead. The SCP-███-1 interaction ("Which one?" in his own voice) is a superb escalation—brief, devastating, and better than any extended description would have been. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally leans on aphoristic constructions ("the language people use when they are naming a mystery instead of solving it") that flirt with preciosity. The "boy with paper lungs" contradiction is a good beat but the surrounding explanation of why it frightened him is slightly over-explained. Dialogue is minimal and functional rather than memorable, though the format doesn't demand much of it. The ending is appropriately unresolved without feeling like a cop-out—the refusal to look at the footage, and the uncertainty about whether refusal was "caution or obedience," is a genuinely earned final note. The closing image (the pause where you can hear breathing) is evocative rather than overwrought. The piece trusts its reader, shows rather than tells in most instances (the camera glitches, the dust in the sleeve, the damp paper), and maintains tonal consistency throughout. Minor deductions for a few over-polished lines and the slight risk of the piece's self-awareness curdling into cleverness.
