+ Epistolary: The Lighthouse Keeper — Score: 83.7
Prompt:
The Lighthouse Keeper Epistolary Narrative: Write a story told entirely through a series of brief correspondences: telegrams or letters or emails between two characters. The correspondence should span several months or years, and reveal a gradually unfolding plot. Use distinct voices for each character, and include details that provide insight into their personalities and motivations. The story should build to an emotional climax, and the final letter should provide a satisfying resolution. The setting is a lighthouse keeper writing to his mother. He is working class and Scottish. He is struggling with the isolation of his posting. Write naturally and without cliches. 1000 words.
Model Output:
12 March 1978 Eilean Dubh Light Station Dear Mam, I am arrived safe, though soaked through from the transfer boat and near sick with the pitching of it. The island is no more than a black tooth in the sea. The tower stands white enough against it, but all round is rock and wind and the cries of birds that sound like folk arguing in the dark. The quarters are clean, if bare. Iron bed, table, little range, shelves with old tins left by the last man. I have polished the lens this morning under Mr Fraser’s instruction and learned the clockwork for the lamp. It is work I can do well. There is comfort in a thing that must be done in the right order. You need not fret. The pay is better than the yard and there is less chance of a crushed hand or a back gone wrong before forty. I will send money when I have my first month. If you are passing Mrs Donnelly, tell her I found the scarf she knitted in the bottom of my trunk. I laughed seeing it. Orange enough to guide ships itself. Your loving son, Alec --- 18 March 1978 8 Kirkgate, Greenock My dear Alec, Your letter came yesterday and I read it twice before putting the kettle on. Then I read it again with tea. A black tooth in the sea is a fine thing to call an island, though I wish you were on a softer bit of ground. I am glad the work suits you. You were always steadier with careful things than your brother, God rest him. Do not skip meals because there is no one there to ask if you’ve eaten. Men alone are bad for that. I’ve sent a parcel with oatcakes, two jars of jam, and your father’s old cardigan if the post office women have not laughed me out the door for the size of it. Mrs Donnelly says to wear the scarf and be grateful. She made a face when I told her what you wrote, but she was pleased all the same. I know why you chose the light. You do not need to explain it to me. Quiet can be a kindness after too much sorrow. Still, quiet has its own teeth, so write often. All my love, Mam --- 2 April 1978 Eilean Dubh Mam, The oatcakes arrived broken but no worse for that. The jam did not survive. Raspberry over everything, even my spare socks. The gulls had a feast from the paper at the door before I could sweep it. I have settled to the routine now. Wind measurements at six. Check the mechanism. Scrub salt from the panes. Record visibility. Wind again at noon, lamp at dusk. It is strange how quickly a man begins speaking aloud to himself when no answer is expected. I caught myself saying “there now” to the kettle as if it were a bairn. There is one thing on the island I like beyond the work. In a drawer under the chart table I found a small carved bird, no bigger than my thumb joint. It is made of whalebone, yellowed smooth with handling, and the wings are not spread but tucked close, as if against weather. The eye is a pinprick of black glass. Someone has worked tiny feather marks along the breast with a very patient knife. It sits in my pocket through the day. I do not know why that should help, but it does. Some nights the sea is all steel and order. Other nights it bangs at the rocks like a man locked out. Those are harder. Alec --- 10 April 1978 Greenock Dear son, I like the thought of your little bird. Keep it if no one comes claiming. A thing held by many hands can have company in it. Your grandfather carried a brass button in his pocket all through the war and called it his “spare nerve.” Men make their own medicine where they can. I have washed and re-knitted the cuff of your father’s cardigan before sending it, because moths had made a meal there. It still smells of his pipe if you put your nose to it. That may be comfort or nuisance depending on the day. You say the loud nights are harder. Then say more on them. You needn’t be brave by post for me. I have already seen what bravery costs and I’d rather have honesty. I was at the cemetery Sunday. I brought daffodils for your brother. The ground is greening up. You were right not to come if you could not bear it yet. There’s no shame in grief taking its own road. Love, Mam --- 1 June 1978 Eilean Dubh Mam, I did not answer at once because there was no clean way to say it. The hard nights are the fog ones. When the horn goes and goes, the sound comes through the walls and into the bones. It is like hearing something mournful from inside your own chest. Last Tuesday, after forty hours near without sleep, I thought I heard Jamie on the stair. Not his voice exactly. More the tread of him, the quick uneven way because of the old football knock to his knee. I opened the door and of course there was no one but wet stone and blowing white. I stood there too long in the cold because I could not make myself shut the door on what I knew was not there. I am ashamed writing this. You told me to say more, so I am saying it. Since the accident at the yard there are times I think if I had not asked him to swap shifts, if I had taken the crane run myself, if I had looked up sooner— I know all the answers. None of them help. Do not worry overmuch. I have not neglected the light. If anything I tend it like a man possessed. No ship will come to harm here for want of me. Alec --- 8 June 1978 Greenock Alec, my son, Listen carefully to me. You did not kill your brother. A snapped cable killed your brother. A foreman who hurried men in bad weather maybe helped. A yard that runs old gear till it breaks helped. But not you. Not because you swapped a shift. Not because you were young enough to think one day was like another. I have held my tongue because I thought time would do what words could not. I was wrong. So here it is plain: Jamie chose the overtime because he wanted the extra money for the motorcycle, foolish creature. He kissed my cheek at the door and said if he was lucky he’d have it by August. He was cheerful. He was not sacrificed. He was alive in his own life, making his own daft plans, till a bad machine ended them. You are not honouring him by punishing yourself on a rock. If hearing things grows worse, you must tell your supervisor or the doctor on the mainland. Men break from loneliness as surely as from falls. There is no disgrace in that either. I wish I could box your ears and hold your face both at once. Mam --- 27 August 1978 Eilean Dubh Mam, I have read your last letter many times. I kept it in the lamp room for a week and the paper smells faintly of paraffin now. There was an incident on the 19th. A trawler from Oban lost bearings in a gale after midnight. I saw her light where no light should be, much too near the west reef. The radio was failing in bursts. I kept the beam on and sounded the horn and, against instruction, burned a hand flare from the gallery when she vanished in the spray. I thought of Jamie then, but not in the old way. Just that I would not let another family get the knock at the door if I could help it. They made harbour by morning. Yesterday I had a telegram from their skipper: LIGHT KEPT US OFF THE TEETH STOP BLESS THE MAN ON IT STOP. I stood with that paper in my hand and cried like a fool. Maybe from relief. Maybe from being tired. Maybe because for the first time in months I did a thing and it did not end in blame. I have written requesting one shore leave week in October. If granted, I will come home and fix the loose gate as promised these three years. Your son, Alec --- 3 September 1978 Greenock My dear boy, I am smiling so hard my face aches. Let them call you foolish for crying if they like. Better tears than all that stony silence you’ve been swallowing. Come in October. The gate hangs like a drunk and the back window sticks. I have saved those jobs for you out of fairness and because I am not climbing ladders with this knee. I’ll make stew and a treacle tart. Mrs Donnelly will pretend not to notice if you wear the orange scarf to the shop. One more thing. I took out your brother’s last things from the hall cupboard last week. Among them was the little tin where he kept bolts and oddments. On top was a note in his writing, likely meant for no one: ASK ALEC ABOUT THE LIGHTHOUSE JOB. BETTER HIM THAN THIS RATTING YARD. He was thinking of you. Proud, I’d say. Bring your bird if you come. I want to see the face of the man who carries a bone seabird for courage and still calls himself ordinary. Love always, Mam --- 14 October 1978 Greenock Mam, I am writing from your own kitchen though you are in the front room asleep with the wireless low, because I wanted to put this down while the house is breathing round me. The leave has near undone me with goodness. The sound of cups in a cupboard. Your slippers on the linoleum. Rain on a street instead of naked sea. Today, while fixing the gate, I found myself whistling. I stopped because I did not recognise the man doing it. Thank you for Jamie’s note. I carried it in my pocket beside the bird all day. They made a strange pair: his rough pencil scrawl and that little pale carving, both saying in their fashion the same thing — go on. I have decided not to resign. That may surprise you after all my complaining, but hear me out. The island is lonely, yes. Some nights it opens a hole in me. But it is also plain. It asks what needs done and then lets a man do it. I think I need that for a while longer. Not to hide. To mend. There is a difference, and I am only just learning it. I have also spoken with Mr Fraser about rotating shorter spells and he agreed more readily than I expected. “No use having a cracked keeper,” he said, which is as close to kindness as the man gets. When I go back tomorrow I will take your parcel, the repaired cardigan, Jamie’s note, and the bird. I will keep the light. I will write. I will come home. That is the resolution, if not of all things then of enough. Your loving son, Alec
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This epistolary story about a Scottish lighthouse keeper writing to his mother is a strong piece of work that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with skill and restraint. The two voices are distinct and consistent. Alec is plain, methodical, and emotionally guarded — his prose rhythms ("Wind measurements at six. Check the mechanism. Scrub salt from the panes") mirror his need for order. The mother is warmer, wry, and gently wise ("I wish I could box your ears and hold your face both at once"), with a Scottish working-class idiom that feels authentic rather than performed. Both voices remain stable across ten letters spanning roughly seven months. The plot unfolds gradually and well: the initial posting, the hints of grief ("your brother, God rest him"), the carved bird as a coping talisman, the confession of auditory hallucinations, the revelation of the brother's death in a yard accident Alec blames himself for, the trawler rescue as a turning point, and the final decision not to resign. The telegram from the skipper ("LIGHT KEPT US OFF THE TEETH STOP") is a clever touch that uses the form itself. The discovery of Jamie's note is perhaps slightly convenient as a device, but it is set up plausibly enough and lands emotionally. The piece largely shows rather than tells. The grief is dramatized through concrete details — the tread on the stair, the uneven knee, the jam-soaked socks, the paraffin-scented letter. The mother's direct confrontation ("You did not kill your brother") is the one moment of telling, but it is earned and appropriate to the epistolary form; a mother would say it plainly. Weaknesses: the resolution is a touch tidy. The final letter explicitly names its own themes ("Not to hide. To mend. There is a difference"), which edges toward self-annotation, and "That is the resolution, if not of all things then of enough" is a writerly flourish that Alec's established plainness might not produce. The emotional arc — guilt, confession, catharsis, acceptance — is somewhat familiar in shape, and the trawler incident arrives right on schedule as narrative medicine. The mother is nearly flawless in her wisdom, which slightly flattens her. But these are minor reservations against genuinely fine execution. The prose is clean, unpretentious, and often quietly beautiful ("a black tooth in the sea," "the sea... bangs at the rocks like a man locked out"). The period detail (1978, telegrams, paraffin lamps) is consistent. The ending is hopeful but not saccharine — Alec returns to the island, acknowledging the loneliness will persist — so the positivity feels congruent with what has been earned. + First-person unique perspective: Hacker Mindset — Score: 80.5
Prompt:
Hacker Mindset Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a reformed (now) white hat hacker who cannot help but notice exploitable weaknesses in both systems and people they encounter. They habitually look for vulnerabilities and exploit vectors. The narrative takes place during a first date at a restaurant, where they're trying to focus on human connection. It's going surprisingly well due to a discovered shared nerd-fandom (magic the gathering). Things go a little sideways when the date reveals a noticeably insecure phone unlock pattern, which protagonist can't help but comment on. They are then left to negotiate the fallout of this faux pas and attempt to salvage (or perhaps sabotage) the remainder of the date. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I can’t walk into a room without threat-modeling it. Not in the dramatic, movie-montage way where code scrolls over my pupils and every lock clicks open in my imagination. It’s quieter than that. More habitual. More like a second layer of subtitles on reality. Exit signs, camera placement, point-of-sale terminals, the deadbolt on the staff door with the strike plate hanging half a screw loose, the little acrylic sign by the register that says GUEST WIFI PASSWORD: penne2024 in cheerful marker as if “password” still means anything when it’s taped to the counter for all to see. I notice. I catalog. I build attack trees for fun and by accident. Reformed, they say, as if it’s a conversion and not an ongoing maintenance problem. As if my brain got a patch and no longer defaults to exploit vectors. I’m white hat now. Consulting, audits, conference talks where I say things like security is about trust boundaries and human factors and everyone nods and writes it down because it sounds wiser than I actually feel. I disclose. I document. I ask permission. I leave systems better than I found them. People are harder. Especially across a little restaurant table under an amber pendant light, where the objective is not “enumerate vulnerabilities” but “be charming” and “ask follow-up questions” and “do not, under any circumstances, compare a person to a badly configured firewall.” I got here twelve minutes early because punctuality is one of the few social protocols I can execute without packet loss. Long enough to inspect the place in the ambient way I inspect everything. The Wi‑Fi password on the counter. The QR code menu with no domain verification. The tablet at the host stand smudged with fingerprints and left unlocked while the hostess refills water. The waiter reusing the same four-digit code to log into the payment terminal because his fingers tapped it with the weary confidence of muscle memory. A whole ecosystem of trust assumptions lacquered over with rustic décor. And then Maya walks in and all of that recedes enough for me to remember I am here for a reason other than passive reconnaissance. Okay. She is prettier than her pictures, which feels unfair in my favor, like someone undersold an asset before acquisition. No, terrible. Stop. She has that competent stride people have when they know where their body is in space. Denim jacket, black dress, silver ring on her thumb. She spots me, smiles in a way that reaches her eyes, and my pulse immediately starts behaving like a service under load. Say something normal. I stand. I do not salute. Good start. “Hey,” I say, which is operating within acceptable parameters. “Hey. Sorry, parking was chaos.” “Threat model failure in urban design,” I almost say, but reroute in time to “No worries.” We sit. Menus up like little privacy screens. The waiter appears, takes our drink order, vanishes. I am trying to remember all the advice ever given to me by better-adjusted friends. Ask open-ended questions. Listen for understanding, not merely response latency. Don’t monologue. Don’t perform. Don’t mention cybercrime in the first seven minutes. Maya saves me from myself by asking what I actually do all day, and I give her the cleaned-up version. Security assessments. Resilience testing. Helping companies find the holes before someone worse does. I can hear how ominous that sounds and add, lightly, “Legally. These days.” “These days?” she says, and there is the tiniest spark in her grin. There are moments where honesty is a risk worth taking. “I was an idiot with a terminal and poor impulse control in my twenties.” “Only in your twenties?” I laugh, surprised into it. Good. Humor handshake established. It goes better from there. More than better, actually. She works in library systems, which means she is exactly the kind of person who can make metadata sound heroic. She tells a story about migrating a county archive off a catastrophically old database and I fall a little in love with the phrase catastrophically old database in her mouth. Then somehow—beautifully, improbably—we hit Magic: The Gathering. Not just “oh yeah, I played in college” Magic. Not “I know what a planeswalker is” Magic. Actual, dangerous, specific Magic. Commander salt levels. Draft archetypes. The moral legitimacy of counterspells. The fact that she once built a deeply annoying blue-black deck “as a social experiment,” which is both hilarious and a mild red flag in exactly the way I appreciate. “Okay, but answer carefully,” she says, leaning in. “Do you destroy Sol Rings on sight, or do you let people have their happiness for one turn?” “Depends,” I say. “Are we talking table politics or optimization?” Her eyes light up. “Optimization.” “Then happiness is an attack surface.” She laughs hard enough that the couple at the next table glances over. There it is, that little endorphin burst, reward circuitry lighting up because a line landed. Human connection through shared cardboard neuroses. This I can do. This I understand. Structure, rules text, mana curves. A game where everyone admits they are trying to outmaneuver each other and the social contract is explicit enough to parse. We order. Pasta for her, salmon for me. The waiter leaves. We are now in the warm middle phase of a date where possibility starts to feel less theoretical. She tells me about her cat, who is named after a fantasy novelist but behaves like a tax auditor. I tell her about the time I had to explain to a CEO why “password123!” was not transformed into a good password by the addition of punctuation. She snorts water through her nose. I apologize while secretly treasuring the moment because it means she is relaxed. This is going well. This is going so well. And then her phone buzzes. It’s faceup on the table, because of course it is. A bright rectangle of modern compulsion. She glances at the notification and says, “Sorry, my sister,” with the automatic guilt reflex of our age, and picks it up. I look away because I am not a monster. Which would be easier if my peripheral vision weren’t trained like a heat-seeking missile for exactly this class of event. She unlocks the phone with a pattern. Not just a pattern. A pattern. A simple corner-to-corner shape, visible in one smooth movement, with the kind of greasy screen residue that probably reproduces it from orbit. An L-shape with a flourish. I catch it in less than a second, not because I’m trying to steal it but because my brain flags weak authentication the way some people notice off-key singing. It is immediate and involuntary and accompanied by a full internal advisory bulletin. No no no no. Do not say anything. You are on a date, not in an awareness training seminar. She types a quick reply, sets the phone down, and keeps talking about—something about a local game store opening a new Commander night—but I am only half processing because a whole section of my cortex is vibrating at the insecurity of what I just saw. Pattern unlocks are bad enough. Simple visible pattern unlocks are practically a consent form for shoulder surfing. Combined with the smudge trail? Combined with the fact that her phone has probably everything on it? Banking, email, password reset vectors, social graph, two-factor intercept— Do not say anything. What I should do is let it go. This is what normal people do. They do not turn every intimate interaction into an impromptu penetration test. They do not confuse concern with compulsion. They certainly do not interrupt a flirtatious debate about whether Cyclonic Rift should be a bannable offense to critique someone’s endpoint security hygiene. I open my mouth. “That unlock pattern is really guessable.” There is a silence so sudden and complete it feels like the restaurant has lost power. I actually hear the clink of silverware from two tables over. Maya blinks at me. Once. Twice. “I’m sorry,” she says, in a tone of voice people use when they’re giving you a chance to reverse into a less stupid statement. Abort. Roll back. Patch now. “I just—” No, that’s already bad. “I noticed—” Worse. Catastrophic. “Occupational hazard,” I say, which is true and also sounds deranged. “I wasn’t trying to look.” Her face changes. Not dramatically. If I weren’t calibrated to microexpressions I might miss it. A slight withdrawal around the eyes. Her mouth flattening by a degree. Not anger, exactly. Alarm. Recalculation. She is rerunning the model of me with new data and the confidence score is dropping. “You noticed my phone password,” she says. “Pattern,” I say automatically, because apparently I am committed to dying on technical distinctions. Excellent. Bury yourself with precision. She leans back. “That’s… kind of weird.” Correct. Accurate assessment. Vulnerability confirmed. I can feel multiple response strategies presenting themselves, all flawed. Minimize. Joke. Explain. Apologize cleanly. Double down into educational concern. Pretend to receive an urgent text and launch myself bodily through the taped Wi‑Fi sign. The waiter appears at exactly the wrong moment with our food, setting plates down into the blast radius. “Can I get you anything else?” A new identity, I think. “We’re good,” Maya says, not looking at him. When he leaves, I choose honesty because it is the only tool left that isn’t also an exploit. “You’re right,” I say. “That was weird. I’m sorry. My brain catches stuff like that before I can stop it, and sometimes I mistake noticing for needing to comment. That’s not fair to you.” She studies me. I force myself not to fill the silence. Silence is where people authenticate. “I get noticing,” she says finally. “I don’t get saying it out loud on a first date.” “Neither do I, apparently.” That earns the smallest exhale through her nose. Not quite a laugh. But maybe not a total shutdown either. I continue, carefully. “For what it’s worth, I wasn’t trying to show off or make you feel stupid. It’s more like… if someone came in with their backpack unzipped and their wallet sticking out, and you spent your whole life noticing unsecured bags, your brain would scream. Mine just has terrible timing and worse social skills.” “And you think my phone is an unzipped backpack.” “I think modern phones are entire lives with glass screens.” She cuts a piece of pasta, thinking. “That was almost smooth.” “Accidental. I don’t recommend relying on it.” There. A real smile, brief but extant. System partially recovered. I let her eat before I say anything else. Important lesson from incident response: stop making changes during active instability. Inside, though, I am still triaging. Did I torpedo this? Maybe. Maybe not. There is a version of tonight where this becomes a story she tells friends—funny, exasperated, weirdly endearing. There is another where I become “that cybersecurity guy who clocked my unlock pattern over appetizers,” and honestly I would deserve it. She twirls pasta, then says, “So if my phone security is terrible, what’s the damage?” The worst possible thing for me is an opening. I take a breath. “Do you want the answer as a person who’s trying not to be insufferable, or as a person whose entire job is evaluating worst-case scenarios?” She points her fork at me. “See, this is your problem. You think those are different people.” That lands cleanly because it is true. I smile despite myself. “Fair.” She sets her fork down. “One sentence. Maximum.” I can work with constraints. Constraints are kindness. “Use a six-digit PIN or a better alphanumeric password, because visible patterns are easy to shoulder-surf and easier to reconstruct from screen smudges.” “Two sentences.” “Semicolon.” She laughs. Genuine this time. The knot in my chest loosens by a measurable percentage. “Okay,” she says. “I’ll change it. But if you quiz me on two-factor authentication before dessert, I’m leaving.” “I would never,” I say, while mentally deleting at least four pending observations about the restaurant’s payment flow. For the next ten minutes I behave. I ask about her favorite set. She says Innistrad, which is objectively defensible. I confess a weakness for artifact synergies and she accuses me, rightly, of being the sort of person who says the phrase value engine without irony. We recover the thread. Maybe not fully, maybe with a visible patch, but functional. Still, some tiny malicious goblin in the back of my head wonders if this is what sabotage looks like when you’re trying to quit it. Not attacking systems anymore, so instead you stress-test moments. Probe boundaries. Introduce failure into anything that starts to matter, just to prove you can predict the collapse. There’s a comfort in broken things. They make sense. They can be mapped. Connection is the real zero-day. No documentation. No guaranteed rollback. Every disclosure a gamble. When dessert menus arrive, Maya glances at the counter and says, “By the way, their Wi‑Fi password is literally taped up over there. Does that upset you too?” I follow her gaze to the cheerful PENNE2024 sign. She caught it. Of course she caught me catching things. “It does,” I admit. She smiles over the candle between us. “You don’t have to tell them.” I look at her, at the amused challenge in it, at the possibility she’s offering me: notice, and choose. For once, maybe that’s the harder trick. Maybe that’s the whole reform. Not losing the instinct, but deciding where it ends. So I leave the sign on the counter. I leave the host stand tablet alone. I leave her future phone settings to her. I cut into tiramisu and ask what commander she’d build if budget weren’t a constraint, and when she answers without hesitation, I listen like it’s the only signal in the room worth capturing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong, well-executed piece that hits nearly every beat of the prompt: first-person internal monologue, habitual threat-modeling, a first date at a restaurant, the MTG shared fandom, the insecure unlock pattern faux pas, and the negotiation/salvage of the aftermath. The voice is consistent and distinctive — dry, self-deprecating, technically flavored without drowning in jargon. The tech metaphors ("pulse behaving like a service under load," "silence is where people authenticate") are used with restraint and mostly land as characterization rather than showing off. The pacing is well controlled: the pre-date reconnaissance establishes the compulsion, the MTG connection earns genuine warmth, the pattern moment is a clean inciting incident, and the recovery is negotiated through dialogue rather than narration. Maya is given agency and wit ("You think those are different people"), which keeps her from being a prop. The dialogue is a highlight — natural, funny, and character-revealing, particularly the "one sentence / two sentences / semicolon" exchange. Weaknesses: the ending is slightly tidy and leans toward redemptive affirmation ("Maybe that's the whole reform") — the thematic statement is spelled out a bit too explicitly, edging toward tell-don't-show in the final paragraphs. The "tiny malicious goblin" passage gestures at sabotage but resolves it quickly and safely; the piece flirts with darker self-sabotage impulses without fully committing, which makes the recovery feel a touch frictionless. Some metaphors are near-cliché for this genre ("second layer of subtitles on reality" is fresh; "heat-seeking missile" is not). The smudge-reading detail is a well-worn trope, though it's deployed knowingly. Minor overuse of the "No. Stop. Terrible." self-interruption tic, though it's arguably voice. Overall: coherent, engaging, emotionally layered, with a consistent comic-melancholy register. The flaws are those of polish, not of competence. + First-person unique perspective: Overthinking It — Score: 60.9
Prompt:
Overthinking It Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of an intelligent 8th-grade girl with social anxiety who has developed a crush on a classmate. The narrative takes place during a group science project where they're paired together, as she cycles through rehearsed conversations while second-guessing each potential approach. Her inner thoughts should reveal the gap between her articulate internal voice and her difficulty expressing herself aloud, her fears of coming across as desperate or weird, and the exhausting process of monitoring her every word, expression, and movement for potential embarrassment. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
When Mr. Garza says, “Okay, lab groups of two,” the whole room erupts into that scraping-chair, half-yelling chaos that always makes my skin go hot. Everyone starts swiveling around and calling names and acting like this is normal and easy, like it doesn’t require an advanced strategy and three backup plans. I’m already doing the usual thing where I pretend to look calm while my brain begins sprinting in seven directions at once. Then Mr. Garza looks at the paper in his hand and says, “Maya, you’re with Eli.” I have exactly one second to react, which is one second too few. Eli. My face probably does something humiliating and visible, like widening or freezing or becoming a human stop sign. I hope not. Maybe I’ve trained myself out of obvious reactions by now. Maybe years of trying not to look weird have finally produced at least one useful skill. He glances over at me and smiles, quick and easy, like this is fine, like I am fine, like pairing with me is not some kind of social test I’m definitely going to fail. “Cool,” he says. Cool, I think back, because apparently my internal voice is a person who can answer normally. What comes out of my mouth is: “Uh—yeah.” Amazing. Incredible. A truly memorable opening. “Uh—yeah,” said in the tone of someone who has just been informed of a minor plumbing issue. I gather my notebook and pencil and move to the lab table trying to walk in a way that suggests I have walked before. Not too fast, because then I’ll look overeager. Not too slow, because then I’ll seem reluctant, which is worse, because what if he thinks I don’t want to work with him? But if I smile too much, that’s weird. Neutral pleasant. Friendly but not intense. Casual shoulders. Is there such a thing as casual shoulders or did I just invent a new thing to fail at? He sits across from me and unfolds the assignment sheet. Photosynthesis and environmental variables. We have to design a mini experiment with aquatic plants and light exposure and then present our results next week. This is actually the kind of thing I’m good at. This should be the part where I become a person who can function. I should say something first. People who are socially normal say something first. Option one: Hi. No, too late for hi. We have already crossed the threshold where hi would be natural. If I say hi now it’ll sound like my brain rebooted. Option two: So, do you want to read through it or should I? Too controlling? No, not controlling. Efficient. But also maybe weirdly formal, like I’m a substitute teacher. Option three: I think this one looks kind of interesting. Too vague. What one? We are both literally looking at the same paper and yet somehow I’d still find a way to be unclear. Option four: Have you ever done this lab before? No, because that sounds like I think he got held back, which is not only rude but insane, and now I can never say any sentence with the phrase “ever done this before” again. I am still deciding among the least bad openings when he says, “Do you want to test different light colors? That might be easier to measure.” “Yes,” I say immediately, too quickly, with enough force to suggest I have been held hostage by my own silence and finally released. He doesn’t seem to notice. “Like maybe white light versus blue and red?” I nod. Then I realize nodding without words is not ideal because it can come off as me being blank or uninterested or incapable of speech, all of which are, unfortunately, partially true at the moment. “That makes sense,” I add, aiming for intelligent and calm. Good. Fine. Actual words. Maybe this will be okay. My internal voice, meanwhile, is giving a TED Talk. It would like to note that blue and red wavelengths are more strongly associated with photosynthetic activity, and that if we keep all other variables controlled, the data could be fairly clean. It would also like to make one casual joke, something light and not overdone, maybe about our plant becoming a tiny celebrity under stage lighting. The internal version of me is witty but restrained, informed without showing off, maybe even charming in a quiet way. External me is trying not to hold the pencil like it’s a distress flare. He says, “Do you want to write, or should I?” This is dangerous. Too much depends on the answer. If I say I’ll write, then my handwriting will be visible, and what if it suddenly looks childish today for no reason? What if my hand shakes? But if I let him write, then I look passive, like I’m just sitting here contributing oxygen. Also if he writes, I’ll have to look at him more, which is a whole separate issue because eye contact has to be measured in exact fractions of a second or else I become either rude or creepy. “I can write,” I say. Not bad. Simple. Useful. “Okay,” he says, sliding the sheet toward me. I write our names at the top. His first, then mine, because that feels less self-centered, although now I’m worried that was too noticeable, like maybe only someone who had spent weird amounts of time thinking about him would consciously decide name order. Maybe normal people also think about that. Maybe no one has ever thought about that except me. Fantastic. He leans in a little and points to the procedure section. “We should probably decide how long each plant gets exposed.” He smells like laundry detergent, faintly, except underneath that there’s still this sharp ammonia scent hanging in the room from whenever the custodians cleaned up after last period. It keeps sneaking into my nose at the worst times, slicing right through my thoughts. Ammonia always smells like something too clean, if that makes sense, like cleanliness with an attitude problem. Every time I start constructing a sentence in my head, the smell barges in and wipes part of it out. Maybe thirty minutes, I think. No, say it aloud. “Maybe thirty minutes?” I manage. “Yeah, that should work.” He says it so easily. He says things and they just arrive in the air properly formed. He doesn’t seem to inspect them first from twelve angles. He doesn’t appear to think, If I suggest thirty minutes, will that sound too eager? Too arbitrary? What if he already thought thirty and now it sounds like I’m trying to impress him by agreeing first? What if thirty is wrong and I’ve revealed myself as secretly incompetent in both science and being alive? I know this is irrational. That’s one of the worst parts. I know, intellectually, that no one is analyzing me this hard because most people are busy being themselves. I know if someone else said “Maybe thirty minutes,” I would think, yes, normal sentence, thank you. But when it’s me, every word feels like it has to pass through customs. He taps the paper with the eraser end of his pencil. “Do you want to be the one who talks during the presentation, or do you want me to?” Absolutely not. Also, if I say absolutely not too quickly, then I’ll sound dramatic and incompetent and like a terrible partner. If I say “I can do it,” then I will spend the next week sick with dread and maybe die in front of the class. There must be a middle option. There is always a middle option. Find the middle option. “We could both do part of it,” I say. That is, annoyingly, a very good answer. Balanced. Cooperative. I should be proud of that, but pride is hard to access when I’m already replaying the sentence to check if my voice sounded weird on the word both. “Sure,” he says. “I’m fine with that.” Of course he is. Because he is one of those people who can just be fine with things. I write down our variables carefully, making my handwriting as neat as possible without making it obvious that I’m trying to make my handwriting neat. There’s a narrow band of acceptable effort. Too sloppy and I look careless. Too neat and I look like I care too much, which is somehow also embarrassing. Existing as a person in public is basically a nonstop calibration problem. Say something casual, I tell myself. This is your chance. Not about the project. Something normal classmates say when they are not malfunctioning. I could ask if he watched the game last night, except I did not watch the game last night and if he says something back I’ll be trapped in a conversation built on ignorance. I could mention the math quiz, but that sounds like I’m trying to be school-only interesting, which is not interesting. I could say I liked his presentation from history last week. No. No, that sounds like I have been paying specific attention to him, which I have, but the point is not to reveal that like some kind of deranged documentary narrator. I could make a joke about our plant. The tiny celebrity under stage lighting. That was good. That was actually funny in a modest, intelligent way. I open my mouth. Nothing. Not exactly nothing. More like traffic. Too many possible tones, too many outcomes. What if he laughs because it’s funny? Good, obviously. But then what if I get too pleased too fast and my face does something enormous? What if he doesn’t laugh and there’s that tiny pause where a joke dies and both people have to stand over the body pretending not to notice? What if it comes out sounding rehearsed, which it is? So instead I say, “Do you think we need three trials?” He answers right away, “Probably, yeah, just to make the data better.” And there it is again, the little stab of disappointment that comes from choosing safe over real. Safe keeps me from embarrassment, but it also keeps me from being known. Which sounds way too dramatic for lab class, except it’s true. Every time I take the safest possible sentence, I leave the better one trapped in my head, and then people meet this edited version of me made almost entirely of caution. He smiles suddenly, looking at the row of colored plastic filters in the supply bin. “If we use the red one, our plant is going to look evil.” I laugh before I can evaluate it, which is probably the most honest thing I’ve done all hour. “Like it has a secret plan,” I say. There. That one made it out. He grins. “Exactly.” And for one whole second I forget to monitor my face. I forget my hands and my posture and whether my voice was the right volume. I’m just there, at the table, with the ammonia smell fading into the background and the paper between us and a stupid joke about an evil plant hanging in the air, and it feels weirdly simple. Then of course I ruin it by thinking about it. Did I laugh too loud? Was “secret plan” too much? Should I have stopped at “yeah”? Was I leaning forward weirdly? Do I look too happy now? Fix your face. Not too much. Relax your shoulders. Casual shoulders. There it is again, the impossible assignment. But still. He’s writing down materials now, and I’m filling in the hypothesis, and every so often one of us says something and the other answers, and even though each sentence still has to drag itself past my internal security system, they are at least happening. Not the perfect ones. Not the ones from inside my head, polished and effortless and bright. Just the real ones, awkward and ordinary and enough to keep the conversation alive. Maybe that counts for something. Maybe overthinking everything doesn’t actually save me from embarrassment as much as it just guarantees I experience it in advance, over and over, like a preview nobody asked for. I write, If aquatic plants are exposed to different light colors, then plants under blue and red light will produce more oxygen bubbles than plants under white light, and Eli says, “That sounds good,” and I say, “Okay,” except this time okay comes out like an actual word a normal person might say. Which, for today, feels almost enormous.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a very specific brief: an internal-monologue-heavy first-person narrative about an anxious, intelligent 8th grader navigating a crush during a lab pairing. The prompt's requirements are nearly all fulfilled: the gap between articulate inner voice and halting speech is dramatized repeatedly and well; the rehearsed-conversation cycling (the numbered "options") directly enacts the second-guessing; the self-monitoring of face, shoulders, handwriting, and word choice is pervasive; and the piece stays almost entirely in internal monologue. The voice is the standout. The narrator's wit ("casual shoulders," "contributing oxygen," "every word feels like it has to pass through customs") is genuinely funny and character-consistent, and the humor feels like authentic anxious overcompensation rather than authorial showing off. The "TED Talk" internal voice vs. the "distress flare" pencil grip is an excellent concrete rendering of the articulate-inside/inarticulate-outside gap. The narrative arc is modest but earned. The evil-plant joke exchange provides a small, believable moment of connection, and the narrator's immediate relapse into self-monitoring afterward is psychologically truthful — this avoids an unearned transformation. The ending's mild hopefulness ("feels almost enormous") is calibrated to the character's scale of difficulty, so it doesn't feel incongruent. The closing insight about experiencing embarrassment "in advance, like a preview nobody asked for" is a strong, earned thematic statement. Weaknesses: The ammonia-smell detail is odd — it's introduced with emphasis but never pays off beyond a couple of mentions; it reads like an injected sensory beat rather than an organic element. Some of the option-cycling runs slightly long and repetitive in the middle, though repetition is arguably the point. The piece is a touch safe and familiar in its beats — the anxious-crush-lab scenario resolves almost exactly as expected, with the small joke breakthrough and gentle uplift. Eli is thin, functioning mostly as a kind, uncomplicated foil; he has no texture beyond "easygoing." The prose occasionally leans on the same rhetorical rhythm (self-correction, "No, because...") enough that it becomes a tic. Dialogue is minimal but serviceable and natural for the setting. Overall this is skilled, controlled, voice-driven writing with minor structural padding and a slightly predictable shape. + First-person unique perspective: Rehearsing Rejection — Score: 62.5
Prompt:
Rehearsing Rejection Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of someone with borderline personality disorder who frequently plays out worst-case scenarios of how friends and loved ones might judge them. They construct elaborate internal dialogues, complete with imagined criticisms and their own defensive responses. The narrative takes place as they prepare to meet a close friend & recent lover, who has been somewhat distant lately, triggering their abandonment fears. Their inner monologue should reveal how they cycle between anticipating rejection, mentally rehearsing confrontations, and developing preemptive resentments as protective measures. Incorporate the *actual* events & interactions that are *not* in fact judgemental or involving rejection (in fact, the opposite), and represent how these are interpreted, how the validation & love is desperately felt & needed -- and then immediately questioned. Capture the cognitive dissonance in this struggle. Include moments where they briefly recognize the pattern but struggle to interrupt it, showing limited (and selective) self awareness, competing with the compelling nature of these imagined scenarios. Write almost entirely in internal monologue. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I start getting ready an hour too early, which is what I call preparedness and what my therapist calls escalation. If I leave too much room before seeing someone, especially someone who matters, the time fills itself. It breeds. Every minute generates three more possible versions of what might happen, and each one gets worse in the retelling. He texted this morning: **Still good for tonight? Looking forward to seeing you.** Normal text. Warm, even. There was a heart on the end, not even the red one, the stupid soft pink one that somehow feels more earnest. I stared at it for ten minutes because if he was looking forward to seeing me, why has he been distant all week? Why did it take him two hours to answer me yesterday? Why did his “sorry, long day” feel copied from a script written for someone you don’t want but don’t know how to stop being kind to? I know. I know how that sounds. Two things can be true, allegedly: he can be tired and he can love me. He can answer late and not be leaving. But my brain is not interested in coexistence. My brain likes verdicts. So I put on one shirt, then another, then the first one again, because if he looks at me and there’s even a flicker—if his face does that infinitesimal shift people do when they’re disappointed but trying to be decent—I want to have at least chosen correctly. Not that there is a correct choice. There is only minimizing evidence. He’s going to say, I think we moved too fast. No, more likely: I care about you, but lately it’s felt intense. Or the cleaner version, the one that hurts because it sounds responsible: I don’t think I can give you what you need. I practice my face in the bathroom mirror, but on the way back through the hallway I catch myself in the long narrow mirror by the coat rack. My shoulders are up near my ears. My hand is twisted in the hem of my shirt so tightly it makes the fabric pucker. I look like someone waiting outside the principal’s office. I look guilty, pre-rejected. I turn away fast, as if being seen by myself is its own humiliation. Okay, so if he says, this is too much, I’ll say, “You knew who I was from the beginning.” No, too accusing. Better: “You don’t have to make me into a problem just because your feelings changed.” That’s good. Calm, sharp. Then if he backpedals and says no, it’s not that, I’ll say, “You’ve been distant. I’m not imagining that.” Which I’m not. I’m not imagining the distance. I’m only imagining the meaning, the motive, the inevitable outcome. Important distinction. Supposedly. I pick up my phone to check whether he’s texted again and there’s an old message still visible from three nights ago: **Made it home. Thanks for tonight. I feel really close to you.** That should help. It doesn’t help. It almost makes it worse, because if he felt close to me then and is pulling away now, then something changed. And if something changed, it was probably because I did too much. Said too much. Wanted too visibly. Needing is always the crime scene, and I am always covered in fingerprints. He said “I miss you” on Monday. People who are planning to leave don’t say that. Yes they do, my mind answers immediately. People say all kinds of tender things while they’re halfway out the door. People say nice things because they don’t want to be the villain. People soften the blow in advance. You are doing it again. I actually think that in a voice that sounds almost sane, almost not mine. You are building a courtroom before the person has even arrived. You are writing his testimony and yours and pretending this is intuition. For maybe five seconds, I can see the mechanism exposed. The gears. The old panic dressed as foresight. If I expect the worst, I can’t be ambushed by it. If I accuse him silently first, then I’m not the one standing there empty-handed when he decides I’m too much. Then the five seconds pass, and I think, or maybe this time it’s just true. I replay the last time I saw him. He brushed my hair back from my face in that absentminded gentle way that almost hurts because it’s not performance, and when I made that joke about being difficult he frowned and said, “Hey. Don’t do that to yourself.” He kissed my forehead. He held me afterward like he was in no rush to become separate. He asked me to text when I got home. These are not rejection behaviors. These are, objectively, if anyone else told me this story, signs of care. But care is slippery. Care can evaporate. Care can be genuine and temporary, and temporary feels like a trick even when nobody meant it as one. Maybe he was already doubting and trying to be nice. Maybe he could feel me wanting reassurance and gave it to me because I’m pathetic when I’m hungry like that, because it’s embarrassing how quickly one kind word can straighten my spine. There is something disgusting about how much I need softness. One hand at the back of my neck and suddenly I’m devoted, suddenly I’m safe, suddenly all the alarms pause and I could cry from gratitude. Then, immediately, I hate him a little for having that power. Then I hate myself more for handing it over. I put on earrings and take them off. Too much. Trying too hard. If I look too good, he’ll think I’m manipulative; if I look too casual, he’ll think I don’t care. He won’t think either of these things. He’ll probably just say I look nice, and I’ll feel flooded and suspicious at once. I can hear it already. “You look nice.” You say that to everyone. “No, I don’t.” You’re being careful with me because you know I’m unstable. “I’m not—” See? You hesitated. I do this all the time: build a tiny theater in my head where he says his lines wrong and I still punish him for them. I cross-examine imaginary tenderness until it confesses to fraud. Last night he called, just for ten minutes, because he was exhausted and had to be up early. “I wanted to hear your voice,” he said. I let that warm me for exactly one breath before thinking, He’s doing maintenance. Keeping me calm until he can do this in person. But then why ask how my meeting went, remember the name of my coworker, laugh at the dumb story about the grocery store, say “I’m proud of you” when I told him I spoke up? Why sound soft in that particular way that makes my chest ache? Because maybe he loves me. That thought comes in quietly, almost shy. It is the most dangerous thought of all. Rejection hurts, but hope dismembers. If I let myself believe he loves me, then every delayed text becomes a referendum, every shift in tone a collapse. Better to stay braced. Better to call him selfish in my head, inattentive, cowardly, before he has the chance to become the judge and I become the one awaiting sentence. Resentment is such efficient armor. It keeps the pleading out of my voice. Except not really. It just makes me brittle. I sit on the bed and unlock my phone again. Another text: **Running a few minutes late, traffic. I’m sorry. Bring your sweater if you want, it’s cold out.** My stomach drops so hard it’s almost comical. Late. Of course. This is how it starts. Delays become cancellations become distance with explanations become “you deserve someone better” which is just a polite translation of I am relieved to be rid of you. He said he was sorry. He told you to bring a sweater because he knows you get cold. Controlling, another part of me snaps back. Performatively considerate. Bare minimum disguised as intimacy. That is insane, and I know it is insane, and still the accusation blooms because it feels better than helplessness. Anger has edges. Fear is just falling. I type **No worries** and erase it because that sounds too eager. I type **Okay** and erase it because that sounds mad. I type **Drive safe** and stare at it until it looks unbearably sincere. I send it anyway, then hate that my care always leaks through the cracks no matter how strategically I arrange myself. Maybe tonight I’ll be normal. Maybe I’ll walk in and see his face light up—not politely, not dutifully, but genuinely, the way it has before—and I’ll just let it happen. Maybe when he touches my back I won’t immediately scan for pity. Maybe if he says, “I missed you,” I won’t hear, for now appended invisibly at the end. Or maybe I will. Probably I will. I can know the pattern and still kneel before it. I can name the distortion while it distorts. I can even feel, under all of it, the plain small truth: I want to be loved without having to litigate it. My phone buzzes again. **Parking now. Take your time. No rush.** No rush. See, a healthy person would read that as kindness. Spaciousness. A close friend waiting downstairs, someone who has held me and kissed me and remembered my coffee order and the story about my father and the exact spot under my shoulder blade that knots when I’m tense. Someone who is here. I read it as dangerous generosity. As if he already knows I’m a lot. As if he’s preparing to manage me. Then, traitorously, another feeling rises, immediate and raw: relief so intense it almost buckles me. He came. He’s here. He didn’t disappear while I was dressing for my own execution. I grab my sweater. My hand is shaking. In another life maybe that would mean excitement uncomplicated by dread. In this one, they are the same sensation until proven otherwise. I head for the door, already composing responses to injuries that have not occurred, already hungry for the look on his face that might silence every invented line for one blessed minute, already preparing not to believe it when it does.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of interiority-driven fiction. The narrative stays almost entirely in internal monologue as instructed, cycling convincingly between anticipated rejection, rehearsed confrontation, and preemptive resentment ("Resentment is such efficient armor"). The imagined dialogues are vivid and self-sabotaging, and the moments of partial self-awareness ("You are building a courtroom before the person has even arrived") are well executed, with the narrator recognizing the pattern and failing to interrupt it. The actual events (texts, the phone call, "Parking now. Take your time") are consistently warm and non-judgmental, and the piece renders the desperate hunger for validation followed by immediate suspicion with real fidelity to BPD cognition. The dissonance is captured in lines like "Rejection hurts, but hope dismembers." Strengths: consistent voice, sharp aphoristic phrasing, strong control of the cycle between dread, anger, and relief. The ending resists false resolution—the narrator heads out "preparing not to believe it," which is earned and true to the character. Weaknesses: the piece leans heavily on aphorism ("Anger has edges. Fear is just falling"), which occasionally tips toward the overwrought and performative—several lines feel engineered for quotability rather than emerging organically from the character. The structure is somewhat repetitive by design, but a few cycles could have been trimmed for a ~1000-word target (it runs long). The "therapist calls it escalation" opening is a slightly familiar device. Dialogue exists only in imagined/rehearsed form and text messages, which is appropriate; the imagined exchanges are effective, though the "You look nice / You say that to everyone" exchange is a touch on-the-nose. Minor tell-don't-show moments ("I can name the distortion while it distorts") are largely justified by the premise of self-aware narration. + Physical-spatial: Blood Debt — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
"Blood Debt" Write a vivid third-person narrative depicting an unsanctioned underground duel between two talented but hot-headed martial artists. Their schools have been embroiled in a generations-old rivalry, and despite strict prohibitions from their masters, these two younger fighters arrange a secret confrontation fueled by personal pride and simmering animosity. - **One fighter** represents **Jigen-ryū**, a traditional, aggressive style practiced historically by elite samurai clans. Its practitioners emphasize explosive offense, decisive strikes, and overwhelming speed. Known historically for their arrogance and disdain toward outsiders, practitioners consider their art superior and untouchable. - **The opposing fighter** employs a form of historical **Piguaquan**, a Chinese martial art traditionally practiced by commoners, bodyguards, and street fighters. This style emphasizes whipping, circular strikes, rapid footwork, unpredictable angles of attack, and evasive maneuvers. Practitioners often come from lower social classes and view the traditional elite as pretentious and detached from true combat effectiveness. The fight takes place in the crumbling ruins of an abandoned temple, now functioning as a hidden arena for illicit duels. Passionate supporters from both factions surround them, wagering money, pride, and reputation on the outcome. **Essential Instructions:** Maintain absolute physical coherence throughout—clearly track fighters' positions relative to each other and their environment. Precisely depict strikes, counters, momentum shifts, and spatial dynamics, allowing readers to clearly visualize the mechanics and choreography of the fight at every moment. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Rain leaked through the cracked roof of the abandoned temple in thin silver threads, tapping on broken tiles and the warped planks of the old prayer hall. Moss climbed the stone pillars. Rotten banners hung in shreds behind a weather-darkened altar whose gilding had long since peeled away. In the center of the hall, where monks had once burned incense, someone had swept a fighting ring clear of rubble. The ring was a rough circle twelve paces across, marked with chalk and lamp soot. Men and women stood three deep around it, pressed between leaning columns and fallen statuary, their voices hushed with the electric restraint of gamblers before the first throw. Coins changed hands. Names hissed through the damp air like curses. On one side of the ring clustered the Jigen-ryū faction: hard-faced young retainers, shoulders square, hair tied tight, their red-and-black armbands worn high and neat. Opposite them lounged the Piguaquan supporters: porters, caravan guards, smiths, laborers, broad-palmed and sharp-eyed, their own red-and-black bands knotted around bare biceps or over patched sleeves as if in deliberate mockery of uniformity. At the north edge of the circle stood Hayato of Jigen-ryū. He was tall and narrow-hipped, in a dark training jacket tied close to the body, sleeves rolled to the forearms. His right foot was half a step behind his left, body angled, weight light on the balls of his feet. His shoulders looked almost relaxed, but his chin was slightly tucked and his right hand hovered near the line of his hip as though every tendon in him had been wound around a hidden spring. The red-and-black armband on his left arm was fresh and immaculate. He wore the expression of a man already offended by the fact that the bout had been deemed necessary. Three paces south of him, at the opposite side of the ring, crouched Liang. Liang’s jacket had no uniform elegance. It was sleeveless, open at the throat, damp with rain and sweat. He stood wider than Hayato, left foot forward, knees loose, spine supple rather than erect. His arms moved in small lazy circles, wrists loose, shoulders rolling to keep the whole frame alive. His armband was tied over the right biceps, the cloth darkened where rain had soaked it. There was a split in his lower lip from some previous evening’s argument. He smiled through it with open contempt. Between them, an old bronze incense brazier lay on its side at the eastern edge of the ring, half inside the chalk boundary. A cracked stone lion crouched just beyond the western edge, reducing the usable space there by a pace. The floor itself sloped subtly toward the altar in the north, and both men had noticed. No master had sanctioned this. No elder would have permitted it. Which was why everyone present watched with the hungry focus reserved for forbidden things. Hayato spoke first. “When this is done, your people will stop saying our name.” Liang rolled one shoulder, never taking his eyes off him. “When this is done, yours will stop saying theirs like they invented fighting.” A few harsh laughs came from the south side. The Jigen men answered with silence, which in that hall sounded like insult refined into ritual. No formal signal was given. They had come for a private settling, and both believed yielding initiative was shameful. Hayato moved first. He did not advance in increments. He launched. His rear foot drove against the wet boards and sent him from the north edge of the ring toward center in one violent burst, left foot spearing forward, torso compressed behind the motion. His right hand cut downward from high outside his shoulder in a knife-hand strike aimed diagonally at Liang’s neck, the line of attack direct and murderous, as if trying to cleave through collarbone into chest. Liang had been waiting for exactly that kind of arrogance. As Hayato crossed the centerline, Liang did not retreat straight back. He slipped one half-step to his own left—east, toward the fallen brazier—rotating clockwise on the ball of his front foot so the descending strike sliced past the front of his throat by inches. At the same instant his right arm whipped in a short circular backfist toward Hayato’s exposed ribs. The strike landed with a flat smack under Hayato’s right arm, but Liang had clipped muscle rather than liver because Hayato’s momentum carried his torso already through the line. Hayato accepted the glancing blow and pivoted sharply on his lead foot, converting the missed downward cut into a horizontal elbow with the same right arm. Liang saw the shoulder turn and folded backward at the waist. The elbow skimmed his chest and jacket ties. Before he had fully recovered upright, Hayato’s left foot stamped forward to close the gap entirely, crowding him near the eastern side where the brazier constricted movement. A murmur rushed through the audience. Jigen pressure. Early. Hayato’s style showed in the sequence: no probing, no ornament, only offense layered over offense. His left palm shot to Liang’s face. Liang parried outward with his left forearm. Hayato’s right hand immediately speared toward the throat. Liang knocked it down with his right wrist and slid another half-step east, but the brazier’s rim touched his heel. He could not give more ground without stumbling over the metal lip. Hayato sensed it. His eyes sharpened. He drove in with a rising forearm from low right to high left, an explosive line meant to split guard and chin together. Liang did not try to absorb it. He sank suddenly, knees dropping, torso turning sideways so the forearm shaved across his left shoulder instead of his jaw. From the low angle he lashed both arms in a Piguaquan double swing—left hand checking Hayato’s striking arm upward while the right whipped downward like a flail into Hayato’s lead knee. The blow landed just above the kneecap from outside to inside. Hayato’s left leg buckled half an inch. Not enough to drop him, but enough to interrupt the next step. Liang used that interruption. He hooked his left foot behind the brazier’s far handle, kicked it backward with a scrape of bronze, and opened a lane behind himself. Then he slid diagonally southwest, out from the trap by the ring’s eastern edge, his shoulders turning as his right arm snapped around in a long, circular chop toward Hayato’s temple. Hayato brought his left forearm up in time. The whipping hand cracked against bone. He gave one short retreating step—his first backward motion of the fight—toward the center to reset his balance. Now they were nearly equidistant from east and west, Hayato just north of center, Liang south-southeast of him. Rain pattered through the roof between them. Both were breathing harder, but Liang’s face had changed. The smile was gone. Hayato flexed his jaw once; his left forearm was already reddening. Liang began to circle clockwise, moving westward around Hayato. His feet were quick and skimming, never crossing. His shoulders rolled, arms drawing loose figure-eights that could become strikes from either side. Hayato turned to keep him in front, taking small precise adjustments, unwilling to lunge blind. “Come on, nobleman,” Liang said, voice low. “Don’t think. Cut.” Hayato obliged. He burst again, but this time with a feint. His left hand flicked high toward Liang’s eyes. As Liang’s right arm rose to intercept, Hayato dropped his level and drove his right shoulder forward, aiming to smash into Liang’s chest and uproot him. Liang pivoted away to his left, but Hayato had not overcommitted. Mid-drive he converted the shoulder rush into a low sweeping strike with his left arm at Liang’s floating ribs. The forearm slammed home. Air burst from Liang’s mouth. He staggered two steps west, heels thudding near the cracked stone lion. Hayato pursued instantly, crossing the centerline and herding him toward the obstructed western edge now as effectively as he had pinned him in the east before. A right knife-hand slashed for the neck; Liang ducked. A left elbow chased the duck; Liang twisted, taking it glancing across the upper back. Hayato’s rear foot advanced again, cutting off escape to the north. Liang was now at the west boundary, the stone lion just behind his left calf and the chalk line under his right heel. Hayato stood a pace in front of him, slightly south of centerline, blocking the path east with his body. If Liang retreated further, he would collide with stone. If he rushed straight forward, he would rush into Jigen power. Hayato drew his right hand high over his shoulder, telegraphing nothing but destruction. The crowd inhaled as one. Liang saw the finishing blow gather and made a choice born of street fighting rather than honor. Instead of fleeing the line, he stepped into it. As Hayato’s right arm came down in a brutal descending strike, Liang shot forward from the wall, jamming both forearms upward between Hayato’s elbow and wrist before the blow reached full acceleration. The impact still drove Liang half a step back into the lion, but it shortened the arc. At the same moment Liang’s forehead smashed into Hayato’s mouth. Cartilage crunched. Hayato’s head snapped back. Before Hayato could reestablish distance, Liang uncoiled. His right arm whipped across Hayato’s face from left to right. The backfist caught the cheek. As Hayato turned with it, Liang spun his torso the opposite way and brought the left arm around in a long circular hammering strike into the side of Hayato’s neck. The mechanics were pure Pigua: waist, shoulder, loose arm, cracking at the end of the arc like a rope weighted with iron. Hayato stumbled eastward toward center, feet crossing for the first time. Liang pursued not in a straight line but on a slight outside angle to Hayato’s right flank, keeping off the direct center where Jigen counters were deadliest. His right foot planted outside Hayato’s right foot. His left hand checked Hayato’s elbow inward. His right palm chopped down behind the ear. Hayato dropped to one knee. A roar tore through the temple, half exultation, half outrage. But Hayato was not finished. Kneeling on his right knee near the center of the ring, left foot planted, he twisted violently and launched a backhand strike toward Liang’s knee, trying to cripple the leg nearest him. Liang had anticipated some last eruption. He hopped his right leg back, the strike missing by inches, then used the loaded left leg to drive a downward forearm across Hayato’s collar and upper spine. Hayato collapsed from kneel to both hands. Liang did not overstrike. He stepped back one pace, chest heaving, and held his right arm cocked in case the samurai rose again. Hayato tried. One hand pushed against the slick boards. Blood dripped from his split lip to the floor. His left knee came under him, but when he lifted his head the hall swayed in his eyes. He looked up at Liang—still defiant, still furious—but his body no longer answered his pride. His arm buckled, and he dropped back to a single knee, unable to stand before the count of breaths demanded by the crowd. It ended there, not with grace but with certainty. Coins erupted into motion. The commoners shouted themselves hoarse. The Jigen side stood rigid, faces gone pale with insult deeper than loss. In the ruined temple, beneath the leaking roof and the blind gaze of shattered gods, Liang raised the red-and-black band on his arm for all of them to see, while Hayato knelt in the center of the ring, defeated not by a better pedigree but by a man who had learned to survive in narrower places.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of martial arts fight writing. The narrative delivers on nearly all of the prompt's core demands: an unsanctioned duel in a ruined temple, two hot-headed fighters from rival traditions, wagering factions, and—most impressively—sustained physical coherence. The choreography is the standout: positions are tracked relative to environmental features (the fallen brazier, the stone lion, the sloping floor), and the fight's geography is used tactically. Hayato first pins Liang against the brazier in the east, then Liang escapes and is later pinned against the lion in the west—a satisfying symmetry that shows deliberate structural design rather than improvised chaos. The stylistic contrast between the two arts is well rendered. Hayato's Jigen-ryū is characterized by explosive linear offense, no probing, layered attacks; Liang's Piguaquan by whipping circular strikes, angle changes, and evasive footwork. The prose itself mirrors these rhythms—short percussive sentences for Hayato's bursts, looser rolling description for Liang. The tactical logic is believable throughout: Liang's escape via kicking the brazier, his jam-and-headbutt counter when cornered, his pursuit on an outside angle to avoid Jigen counters, and Hayato's final kneeling backhand attempt all follow coherent martial reasoning. Characterization is functional but somewhat thin. The fighters are defined primarily by their styles and class postures rather than interiority; the pre-fight dialogue is minimal and serviceable, with the "nobleman... don't think. Cut" exchange being the sharpest moment. The class tension (samurai arrogance vs. commoner pragmatism) is present but delivered mostly through the narrator's framing and the closing line, which edges toward telling. The ending—"defeated not by a better pedigree but by a man who had learned to survive in narrower places"—is a touch explicit in its moral, though it lands as thematic closure rather than a failure. Weaknesses: the crowd remains undifferentiated backdrop; the emotional arc is relatively simple (pride → attrition → defeat) without much complexity or surprise; the outcome is fairly predictable given the setup's sympathy for the underdog; and a few phrases ("insult refined into ritual," "blind gaze of shattered gods") flirt with over-polish without tipping into purple. The prose is disciplined, concrete, and kinetic—rarely overwrought. Momentum shifts are clear and earned, and the physical stakes escalate logically to a decisive but non-lethal finish.
