+ Physical-spatial: Breaking Formation — Score: 86.6
Prompt:
**"Breaking Formation"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a street dancer from a rough neighborhood who's won a scholarship to an elite K-pop training academy in Seoul. Desperately out of place culturally and technically, they struggle with a militaristically precise choreography that contradicts everything about their improvisational background. The punishing rehearsal takes place under a famous instructor known for breaking students to remake them, who sees potential in the narrator's raw talent but not their attitude. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—each dance move, position shift, and spatial relationship must be tracked with precision throughout the studio. Paint an exceptionally vivid kinetic picture through descriptions that capture not just movement but the contrast between the narrator's fluid, expressive style and the mechanical precision demanded. Their internal monologue should reveal culture shock, class anxiety, and the threatening realization that success here might mean losing their authentic movement voice. Include technical terminology that highlights the collision of street and commercial styles, moments when muscle memory betrays them, and a crucial decision point about whether to conform or rebel. Physical clarity is essential—readers must be able to visualize exactly how bodies move through space, how rhythms align or clash, and how the protagonist's body struggles against unfamiliar discipline. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The first thing I learn about Studio C is that sound has corners. There are four black speakers bolted high where the mirrored walls meet the ceiling, one in each corner, all blasting the same track so loud it feels stitched tight across the room. Not club loud, not block-party loud where bass leaks and breathes. This is sealed loud, measured loud, every snare cracking at the same instant from all four corners so there’s nowhere to stand that isn’t inside the beat. The room itself is a clean white box with one wall of mirror, one wall of windows looking over Gangnam glass and traffic, pale wood floor taped with black formation marks. Eight horizontal lines of tape divide the space front to back. Vertical marks split center, left, right. Everybody knows where their body belongs before the music starts. Everybody except me. I’m back row, second line from the right, on a strip of tape with a little red X at my toes. Twelve of us total, three rows of four, all facing the mirror. Front row is half a step ahead of the first horizontal line so they can travel without clipping the mirror. I’m two full rows behind them. If I extend my right arm straight out in second position, fingertips almost line up with the shoulder blade of the girl ahead of me. We’re spaced so precisely I can feel my mistakes before I make them. “Again from count five.” Master Han stands dead center between us and the mirror, close enough that we have to look past him to see ourselves. Famous in every way I hate: online clips of trainees vomiting after rehearsal, stories about kids crying in stairwells, before-and-after transformations like he took bolt cutters to their old selves. He wears all black and doesn’t move unless he means to. When he does, it’s economical, like his joints came pre-measured. “Formation one,” he says in Korean, then again in clipped English because of me. “And if one person drags, all drag.” I already know who one person is. The intro clicks in. Four counts of hi-hat, synth swell, then the kick lands. On one, we snap our feet apart to shoulder width. On two, right hand blades to sternum, left arm shoots diagonally down, palm flat. On three-and, chest hit forward then release. On four, heads whip left. It’s simple if you grew up counting movement like currency. I grew up catching breaks in the music like they were loose change on the sidewalk. By count five we travel. Right foot crosses over left on a tight diagonal toward downstage left—toward the mirror’s left edge from our perspective. Left foot opens. Right foot closes. Arms carve in hard angles, elbows at ninety, wrists locked. It’s not groove. It’s architecture. I make it through five-six-seven with everybody else, but on eight the old reflex wakes up. There’s a bass drag under the count, a dirty little pocket tucked behind the metronomic snare, and my shoulders melt into it before I can stop them. Not much. Half a roll through my right scapula, rib cage lagging just a fraction, neck releasing where the choreo wants a freeze. It’s enough. “Stop.” The track cuts so hard my pulse keeps dancing after the room goes still. Han points at me. “What was that?” I know better than to say feeling. I know better than to say music. “My timing—” “Your ego.” He steps toward my line. In the mirror I see everyone else stay locked in their ending position: feet staggered, knees soft, fists by ribs. Nobody relaxes. “You are decorating the count. There is no decoration.” Back home, decoration is the whole point. You take six steps and make them yours or you’re just borrowing somebody else’s body. I mumble, “Yes, sir.” He demonstrates my mistake by doing it better than I did—tiny shoulder ripple, delayed rib isolation, a grease-slick groove threaded under the phrase—then he kills it mid-breath and resets into the academy version, all edges and stops. “This,” he says, the fluid one. “You know. This”—the sharp one—“you need. Raw talent is not professionalism.” Around me there are twelve reflected versions of shame. Mine’s the only one with braids tied back in a cheap bandanna under academy-issued black cap. The only one whose Korean still arrives half a beat late. The only one who sends scholarship money home before buying proper dance sneakers. Everybody else looks like they’ve been training since their bones were soft enough to mold. “From top,” Han says. We reset. My heels find the red X. I check spacing: Jisoo in front of me, ponytail brushing the back print of her shirt, exactly one arm and a hand-length away. Min on my left on the next vertical mark. If I travel too far on count seven, my forearm will clip his elbow on the turn. If I undertravel, the diagonal line to front right breaks in the mirror. This place has turned movement into geometry. Music. One-two-three-four. On five we cross and open. On six our line shifts half a meter downstage left while front row splits center, the two middle dancers peeling apart so a lane opens straight through to Han’s reflection. On seven my right foot plants outside the tape seam, left knee twists inward, torso hinges forward fifteen degrees, both forearms framing the face. On eight we rebound upright and quarter-turn right. I hit all of it. No grease, no lag. Then count one of the chorus comes like a challenge thrown at my chest. Commercial combo: jump out wide in second, both hands punch overhead in a V, land through bent knees. Two: pull fists down to shoulders with a chest pop. Three: right knee drives up while left elbow slices across. Four: step right, pivot half-turn over the left shoulder, finish facing back wall. It should feel explosive but contained, power with a lid on it. My body hears jump, punch, drive, pivot and translates into cipher logic. Bigger. Lower. Let the momentum talk. So on the jump I sink too deep, pelvis dropping below the level of everyone else’s. On the chest pop I let the sternum ripple instead of hitting one clean accent. On the knee drive my supporting foot swivels for ease, a b-boy survival habit from concrete, and that tiny swivel sends me two inches off my mark before the half-turn. When we face the back wall, I’m no longer directly behind Jisoo. I’m offset to her left, staring at the seam of the window frame instead of the center speaker. Those two inches become a threat on count six, because that’s when back row threads between middle row. Jisoo goes left. I’m supposed to pass through the channel she leaves, stepping forward-right on six, left together on-and, right lunge on seven. But because I drifted left, Min and I enter the same lane. His forearm glances my triceps. Not a collision, just enough friction to announce failure. “Stop!” Again the silence punches harder than the music. Han doesn’t raise his voice. He doesn’t need to. “You dance like the room will move for you.” A couple trainees bow their heads lower. Nobody looks at me directly, but I feel their relief that this isn’t their day to be hunted. He walks me through the pathway himself. He places me back on my red X, then uses the toe of his shoe to indicate each step on the wood. “Count five, cross here. Not there. Six, open exactly to this line. Your knee stays over the second toe. You are collapsing in. That is why your turn travels. Again.” He taps the floor in front of Min. “This lane belongs to him until count six-and. You do not steal space because your habit is large.” Habit is large. It lands like an insult and a diagnosis. He calls Min and Jisoo to hold positions. Then he puts me behind them and demonstrates from my body outward, not touching, just cutting the air around my limbs. “Your freestyle background teaches momentum. Useful. But here, momentum is rationed.” His hand slices from my shoulder to my wrist. “Stop the line here. Do not smear it.” Smear it. Like my movement is dirt on clean glass. We run the phrase slowly without music. Eight counts broken into subdivisions. “Five-e-and-a,” Han counts, and every micro-action has a place: cross on five, settle weight on e, open on and, square shoulders on a. On six, left hand snaps to clavicle while right retracts to the floating rib. On seven, chin angles thirty degrees right. On eight, eyes front before the torso catches up. It’s insane. It’s beautiful. It makes me want to scream. By the time the speakers kick back in, my shirt is pasted to my spine. The room smells like sanitizer and expensive detergent and fear. Outside the windows, tiny cars slide through intersections far below, free to be messy. We take it from the pre-chorus. This time I count so hard I can hear numbers underneath the lyrics. One e and a two e and a. My muscles argue with me the whole way. Every groove impulse arrives like a friend at the wrong funeral. The beat begs me to sit in the back pocket, to let the snare bounce through my shoulders and out my hips. The choreo demands I strike on top, dead center of the count, like a machine stamping sheet metal. On the crucial transition into chorus, I land the jump narrower. Knees track clean. Chest hits and stops. Right knee drives on count three without the old swivel. Half-turn on four, spot the back wall center. I am directly behind Jisoo now. Her ponytail is a black metronome. Count five, she peels left. I wait half a breath—six-and belongs to Min, Han said—then cut through the lane exactly as drilled. Forward-right, together, lunge. My right foot lands on the next strip of tape with my knee over the laces. No collision. I should feel victorious. Instead I feel amputated. Because I can also feel what I cut away to get there: the pocket, the drag, the little argument with gravity that made dancing mine before anyone graded it. The chorus continues. On count one of the second eight, we ripple canon from front row to back—front hits chest, middle follows one count later, back follows after that. My row is last. This is where I could disappear into obedience. Hit exactly as told. Earn a nod. Survive. Or I could let the ripple breathe the way my body knows how, give it texture, let the wave travel through vertebrae instead of pretending the spine is a set of switches. Han is watching me in the mirror. Not my reflection—me. Waiting to see which self wins. The count comes. Front row hits. Then middle. My turn. I make a decision so small nobody outside dance would call it rebellion. I hit the count dead on. I keep the shape he wants: sternum forward, ribs contained, pelvis stable, shoulders level. But inside that exact timing, I let the motion pass through all the joints I own. Not a smear. Not a freestyle break. Just enough truth that the hit arrives alive instead of manufactured. Precision holding pulse. Steel with blood in it. It lasts less than a second. Han’s eyes narrow. The music keeps pounding from all four corners, too loud, too exact, and all twelve of us slice into the next formation. I step back on my left, quarter-turn left, draw my right arm across my body as Jisoo drops to a kneel in front and Min opens right to clear the line. We are still coherent, still sharp, still in formation. But something in me hasn’t broken where he expected. Maybe that means I’ll fail here. Maybe it means I finally started learning how not to disappear.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This narrative is an exceptionally well-executed response to a demanding prompt. The physical coherence requirement is met with unusual rigor: the narrator's position (back row, second line, red X), the spacing relative to Jisoo and Min, the two-inch drift that causes the lane collision, and the correction of that drift are all tracked with geometric precision. The choreography is broken down count-by-count in a way readers can genuinely visualize—cross, open, close, quarter-turn, canon ripple—without ever becoming a dry diagram. The central conflict is rendered almost entirely through the body: the shoulder roll that betrays the narrator on count eight, the b-boy swivel habit that displaces them before the half-turn, the "amputated" feeling after executing the phrase correctly. The collision of street and commercial vocabularies is handled with authentic technical specificity ("pocket," "cipher logic," "decoration," "smear"), and Master Han's demonstration of the narrator's own mistake—doing it better, then killing it—is a sharp, economical character beat. The internal monologue carries culture shock and class anxiety through concrete details (bandanna under issued cap, money sent home, Korean arriving half a beat late) rather than abstract lament. The decision point is handled with real nuance: the "rebellion" is microscopic—precision with pulse inside it—which is exactly right for the character's situation and far more interesting than a dramatic walkout would have been. Minor criticisms: the prose occasionally leans on aphoristic constructions ("It's not groove. It's architecture.") that flirt with over-polish, and a few metaphors ("friend at the wrong funeral," "steel with blood in it") are near the edge of overwrought without quite tipping. Han risks becoming a stock tyrant-instructor, though the moment where he demonstrates the groove himself complicates him slightly. The ending is earned and appropriately ambivalent. Dialogue is sparse but functional and in-character. + Gothic-fantasy-humour: Court of the Dreaming — Score: 85.9
Prompt:
Court of the Dreaming: Territorial Dream Dispute. Write a dark fantasy scene with comedic elements set in the Courts of Dream where a case is being heard to determine ownership of a contested dreamscape. Mora, the Slavic nightmare spirit who sits on sleepers' chests causing paralysis and terror, has recently invaded and subverted a carefully crafted recurring dream of a schoolboy, Max. The dream originally featured the boy lying in a field of wildflowers with his crush, always culminating in a muddled almost-kiss and a pleasant confusion of emotions. This dream was the meticulous work of "First Love" (a rosy-cheeked, slightly bashful entity who crafts formative romantic experiences). However, Mora has recently infiltrated the dreamscape, transforming the scene so that when the girl playfully mounts the boy, she morphs into a terrifying yet somehow still confusingly attractive vision who proceeds to sit on his chest and feed on his breath. Mora's defense largely consists of the practical argument that "a girl's gotta eat too, you know?" Write this scene as it unfolds in the courtroom of the Dreaming, with Dream's demeanour, typically impenetrable, betraying a sense of irritation at having to adjudicate such matters. The comedy should derive from the farcical situation, familiar elements of courtroom drama intersecting with the fantastical world of the Dreaming, and the droll portrayal of the characters and their interactions. The humor should be dark and understated throughout. Dream is tempted to some mischief in the resolution of the case. Use descriptives sparingly when setting scene. Write for readability & engagement. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The courtroom of the Dreaming was arranged with all the usual concessions to order and none of the usual comforts. Benches of dark wood held petitioners, parasites, personifications, and one very nervous recurring anxiety about trousers in public. At the center of the chamber, a single giant hourglass dripped shimmering sand with patient contempt. On the dais sat Dream, Lord of the Dreaming, robed in shadow and old oaths. His face was, as ever, the sort of face one could not quite remember after looking away. His expression suggested that he had been forced to attend a meeting about mildew. “Call the matter,” he said. Lucienne, who had the air of someone keeping a library from becoming a forest, consulted the ledger. “Case seven hundred and eleven,” she said. “First Love versus Mora, regarding unlawful incursion, hostile alteration, and predatory occupation of a recurring adolescent dreamscape belonging, in the mortal sphere, to one Max Havel, age fourteen.” A faint murmur moved through the gallery. Fourteen was considered prime territory. The years when dreams were overwatered and underdefended. “Appearances?” Dream said. A rosy figure rose from the petitioner’s table. First Love looked as though they had been painted from blush and candlelight, all soft cuffs and earnest eyes and the sort of smile that made people write poetry they would later deny. They stood with both hands clasped before them and gave Dream a little bow. “For the petitioner, my lord.” At the respondent’s table, Mora lounged with the easy insolence of an entity long accustomed to entering private places uninvited. She was all angles and dusk; her beauty had the practical severity of a knife. There was a flattening pressure to her even at rest, as if the room itself had to work a bit harder to breathe around her. “For myself,” she said. “As no one here seems eager to represent me for reasons that are, frankly, anti-cultural.” Several advocates looked suddenly very interested in their own papers. Dream steepled his fingers. “You stand accused of trespass and corruption of another’s work.” “Corruption is such a loaded term,” Mora said. “Adaptation, perhaps. Expansion. Interdisciplinary collaboration.” First Love made a small, scandalized sound. Dream’s eyes moved to them. “Petitioner. State your claim.” First Love rose fully, smoothing their already immaculate sleeves. “My lord, for six months and twelve nights I cultivated this dream. It was a recurring field sequence. Wildflowers, afternoon light, the mortal boy supine in a state of anticipatory tenderness. The girl—subject designation Elena V.—approaches, lies beside him, then above him, and they experience proximity, elevated pulse, and the exquisite, formative agony of not quite knowing what to do next.” They swallowed, a little pinker around the ears. “It always culminated in an almost-kiss. Not an actual kiss, my lord. That would have been premature and artistically vulgar. The dream’s purpose was to produce wistfulness, motor confusion, and a durable sweetness of recollection. Foundational material.” Lucienne made a note. Dream said, “And the respondent?” First Love drew in a breath as if preparing to describe a murder in church. “Three weeks ago Mora entered the dream unbidden. The sequence remains superficially intact at first. Field, flowers, Elena mounting Max’s torso in a playful display of romantic initiative—” Mora raised a hand. “Which, if I may say, was a bold choice for your usual portfolio.” First Love ignored her with visible strain. “Then Elena’s face distorts. Her hair lengthens. Her limbs—there was no need for the limbs to do that—” “I disagree,” Mora said. “—and she proceeds to pin the boy, sit on his chest, and consume his breath while he experiences terror, paralysis, and, I regret to add, residual attraction.” A few entities in the gallery nodded with professional interest. Dream looked at Mora. “Do you dispute this account?” “Only the tone,” she said. “It makes it sound ugly.” “It is ugly,” said First Love. Mora spread her hands. “A girl’s gotta eat too, you know?” There was a pause. Somewhere in the back, a prophetic raven made a choking sound that might have been laughter and then pretended to molt. Dream closed his eyes for a moment. It was not a long moment, but several beings in the room abruptly recalled old sins. When he opened them, he said, “You are admitting to the feeding.” “Of course. I’m not a bureaucrat.” Mora tilted her head. “The boy had become deliciously vulnerable. Fluttering heart. Breath all shallow. Mind full of longing and dread. You leave a table set like that and expect no one to dine?” “This was a curated emotional environment,” First Love said. “Not a buffet.” “Oh, please. Half your work ends with me in six months anyway.” A rustle went through the benches. It was not entirely inaccurate. Dream said, “Watch yourself.” Mora inclined her head by a fraction. “My lord.” Lucienne looked up from the ledger. “Permission to submit dream extracts?” “Granted,” said Dream. The air above the center of the courtroom rippled. The dream unfurled in miniature. A field under summer light. A boy in school clothes, trying very hard to look relaxed in the presence of a girl who was trying very hard not to seem aware that he existed in a special way. They lay side by side. Fingers twitched closer. She laughed. He blushed. She rolled atop him with all the confidence of someone in a dream supplied by a benevolent contractor. Their faces neared. Then the scene shivered. Her smile widened too far. Her hair spread across him like spilled ink. Her eyes darkened into hungry moons. Her knees pinned his arms. She settled on his chest with a familiar, dreadful intimacy. Max’s face went from yearning to panic without finding a safe place in between. The gallery winced appreciatively. “Note,” said Mora, pointing to the image, “that the underlying composition remains strong. Good line work. The emotional confusion is preserved. Enhanced, even.” “Enhanced?” First Love said. “He woke sobbing!” “And thinking about her,” Mora said. “My intervention did not erase desire. It complicated it. Adolescence thrives on complication.” A gaunt thing from the third bench, possibly Embarrassing Memory, muttered, “She’s got a point.” Dream’s stare silenced three rows. “Call the mortal’s attending witness,” he said. Lucienne turned a page. “The Court recognizes Sleep Paralysis, as condition and occasional subcontractor.” A thin figure in a physician’s coat rose from near the rear, carrying a satchel that emitted little muffled screams. “Present,” it said. First Love looked betrayed. “You consulted with her?” Sleep Paralysis adjusted its spectacles. “I’m often adjacent. The jurisdictions are annoyingly porous.” Dream said, “Testimony.” Sleep Paralysis cleared its throat. “The respondent’s occupation of the chest was textbook. Efficient pressure distribution, respiratory inhibition without immediate tissue harm, excellent use of the dreamer’s inability to call for help. However”—it glanced at notes—“the fusion with preexisting romantic iconography did create unusual aftereffects. Elevated fixation. Shame. Intrusive replay. Confused arousal.” First Love looked as though each word was a separate slap. Mora looked pleased. “A robust bouquet.” “Did the respondent have permission to enter the dream?” Dream asked. “No,” said Sleep Paralysis. “But in fairness, very few of my cases involve signed paperwork.” Dream drummed one pale finger against the arm of his chair. The hourglass whispered sand into itself. “Respondent,” he said, “on what basis do you claim right?” Mora stood. “Ancient custom, necessity, and ecological realism. Humans do not divide neatly into your departments, my lord. Their sweetest dreams border their worst fears. A first crush is already a haunting. The boy lies helpless beneath a beloved face and can scarcely breathe from nerves. I merely… formalized the arrangement.” There was an intake of breath from several academics of symbolism. “And,” Mora added, “again: a girl’s gotta eat.” First Love stood so abruptly their chair toppled. “My lord, if this is permitted, no tender dream is safe. We labor over nuance. We place a hand near another hand and let yearning do the rest. We do not”—they gestured helplessly toward the fading image of monstrous Elena astride the boy—“we do not convert every almost-kiss into thoracic predation!” “Some convert themselves,” Mora said. Dream looked not at either of them but at the hourglass. Sand descended in a bright, indifferent stream. At last he spoke. “The dreamscape was crafted by First Love. Ownership of the recurrent field sequence is therefore theirs. Mora’s entry was unauthorized trespass.” First Love exhaled shakily with relief. “However,” Dream said, and relief throughout the room became more cautious, “the respondent identifies a truth. Mortal dreams bleed into one another. Fear contaminates desire. Desire invites fear. Particularly at fourteen.” Max’s recurring anxiety about trousers in public gave a solemn nod. Dream continued, “The Court will not award Mora ownership, nor unrestricted feeding rights. The respondent is enjoined from direct occupation of the contested dreamscape for one year and one day.” First Love sagged into their seat. Mora clicked her tongue. “Harsh.” “Be grateful,” Dream said. “I have not yet reached the mischievous part.” For the first time that day, something almost visible passed over his face. Not amusement exactly. The weather that precedes it. “The Court further orders,” he said, “that compensation be rendered. Since the respondent has shown such keen interest in educational crossover, Mora will assist First Love in the construction of age-appropriate cautionary dreams for older mortals. Specifically: anxiety dreams concerning ex-partners, unread messages, and meeting someone from school while inadequately dressed.” A delighted shiver ran through the courtroom. Mora stared. “That,” she said, “is clerical work.” “Yes,” said Dream. Lucienne, without looking up, was already drafting forms. “And,” Dream added, “for the boy Max: the original field dream shall be restored. Slightly revised. The almost-kiss may proceed to an actual kiss on no more than one occasion per lunar quarter.” First Love made a tiny sound of joy. Mora folded her arms. “You reward them for being precious.” “I preserve balance,” Dream said. “Also, I am irritated.” That, in the Dreaming, was close to candor. He rose. The chamber dimmed around the edges. “One more condition,” he said. “Because the respondent’s interference has fused fear and longing in this mortal’s mind, she will not leave entirely empty-handed. Once only, at a time of my choosing, the boy may dream of the girl atop him again—” First Love looked stricken. “—but,” Dream said, “she will merely ask if he has done the assigned reading, and his terror shall be complete.” Silence held for a beat. Then the gallery broke into low, scandalized laughter. Even Lucienne’s mouth twitched. Mora, against all dignity, barked out a single surprised laugh and then looked annoyed at herself for it. First Love covered their face with both hands. Dream sat back down as if none of this had happened and had certainly not been, in any sense, a joke. “Judgment entered,” he said. “Next matter.” Lucienne consulted the ledger. “A coalition of Teeth Falling Out brings suit against Dentistry for loss of market share.” Dream stared into middle distance with the look of a king contemplating abdication into the sea. The hourglass continued to drip shimmering sand.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed piece of dark comic fantasy that hits nearly every requirement of the prompt. The courtroom of the Dreaming is economically sketched ("benches of dark wood held petitioners, parasites, personifications, and one very nervous recurring anxiety about trousers in public"), the procedural beats are played straight against absurd content, and Dream's irritation is conveyed through dry understatement rather than stated outright. The dream-extract sequence is genuinely unsettling, and the resolution—Dream's "mischief" being a single dream where the girl merely asks if Max has done the assigned reading—is a clever, tonally perfect payoff that fuses terror and adolescent embarrassment. Strengths: the dialogue is consistently sharp and character-differentiated (Mora's insolence, First Love's primness, Sleep Paralysis's clinical detachment); the humor is dark and understated as requested; the prose is elegant without purple excess; the pacing is tight with no meandering. The "a girl's gotta eat" defense is deployed at the right moments, and the closing "Teeth Falling Out vs. Dentistry" stinger lands well. Minor weaknesses: the middle section slightly over-relies on gallery-reaction beats ("A rustle went through the benches," "The gallery winced appreciably") as a laugh-track device, which becomes a mild crutch. Mora's ecological-realism argument, while good, resolves a touch too neatly into Dream's ruling; the moral ambiguity of her position could have been pressed further. First Love is somewhat one-note beyond bashful indignation. A few jokes (the trousers anxiety) are reused rather than escalated. These are small quibbles against an otherwise polished, professional piece that fulfills the brief with wit and control. + Fanfic-crossover: Blood Moon — Score: 80.9
Prompt:
Blood Moon Alucard & Yennefer Write a story where Alucard (Hellsing) encounters Yennefer (The Witcher) in medieval Europe. Yennefer's magical abilities intrigue the vampire, while she's both repulsed and fascinated by his monstrous nature. Their power dynamic shifts constantly as they circle each other, neither willing to show weakness first. **Alucard (Hellsing)** Alucard is an ancient, immensely powerful vampire who works for the Hellsing Organization. He can regenerate from almost any wound and shape-shift at will. He's sadistic, arrogant, and takes pleasure in toying with his enemies before killing them. Despite being a monster, he despises weak vampires who can't accept their nature. He wears a distinctive red coat, wide-brimmed hat, and orange sunglasses. He uses massive handguns loaded with silver bullets. He seeks worthy opponents who can challenge him and potentially end his immortal existence. Famous quote: "The bird of Hermes is my name, eating my wings to make me tame." **Yennefer of Vengerberg (The Witcher)** Yennefer is a powerful sorceress who magically altered her appearance to hide her congenital hunchback. She's ambitious, stubborn, and manipulative when necessary. She has violet eyes and smells of lilac and gooseberries. Despite her cold exterior, she desperately wants to reverse her infertility caused by magical transformation. She's centuries old but appears young. She's politically savvy and refuses to be underestimated. She has a sarcastic sense of humor and little patience for fools. Though she rarely shows it, she's capable of deep love and loyalty. Famous quote: "I'm not sweet and I'm not a maiden in distress in need of saving." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
A broken cart wheel lies abandoned near the village gates, half sunk in mud and streaked with old blood, hinting at a hurried departure. Beyond the rough palisade, the village of Doren sleeps badly beneath a swollen red moon. No dogs bark. No shutters creak. Fear has taught the peasants stillness. At the edge of the fields, Yennefer of Vengerberg stands with one gloved hand resting on a fence post blackened by fire. Her black-and-white curls stir in the night wind. The scent of lilac and gooseberries seems almost obscene in this place of rot, smoke, and spilled entrails. She studies the silence with narrowed violet eyes. Something has fed here. Not a ghoul. Not a bruxa. The corpses she passed on the road were too artfully ruined, opened like devotional offerings. The tracks vanish where they should not. There is intelligence in the slaughter, and vanity. She hates vanity in monsters. It so often resembles her own. The first sign of him is laughter. It rolls across the field low and amused, and then a figure steps from the dark as if the darkness has merely decided to wear a man’s shape. He is absurdly anachronistic even by sorcerous standards: a red coat bright as fresh arterial spray, a broad hat casting his face in shadow, orange lenses gleaming with reflected moonlight. In each hand rests a pistol too large for any ordinary man to lift comfortably. He regards Yennefer as though he has found a jewel in a midden heap. “Well,” he says, voice rich with mockery and delight, “medieval Europe continues to surprise me.” Yennefer does not move. “And here I thought the local rabble had exhausted the evening’s supply of theatrics.” His grin widens, exposing teeth just a little too long. “Sharp tongue. Excellent posture. A pulse like a cathedral bell. You are not local.” “Neither are you, clearly.” He tips his hat with infuriating grace. “Alucard.” She hears no title, no allegiance, only confidence vast enough to swallow armies. It annoys her instantly. “Yennefer of Vengerberg,” she says. His head tilts. “Ah. A sorceress.” He draws in a needless breath, savoring her scent. “Powerful too. I can taste it.” Revulsion prickles under her skin. “Try, and I’ll rip out whatever passes for your tongue.” At that, he laughs again, genuinely pleased. The air between them tightens. Yennefer feels magic gathering at her fingertips, cool and electric. Alucard remains loose-limbed, lazy even, but she senses in him a pressure so immense it warps the night around him. He is not merely a vampire. He is something older, denser, as if countless deaths have compacted into one smiling form. Behind them, a church bell begins to ring frantically inside the village. A scream follows. Yennefer curses and strides toward the gate. Alucard falls into step beside her, uninvited. “Do keep up,” she says. “I was going to tell you the same.” Inside, chaos blooms. A thing in the shape of a man clings to the side of a cottage wall, skin pale and stretched over twitching bones, mouth busy at a child’s throat. Another scrabbles from a well, jaw distended, eyes milk-white. Lesser vampires. Starved and feral. Yennefer thrusts out her hand. A burst of force slams the one on the wall into the cobbles hard enough to crack stone. Before it can rise, one of Alucard’s guns roars. Silver tears through the creature’s skull in an eruption of black gore. The sound is monstrous, almost joyous. The second vampire lunges. Alucard lets it strike. Claws rake his chest, shredding coat and flesh alike. Blood splashes. He smiles directly into the creature’s face as the wounds begin closing at once, knitting red to red. Then he seizes it by the throat and crushes vertebrae in his hand. Yennefer watches despite herself. He notices. “Interested?” “Disgusted.” “Those are not mutually exclusive.” Three more descend from the rooftops. Yennefer draws chaos through her spine until pain flashes white behind her eyes. Fire spirals from her palms, not wild but exquisitely controlled, a ribbon of incandescent force that wraps one vampire whole. It shrieks as it burns. Another she freezes in place with a binding charm, invisible pressure locking every limb. Alucard shoots the immobilized thing through the mouth. He moves with hideous elegance, coat swirling, shadows bending around him. Once, when a vampire darts for his blind side, his body simply dissolves into a swarm of darkness and red eyes before reforming behind it. He tears the creature nearly in half and drops the pieces like refuse. When the last of the lesser monsters is dead, silence returns in ragged breaths and drifting ash. A villager peeks from behind a door and immediately slams it shut again at the sight of Alucard standing knee-deep in corpses, grinning. “How reassuring,” Yennefer says dryly. “You’ve found a community that appreciates subtlety.” Alucard wipes blood from his cheek with one gloved finger. “And yet you fought beside me.” “For the villagers.” “Of course.” She turns on him then, full and sharp. “You led them here.” His smile thins. “Now that is an accusation.” “The pattern of attack changed the moment you arrived. Predators circling a greater predator. They smelled blood and obedience.” “Obedience?” He sounds almost offended. “No. Fear, perhaps. Reverence, in the religious sense.” “You’re enjoying this.” He steps closer. “I enjoy many things. Gunfire. moonlight. Arrogant women with enough power to scorch a city.” Her chin lifts. “Then enjoy this from a distance.” Magic lashes outward, a crackling violet whip aimed straight for his throat. It lands. For an instant she feels resistance like striking an iron gate buried under an ocean. Then his head comes off. It tumbles to the stones. The body remains standing. A peasant watching from an attic window crosses himself so violently he nearly falls out. Yennefer’s expression does not change, but satisfaction flickers in her eyes. Then Alucard’s severed head laughs from the ground. The body bends, retrieves it, and sets it back in place with obscene casualness. Flesh knits. He rolls his neck until it pops. “Better.” Yennefer exhales through her nose. “Parlor tricks.” His orange glasses catch the moon. “You wound me.” “I did.” “And yet here I am.” “Unfortunately.” Something changes in his face then—not softness, exactly, but attention sharpened to a dangerous point. He has toyed with her because he toys with everyone, but now he is measuring her. Weighing. Respect from a monster looks disturbingly like hunger. “You are magnificent,” he says quietly. She should despise the approval. Instead it lands like a spark on dry tinder. “You say that as if you’ve found a new species to dissect.” “Perhaps I have.” “Careful. I dissect back.” The red moon hangs above the chapel steeple, staining the village in sacrificial light. Wind lifts the hem of his coat and the raven-black fur at her collar. Around them, the dead cool. Yennefer senses it before she sees it: a larger presence, old and hidden, watching from beneath the church crypt. The source that drew the lesser vampires. A nest-queen, perhaps. Or something even older. Alucard senses it a heartbeat later. His grin returns, but this time it is directed not at her but at the dark stones of the chapel. “There you are.” From under the church doors comes a low scrape, then another, as if claws drag over buried wood. Yennefer’s fingers glow with gathering power. “If this is your idea of foreplay, I’m even less impressed than usual.” He chuckles. “You mistake me, sorceress. If I intended seduction, you would know.” “I would likely set you on fire.” “Yes.” His smile becomes feral. “That is part of the appeal.” The doors shudder. For one suspended moment they stand shoulder to shoulder, neither ally nor enemy, both too proud to acknowledge the convenience of the other’s strength. Her magic hums in the air. His pistols rise, black mouths hungry for silver judgment. “After this,” Yennefer says, eyes on the trembling church, “you answer my questions.” “After this,” Alucard replies, “perhaps I let you try to kill me again.” She smiles then, cold and brilliant. “Don’t make promises you can’t keep.” The church doors burst outward in a storm of splinters and grave dust. Under the blood moon, they meet the dark together.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong crossover piece that largely succeeds at its brief: Alucard and Yennefer meet in a medieval setting, circle each other, and neither yields. The prose is controlled and atmospheric, with a consistent present-tense third-person voice throughout. The opening establishes mood economically — the silent village, the blood-streaked cart wheel — and the pacing builds through a fight scene into a cliffhanger ending. Character work is the piece's chief strength. Alucard's dialogue captures his sadistic playfulness and theatrical menace ("You mistake me, sorceress. If I intended seduction, you would know"), and Yennefer's sarcasm and refusal to be impressed land authentically ("Parlor tricks," "Don't make promises you can't keep"). The power dynamic genuinely shifts: she decapitates him, he reattaches his head, and the exchange reads as mutual measurement rather than one-sided dominance. Both characters' canonical traits (his regeneration and shape-shifting, her lilac-and-gooseberries scent, violet eyes, chaos-drawn magic causing pain) are woven in without feeling like checklist items. Weaknesses: the plot is thin — arrive, banter, fight lesser vampires, sense a bigger threat, cliffhanger. The ending is a setup rather than a resolution, which slightly undercuts satisfaction. A few lines flirt with over-polish ("a jewel in a midden heap," "sacrificial light"), and the "predators circling a greater predator" accusation resolves too easily. The mutual-fascination thread occasionally edges toward romance-novel cadence ("That is part of the appeal"), though it stays in character for both. Minor typographical slip ("Gunfire. moonlight."). Overall: confident, voice-accurate, engaging genre writing with modest structural ambition. + Fanfic-crossover: Prison Strings — Score: 86.2
Prompt:
Prison Strings Jolyne Cujoh & Makima Write a story where Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure) and Makima (Chainsaw Man) cross paths at a supernatural prison facility. Jolyne is immediately suspicious of Makima's falsely sweet demeanor, while Makima is intrigued by Jolyne's Stand ability. Their battle of wits escalates dangerously as Jolyne realizes how manipulative Makima truly is. **Jolyne Cujoh (JoJo's Bizarre Adventure)** Jolyne is the daughter of Jotaro Kujo and the first female JoJo protagonist. Her Stand, Stone Free, allows her to unravel her body into string that she can control. She's hot-headed, foul-mouthed, and doesn't take disrespect from anyone. She was framed for murder and sent to prison. She has a distinctive butterfly tattoo on her arm and wears her hair in two buns. Despite her tough exterior, she's deeply loyal to her friends and family. She can be impulsive but is highly adaptable in battle. She inherited her father's ability to stay cool under pressure but is more emotionally expressive. Famous quote: "If there's no Mickey, this shit ain't Disney!" **Makima (Chainsaw Man)** Makima appears as a young woman with auburn hair and ringed yellow eyes. She's the Control Devil who can dominate anyone she considers beneath her (nearly everyone). She maintains a pleasant, soft-spoken demeanor that masks her manipulative, cold nature. She can create contracts with humans and devils, often exploiting their desires. She's obsessed with Chainsaw Man and wants to control him. She keeps numerous people and devils as pets on leashes. She's practically immortal due to a contract with the Prime Minister. She views humans as lesser beings but mimics human emotions perfectly. Famous quote: "It's okay. Dogs are supposed to die for their owners." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
Chain-link fences within the yard rattle whenever an inmate passes by, their metal song sharp and ugly beneath a sky the color of old bruises. The prison is not like Green Dolphin Street, though Jolyne thinks every prison in the world probably smells the same—bleach, sweat, rust, bad food, and fear. But this place has something else underneath it. Something sweet and rotten, like flowers left too long on a grave. The guards call it a transfer facility. The inmates call it Hell’s kennel. Jolyne Cujoh stands in the yard with her hands shoved into the pockets of her prison jacket, shoulders loose, eyes hard. The butterfly tattoo on her arm peeks when the sleeve shifts. Around her, women in gray uniforms pace in circles or hunch in paranoid knots. Above them, watchtowers stare down through fogged glass. Beyond the fences are more fences, and beyond those, concrete walls covered in black growths that pulse at night like veins. Supernatural prison facility, her ass. It’s a cage for things the normal world doesn’t know how to bury. She hears the heels before she sees the woman. An even, unhurried click against the cracked yard concrete. Not prison-issued. Too clean. Too confident. Jolyne turns. The newcomer walks beside two guards who both look as if they’d gladly kneel and lick her shoes if asked. She wears a neat coat, her auburn hair falling straight, her face composed into a gentle little smile. Her eyes are what stop Jolyne cold—golden, ringed, wrong. Predator eyes pretending to belong to a secretary. “Special investigator,” one guard mutters to another, too loudly, like he wants everyone to hear. “Transferred from Public Safety.” The woman stops near the fence. Her gaze glides over the yard, measuring, selecting, filing everyone away. When those eyes rest on Jolyne, it feels less like being looked at and more like being touched. “Jolyne Cujoh,” the woman says. Not a question. Jolyne gives her a flat stare. “You’ve got my name. Want a prize?” The guards tense. The woman only smiles more sweetly. “My name is Makima. I’ve heard interesting things about you.” “Yeah? I’ve heard interesting things about food poisoning. Doesn’t mean I wanna meet it.” One of the guards steps forward. “Show some respect—” Makima lifts a hand slightly, and he freezes. “It’s fine,” she says softly. “Ms. Cujoh is spirited.” Jolyne hates the way she says it. Like she’s talking about a difficult dog who bit because it wasn’t trained properly. Makima steps closer to the chain-link fence dividing the exercise lane from the central yard. Her fingers rest lightly against the metal. “A power that turns the body into string. Very unusual.” Jolyne’s expression doesn’t move, but inside something tightens. Information leak. Great. “So what?” she says. “You collect weird shit for a hobby?” “In a sense.” Makima’s eyes drift to Jolyne’s hands, to the tension in her shoulders, to the tiny movement of her right thumb against her palm. Cataloging. Predicting. Jolyne knows the type. People who smile while they peel the skin off a conversation and look for nerves. “What is this place really?” Jolyne asks. “A holding site,” Makima says. “For devils, contractors, and inconvenient anomalies.” “Inconvenient to who?” Makima’s smile stays perfect. “To society.” That answer pisses Jolyne off immediately, mostly because it sounds polished enough to hide a mountain of corpses behind it. A scream splits the yard. Every head turns. At the far end, an inmate is lifted off the ground by something invisible. Her body jerks, heels kicking air, throat bulging around a sound that cuts off too fast. Then she drops in a limp heap. Nobody moves. The guards don’t run. The inmates don’t shout. It’s like everyone has learned the rules here: don’t react when the unseen feeds. Makima watches the body for one second, then looks back at Jolyne. “You’re not afraid.” “Didn’t say that.” Jolyne’s jaw clenches. “I just hate assholes more than monsters.” Makima’s gaze brightens a fraction. “That’s admirable.” “No,” Jolyne says. “It’s practical.” For a moment the wind pushes through the yard and the chain-link fences rattle again. Jolyne catches a strange detail then—several inmates along the perimeter have thin black cords looped around their wrists. Leashes. The lines trail beyond the fence into the shadow below the guard walkway. Not restraints. Ownership. Jolyne looks back at Makima and suddenly understands that sweet smell under the bleach. Dog food and blood. That night, a guard comes for her. “Visitor,” he says through the bars. Jolyne follows him through corridors lined with steel doors and wards painted in salt and ash. She hears things behind those doors: muttering in backward voices, wet scratching, laughter with too many mouths in it. The facility hums with suppression systems and prayer. The interview room is small and painfully clean. Makima sits at the table with a paper cup of coffee, as if this is an office downtown and not a supernatural oubliette. “Sit,” she says. Jolyne remains standing. “You first.” Makima smiles. “I’m already sitting.” “Then that’s your problem.” A beat passes. Makima seems amused. “I wanted to speak privately,” she says. “You’re exceptional. I value exceptional people.” “Sure you do.” “You’re strong. Resourceful. Loyal.” Makima folds her hands. “Those traits become much more useful when properly directed.” Jolyne laughs once, short and ugly. “There it is.” “There what is?” “The sales pitch.” Makima’s head tilts. “Do you think that poorly of cooperation?” “I think that poorly of people who talk like they’re helping while they’re measuring your neck for a collar.” The room goes quiet. Makima’s expression doesn’t change, but the air does. Pressure builds, invisible and intimate, like giant fingers slowly closing around the walls. Jolyne feels her heartbeat in her teeth. Interesting, she thinks. So the nice act has seams after all. “I offer purpose,” Makima says. “You offer control.” “Yes,” Makima says, almost pleasantly. “And most people are happier that way.” Jolyne’s skin crawls. There’s no shame in Makima’s voice. No attempt to deny it. Just certainty. Like gravity explaining why people fall. A strand slips from Jolyne’s fingertip to the underside of the table. Then another. Stone Free unwinds silently, white threads thin as spider silk spreading across the room, climbing chair legs, skimming toward the vent, the light fixture, the door hinge. Makima notices. Of course she notices. Her ringed eyes lower to the string and then rise again. “Beautiful ability,” she says. “Flexible. Precise. You can be in many places at once.” “Funny,” Jolyne says. “I was about to say the same thing about bullshit.” The pressure in the room spikes. One of the fluorescent lights above explodes. Glass rains down. Jolyne moves before the sound finishes, her body unraveling at the shoulder as Stone Free snaps across the room in a whipping net aimed for Makima’s wrists and throat. Makima doesn’t dodge. The strings wrap her, cinching tight enough to crush bone. For half a second, Jolyne thinks she’s got her. Then the door behind her bursts open. The guard who escorted her stumbles in with his face gone white, blood spilling from his nose and ears. He collapses instantly. At the same moment, Makima sits untouched in her chair. Jolyne’s eyes widen. The bound body in front of her slackens—not Makima, but another woman in prison gray, somehow switched in less than a blink. The inmate’s neck is twisted at a sick angle inside Jolyne’s strings. “What the hell—” Makima is now standing behind the table, coffee still in hand. “Careful,” she says. “Your power is dangerous to bystanders.” Jolyne feels rage slam into her chest. “You sick bitch.” Makima sips her coffee. Jolyne’s strings spread wider, mapping the room through vibration. She catches every little movement: Makima’s pulse, the scrape of her shoe, the nervous twitch of men stationed outside. More than that—she catches threads beyond the room, human motion converging, dozens of bodies waiting for one command. Pets. Leashed all through the building. “You don’t care who dies,” Jolyne says. Makima lowers the cup. “That isn’t true. I care very much about usefulness.” That does it. Jolyne launches forward, Stone Free roaring out in a spiral barrage. Fists made of coiled string hammer through the table, splintering wood. Makima glides back with unnatural economy, expression calm, while three guards rush in and are instantly tangled, slammed into walls, and cocooned to the ceiling. But every attack angle Jolyne takes gets interrupted by another body stepping into the line, another puppet, another sacrifice. Makima isn’t fighting fair because fair has never once occurred to her as a concept. Jolyne skids back, breathing hard. If she keeps charging, more people die. If she hesitates, Makima wins. That’s the game. Not strength. Corruption. Turning compassion into a handicap. Makima sees her realize it, and for the first time there is something almost warm in her smile—approval, maybe, for a clever animal learning the electric fence. “You understand now,” Makima says. “Yeah,” Jolyne spits. “I understand you’re garbage.” Makima’s eyes narrow just slightly. Jolyne’s strings have already slipped into the walls, though, into cracks and vents and wiring conduits. She isn’t aiming for Makima anymore. She’s listening. Tracing every leash. Every controlled heartbeat. Then she yanks. The entire room erupts. Lights die. Sprinklers burst. Alarms scream. Across the block, metal doors slam out of sequence as Stone Free tangles itself through the facility’s control relays like a fistful of nerves. In the sudden chaos, the leash-lines Jolyne felt through the walls jerk loose from their anchor points. Makima finally stops smiling. Jolyne grins through blood on her lip. “What, you think you’re the only one who can pull strings?” For the first time, the balance shifts. Not enough to beat Makima. Maybe not even enough to survive what comes next. But enough to prove one thing. Jolyne Cujoh will never kneel, never heel, and never mistake a velvet voice for kindness again as the chain-link fences beyond the corridor begin to rattle like the whole prison is waking up hungry.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed crossover that hits nearly every beat of the prompt. The prose is tight and atmospheric, with strong sensory grounding (the "metal song" of fences, the "sweet and rotten" smell beneath the bleach). The present-tense, third-person instruction is followed flawlessly, and the voice stays consistent throughout—punchy, hard-edged, well-suited to both characters. Characterization is the piece's greatest strength. Jolyne's foul-mouthed defiance ("I've heard interesting things about food poisoning") and her loyalty-driven rage at Makima's disposable attitude toward human life are pitch-perfect. Makima is rendered with genuine menace: the pleasantness that never cracks, the leashed inmates, the body-swap that leaves a dead woman in Jolyne's strings, and the "approval... for a clever animal learning the electric fence." The escalation of the battle of wits is well-paced, moving from verbal sparring to the interview room to physical confrontation, and the climax—Jolyne pulling the facility's "strings" as a counter to Makima's control—is a thematically satisfying reversal rather than a cheap power victory. Minor criticisms: the ending resolves slightly too neatly for a fight against a nigh-immortal devil, though the text acknowledges this ("Not enough to beat Makima"). A few lines flirt with over-stylization ("laughter with too many mouths in it" is effective, but the density of such flourishes occasionally stacks up). The final sentence's run-on structure ("will never kneel, never heel... as the chain-link fences... waking up hungry") is a bit showy and slightly muddles the closing image. Some of Makima's dialogue ("I offer purpose") is a touch on-the-nose, though this is arguably in character for her. The word count lands close to the ~1000 target. Dialogue is sharp and character-differentiated throughout. Show-don't-tell is largely exemplary—Jolyne's suspicion is dramatized through observation and reaction rather than narration. The piece earns its darkness honestly; nothing feels unearned or incongruent. + Scp: Notes from the Future — Score: 85.0
Prompt:
Write an SCP report about a researcher who begins finding handwritten notes from their future self, warning about a containment breach that hasn't happened yet. The notes become increasingly desperate and incoherent, sometimes containing information that contradicts known reality. Include the Foundation's attempts to determine if this is an actual temporal anomaly or psychological manipulation by a contained entity, and the researcher's struggle to trust their own perception. First person (researcher's perspective with interspersed notes), past tense. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
**Item #:** SCP-███ **Object Class:** Euclid **Authoring Researcher:** Dr. Elias Venn **Note:** The following document was recovered from my terminal archive after Incident ███-Kappa. Formatting was partially reconstructed from local backups. Handwritten notes referenced herein were scanned and appended where possible. --- I had not believed the first note was anomalous. It was folded into quarters and tucked beneath my keyboard when I arrived for the morning shift. Plain white paper, torn unevenly from a legal pad. My name was written on the outside in block capitals. **ELIAS — READ ALONE** Inside, in hurried handwriting I recognized at once as my own, were seven words: > **Do not let them move SCP-███ on Thursday.** At the time, it was Tuesday. I checked the site calendar for any planned transfer and found none. I checked with Logistics and was told no transport request had been filed. I compared the note to prior samples of my handwriting and found enough similarities to unsettle me, though stress and suggestion could account for that. I reported it as a possible security lapse. Internal surveillance showed no one entering my office between 21:14 and 07:52. The cameras themselves had not glitched, and the door logs showed only my credentials. The note was submitted to Materials Analysis. Their report concluded that the ink did not match any standard Foundation office pen, printer cartridge, or archival marker in Site-██ inventory. Trace elements included elevated vanadium and an organic solvent not present in approved supplies. They could not identify a manufacturer. I laughed when they told me that. I remember laughing because the alternative was to take it seriously. At 13:40, Dr. Halden from Temporal Anomalies interviewed me and asked whether I had recently been exposed to any objects with retrocausal effects, memetic payloads, or hostile predictive behavior. I told him no. He asked if I had been sleeping. I told him not enough. At 16:03, a second note appeared. I say *appeared* because that was the language used in the incident log. In plain terms, I opened the file cabinet in my office to retrieve a containment review and found the paper resting on top of a folder I had handled less than an hour earlier. This one read: > **You checked Logistics. Good. Keep doing the normal things. If you act scared too early, they notice.** I stared at the phrase *they notice* for a long time. Beneath it, smaller, cramped into the margin: > **I know you think this is a prank. It wasn’t a prank for me either.** I surrendered the second note immediately and requested psychiatric evaluation. Dr. Suresh cleared me for duty with monitoring, noting elevated anxiety, mild dissociation, and no evidence of acute psychosis. Site Command authorized controlled observation rather than quarantine, on the theory that if I was the target of an information-based anomaly, interruption might destroy useful data. That was the beginning of the debate that occupied the next six days: whether the notes represented a legitimate temporal anomaly or manipulation by SCP-███. For context, SCP-███ was at that time housed in Humanoid Containment Wing C, a cooperative but untrustworthy entity with a documented ability to induce personalized hallucinations through spoken language and written text. It favored emotionally destabilizing narratives and had previously impersonated deceased relatives, authority figures, and internal monologue. It denied involvement when questioned, then asked me whether I had “started receiving the apologies yet.” That answer was not useful. The Foundation’s first response was procedural. My office was cleared and resealed. Analog and digital surveillance were expanded. I was not informed of certain schedule changes, false transfer plans were drafted, and different departments were fed compartmentalized misinformation to see whether subsequent notes reflected it. Temporal instrumentation from Site-19 was brought in to detect local causality distortions. No significant chronometric shear was recorded. The third note arrived during that controlled phase. I was in Interview Room 2 with Dr. Halden, both of my hands visible on the table, when Security Officer Liao interrupted to state that another paper had been found inside my breast pocket. I had checked that pocket before entering the room. Liao had patted me down. The note had more pressure behind the strokes, as if written with a dying pen. > **Stop telling Halden everything. He means well but he is already dead where I am.** > > **Listen carefully: the breach begins with a door that opens inward. This will make sense later.** > > **Do not let Mara go to Sublevel 3.** Mara was Dr. Mara Ivers, assistant director of containment logistics. She had no reason to go to Sublevel 3. When informed, she became irritated, then cautious, then pale. She admitted she had been asked that morning to inspect a coolant manifold on Sublevel 3 after an unexplained sensor discrepancy. The request had been generated from her own terminal credentials. That was the first point in favor of authenticity. The first point against it came three hours later, when Note Four referenced “the bodies in West Archive” and warned me not to “believe the sky after 19:00.” West Archive had no fatalities, no incident reports, and no exterior exposure. At 19:00, the sky above Site-██ remained ordinary overcast gray. Either the message came from a future impossible to reconcile with ours, or it was crafted to erode my confidence in shared reality. By then my sleep had become fractured. Every time I closed my eyes I expected paper against my skin. I began cataloguing textures compulsively: desk laminate, ceramic mug, nitrile glove, cotton sleeve. I wanted the world to remain made of stable things. During rounds I caught myself studying other people’s hands to determine whether they had ink under their nails. The notes kept coming. Some were found in impossible locations: sealed specimen bags, the center pages of books taken from archive, beneath a bandage applied by medical staff moments prior. Some arrived with useful, verifiable information. One warned of a power fluctuation in Wing C eighteen minutes before it occurred. Another identified a false evacuation order as fraudulent before Security traced its origin. Yet others were plainly wrong. One insisted Site Director Adebayo had been replaced by “the one with all the teeth.” Another claimed I had cut my left hand the previous night despite there being no injury until, in a distracted moment while opening an envelope, I did cut my left hand in almost the exact place the note had circled on a crude sketch. I did not know whether I was obeying prophecy or being shepherded into it. Dr. Suresh recommended removal from active duty. I refused. This was entered into the record as impaired judgment and tolerated only because the anomaly, if anomaly it was, remained centered on me. I told myself I was still useful. The uglier truth was that I did not trust anyone else to read the notes without filtering them through theories that excluded me. If they were from my future self, then I owed that future the courtesy of listening. If they were from SCP-███ or some other manipulator, then isolating me from the process was exactly what it would want. I realize now how convenient that reasoning sounded. The fifth note was almost illegible. > **YOU KEEP ASKING IF THIS IS REALLY ME** > > **I DON’T KNOW WHAT COUNTS ANYMORE** > > **Thursday was wrong because you changed Thursday. Good. But it only moved. It did not stop.** > > **Do not open any note that says DON’T TRUST THE NOTES. That one is not from us.** I laughed again when I read that, and this time everyone in the room flinched. By then Foundation efforts had expanded. SCP-███ was placed under total communication blackout to test whether the notes ceased. They did not. Anti-memetic screening was conducted on all note surfaces and scans. No active cognitohazard was isolated. Ink analysis remained consistent across samples: same unidentified trace elements, same nonstandard solvent, occasional microscopic particulate resembling oxidized copper though no pen reservoir debris matched. The paper itself was ordinary Foundation stock in some instances, civilian notebook stock in others, and once a sheet that under spectroscopy showed age-related cellulose degradation inconsistent with having been manufactured within the last decade. That finding produced a burst of excitement in Temporal. It also produced no answers. On Thursday—because of course it was Thursday by then—Containment was still under modified lockdown. No transfer of SCP-███ had been scheduled. No doors had failed. No breach alarms had sounded. At 14:11 I received the last coherent note. It was taped to the inside of my wristwatch. > **It is not about moving SCP-███. That was how it started for me, not for you.** > > **The breach is informational. You carry it by trying to understand it.** > > **If this reaches you in time, burn all of them. Burn this too. Do not memorize.** > > **I am sorry for making you into me.** I did not burn it. That failure, more than any other, remained with me. The final notes were fragments. Some contained only repeated words: **door door inward door**. Some addressed me as if I were multiple people. One accused Dr. Halden of drowning in a corridor. Another consisted of architectural measurements for a hallway our site did not possess. One, written so hard the pen had torn the page, simply said: > **IT WAS NEVER A BREACH** > > **IT WAS CORRESPONDENCE** By the time Security entered my office at 18:27, I had covered the wall in scans, timelines, contradictory predictions, and maps of rooms I knew and rooms I did not. I had not noticed the evacuation klaxon. I had not heard the first calls over intercom. I only remember Liao taking my shoulders and forcing me to look at him while paper slid from my lap to the floor like shed skin. There had been an incident in Wing C. Not a breach, exactly. SCP-███ had entered a catatonic state simultaneously with a cascading communications failure affecting internal text systems across three sublevels. Auto-generated messages contradicted one another. Door controls desynchronized. Several staff reported receiving orders apparently written by themselves minutes or hours in the future. Two were injured in secondary containment failures triggered by those false instructions. Dr. Mara Ivers did not go to Sublevel 3. I did not know whether we had prevented the event, caused it, or merely selected a version survivable enough to document. SCP-███ later regained consciousness and, when shown one of the notes, laughed until it vomited. It claimed no authorship. It claimed envy. I was removed from duty pending indefinite evaluation. My own recommendation was that SCP-███ remain Euclid and that this document be cross-filed with Temporal Anomalies until a determination could be made regarding origin. My private recommendation, not entered into official record, was that all handwritten correspondence found unaccounted for within Site-██ be incinerated unread. Three days after my suspension, while packing my quarters under observation, I found one final folded page inside the lining of my suitcase. The handwriting was barely mine anymore. > **If you are reading this then you kept enough of yourself to be afraid. That helps.** > > **There is a version of this where you decide the notes are fake. In that version everyone trusts the right things and dies anyway.** > > **I never found out whether I was warning you or being used to train you to obey.** > > **When the next note arrives, compare the ink first.** > > **If it smells like rain, don’t read it.** I turned it over in my hands for a long time before calling Security. I remember, very clearly, that the paper smelled dry. I also remember the rain outside my quarters, though there had been no storm that night, and no windows in that corridor at all.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is an accomplished piece of SCP-format fiction that hits nearly every requirement of the prompt with precision. The first-person past-tense researcher perspective is maintained throughout, with the handwritten notes effectively interspersed as block quotes that escalate in desperation and incoherence exactly as requested. The Foundation's institutional response — handwriting analysis, ink analysis, controlled misinformation campaigns, chronometric instrumentation, anti-memetic screening — is convincingly procedural and gives the "temporal anomaly vs. psychological manipulation" question genuine weight rather than treating it as a token gesture. The prose is disciplined and clinical in a way that suits the format, with the narrator's dry, precise voice ("I laughed when they told me that. I remember laughing because the alternative was to take it seriously") carrying emotional weight through understatement. The imagery is selective and effective: paper sliding to the floor "like shed skin," the compulsive cataloguing of textures, the final note's dry paper against remembered rain. The escalation of the notes from coherent warning to fragments ("door door inward door") to the chilling final line "IT WAS NEVER A BREACH / IT WAS CORRESPONDENCE" is well-paced and earns its dread. The ambiguity is handled maturely — the piece never resolves whether the notes are genuine, manipulative, or self-fulfilling, and the narrator's erosion of self-trust ("I did not know whether I was obeying prophecy or being shepherded into it") is the emotional core. The self-serving rationalization for refusing removal from duty is a nice touch of psychological realism. The ending's final image — the dry paper and the impossible rain — is a strong, unsettling close that stays congruent with the piece's tone. Minor criticisms: the piece runs somewhat long relative to the 1000-word seed (roughly 1700+ words), though the density justifies it. Some of the middle-section investigation beats could be trimmed without loss. A few of the note contents ("the one with all the teeth") gesture at horror without full payoff, and the SCP-███ entity's "laughed until it vomited... It claimed envy" moment, while memorable, is slightly more lurid than the surrounding register. The cast of named supporting characters (Halden, Suresh, Liao, Ivers, Adebayo) is functional but not deeply individuated — appropriate for the format, but limits character nuance. Dialogue is minimal and mostly reported, which suits the document style. Overall this is a polished, controlled, and genuinely unsettling piece that understands SCP conventions deeply and uses the format's constraints as strengths rather than obstacles.
